Main article: [Optical telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optical_telegraph "Optical telegraph")

An [optical telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optical_telegraph "Optical telegraph") is a telegraph consisting of a line of stations in towers or natural high points which signal to each other by means of shutters or paddles. Signalling by means of indicator pointers was called _semaphore_. Early proposals for an optical telegraph system were made to the [Royal Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Society "Royal Society") by [Robert Hooke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Hooke "Robert Hooke") in 1684[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-14) and were first implemented on an experimental level by Sir [Richard Lovell Edgeworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Lovell_Edgeworth "Richard Lovell Edgeworth") in 1767.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-15) The first successful optical telegraph network was invented by [Claude Chappe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Chappe "Claude Chappe") and operated in France from 1793.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-16) The two most extensive systems were Chappe's in France, with branches into neighbouring countries, and the system of [Abraham Niclas Edelcrantz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Niclas_Edelcrantz "Abraham Niclas Edelcrantz") in Sweden.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Holzmann-13):ix–x,47

During 1790–1795, at the height of the [French Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Revolution "French Revolution"), France needed a swift and reliable communication system to thwart the war efforts of its enemies. In 1790, the Chappe brothers set about devising a system of communication that would allow the central government to receive intelligence and to transmit orders in the shortest possible time. On 2 March 1791, at 11 am, they sent the message "si vous réussissez, vous serez bientôt couverts de gloire" (If you succeed, you will soon bask in glory) between Brulon and Parce, a distance of 16 kilometres (10 mi). The first means used a combination of black and white panels, clocks, telescopes, and codebooks to send their message.

In 1792, Claude was appointed _Ingénieur-Télégraphiste_ and charged with establishing a line of stations between Paris and [Lille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lille "Lille"), a distance of 230 kilometres (140 mi). It was used to carry dispatches for the war between France and Austria. In 1794, it brought news of a French capture of [Condé-sur-l'Escaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cond%C3%A9-sur-l'Escaut "Condé-sur-l'Escaut") from the Austrians less than an hour after it occurred.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-17) A decision to replace the system with an electric telegraph was made in 1846, but it took a decade before it was fully taken out of service. The [fall of Sevastopol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Sevastopol_(1854%E2%80%931855) "Siege of Sevastopol (1854–1855)") was reported by Chappe telegraph in 1855.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Holzmann-13):92–94

The [Prussian system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prussian_semaphore_system "Prussian semaphore system") was put into effect in the 1830s. However, they were highly dependent on good weather and daylight to work and even then could accommodate only about two words per minute. The last commercial semaphore link ceased operation in Sweden in 1880. As of 1895, France still operated coastal commercial semaphore telegraph stations, for ship-to-shore communication.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-18)

### Electrical telegraph

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Telegraphy&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Electrical telegraph")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ae/Telegraph-2.jpg/250px-Telegraph-2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Telegraph-2.jpg)

A site in Hammersmith London (UK) where Sir Francis Ronalds constructed the first electric telegraph in 1816

Main article: [Electrical telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_telegraph "Electrical telegraph")

See also: [Electrical telegraphy in the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_telegraphy_in_the_United_Kingdom "Electrical telegraphy in the United Kingdom")

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/Cooke_and_Wheatstone_electric_telegraph.jpg/250px-Cooke_and_Wheatstone_electric_telegraph.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cooke_and_Wheatstone_electric_telegraph.jpg)

[Cooke and Wheatstone's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooke_and_Wheatstone_telegraph "Cooke and Wheatstone telegraph") five-needle, six-wire telegraph (1837)

The early ideas for an electric telegraph included in 1753 using [electrostatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrostatic "Electrostatic") deflections of [pith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pith "Pith") balls,[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-19) proposals for [electrochemical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrochemical "Electrochemical") bubbles in acid by [Campillo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_Salva_Campillo "Francisco Salva Campillo") in 1804 and [von Sömmering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Thomas_von_S%C3%B6mmering "Samuel Thomas von Sömmering") in 1809.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-21) The first experimental system over a substantial distance was by [Ronalds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Ronalds "Francis Ronalds") in 1816 using an [electrostatic generator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrostatic_generator "Electrostatic generator"). Ronalds offered his invention to the [British Admiralty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Admiralty "British Admiralty"), but it was rejected as unnecessary,[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-22) the existing optical telegraph connecting the Admiralty in London to their main fleet base in [Portsmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portsmouth "Portsmouth") being deemed adequate for their purposes. As late as 1844, after the electrical telegraph had come into use, the Admiralty's optical telegraph was still used, although it was accepted that poor weather ruled it out on many days of the year.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Kieve-23):16,37 France had an extensive optical telegraph system dating from Napoleonic times and was even slower to take up electrical systems.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-24):217–218

Eventually, electrostatic telegraphs were abandoned in favour of [electromagnetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnet "Electromagnet") systems. An early experimental system ([Schilling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pavel_Schilling "Pavel Schilling"), 1832) led to a proposal to establish a telegraph between [St Petersburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Petersburg "St Petersburg") and [Kronstadt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kronstadt "Kronstadt"), but it was never completed.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-25) The first operative electric telegraph ([Gauss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss "Carl Friedrich Gauss") and [Weber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_Eduard_Weber "Wilhelm Eduard Weber"), 1833) connected [Göttingen Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%B6ttingen_Observatory "Göttingen Observatory") to the Institute of Physics about 1 km away during experimental investigations of the geomagnetic field.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-26)

The first commercial telegraph was by [Cooke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Fothergill_Cooke "William Fothergill Cooke") and [Wheatstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Wheatstone "Charles Wheatstone") following their English patent of 10 June 1837. It was demonstrated on the [London and Birmingham Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_and_Birmingham_Railway "London and Birmingham Railway") in July of the same year.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-guarnieri1-27) In July 1839, a five-needle, five-wire system was installed to provide signalling over a record distance of 21 km on a section of the [Great Western Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Western_Railway "Great Western Railway") between [London Paddington station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Paddington_station "London Paddington station") and [West Drayton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Drayton "West Drayton").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Huurdeman-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-29) However, in trying to get railway companies to take up his telegraph more widely for [railway signalling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railway_signalling "Railway signalling"), Cooke was rejected several times in favour of the more familiar, but shorter range, steam-powered pneumatic signalling. Even when his telegraph was taken up, it was considered experimental and the company backed out of a plan to finance extending the telegraph line out to [Slough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slough "Slough"). However, this led to a breakthrough for the electric telegraph, as up to this point the Great Western had insisted on exclusive use and refused Cooke permission to open public telegraph offices. Cooke extended the line at his own expense and agreed that the railway could have free use of it in exchange for the right to open it up to the public.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Kieve-23):19–20

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/Morsetaste.jpg/250px-Morsetaste.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Morsetaste.jpg)

A [Morse key](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph_key "Telegraph key") (c.1900)

Most of the early electrical systems required multiple wires (Ronalds' system was an exception), but the system developed in the United States by [Morse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Morse "Samuel Morse") and [Vail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Vail "Alfred Vail") was a single-wire system. This was the system that first used the soon-to-become-ubiquitous [Morse code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Morse_code "American Morse code").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-guarnieri1-27) By 1844, the Morse system connected [Baltimore to Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore-Washington_telegraph_line "Baltimore-Washington telegraph line"), and by 1861 the west coast of the continent was connected to the east coast.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-31) The [Cooke and Wheatstone telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooke_and_Wheatstone_telegraph "Cooke and Wheatstone telegraph"), in a series of improvements, also ended up with a one-wire system, but still using their own code and [needle displays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Needle_telegraph "Needle telegraph").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Huurdeman-28)

The electric telegraph quickly became a means of more general communication. The Morse system was officially adopted as the standard for continental European telegraphy in 1851 with a [revised code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Clemens_Gerke#Revision_of_Morse's_Code "Friedrich Clemens Gerke"), which later became the basis of [International Morse Code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Morse_Code "International Morse Code").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Coe-32) However, Great Britain and the [British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire") continued to use the Cooke and Wheatstone system, in some places as late as the 1930s.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Huurdeman-28) Likewise, the United States as well as most states of Australia continued to use [American Morse code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Morse_code "American Morse code") internally, requiring translation operators skilled in both codes for international messages.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Coe-32)

### Railway telegraphy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Telegraphy&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Railway telegraphy")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ef/GWR_Cooke_and_Wheatstone_double_needle_telegraph_instrument.jpg/250px-GWR_Cooke_and_Wheatstone_double_needle_telegraph_instrument.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GWR_Cooke_and_Wheatstone_double_needle_telegraph_instrument.jpg)

An early Cooke and Wheatstone double-needle railway telegraph instrument at the [National Railway Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Railway_Museum "National Railway Museum") in [York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/York "York")

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/Block_instrument.jpg/250px-Block_instrument.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Block_instrument.jpg)

A block signalling instrument as used in Britain in the 20th century

See also: [Railway signalling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railway_signalling "Railway signalling")

Railway signal telegraphy was developed in Britain from the 1840s onward. It was used to manage railway traffic and to prevent accidents as part of the railway signalling system. On 12 June 1837 Cooke and Wheatstone were awarded a patent for an electric telegraph.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-33) This was demonstrated between [Euston railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euston_railway_station "Euston railway station")—where Wheatstone was located—and the engine house at Camden Town—where Cooke was stationed, together with [Robert Stephenson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Stephenson "Robert Stephenson"), the [London and Birmingham Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_and_Birmingham_Railway "London and Birmingham Railway") line's chief engineer. The messages were for the operation of the rope-haulage system for pulling trains up the 1 in 77 bank. The world's first permanent railway telegraph was completed in July 1839 between London Paddington and West Drayton on the [Great Western Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Western_Railway "Great Western Railway") with an electric telegraph using a four-needle system.

The concept of a [signalling "block" system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signalling_block_system "Signalling block system") was proposed by Cooke in 1842. Railway signal telegraphy did not change in essence from Cooke's initial concept for more than a century. In this system each line of railway was divided into sections or blocks of varying length. Entry to and exit from the block was to be authorised by electric telegraph and signalled by the line-side semaphore signals, so that only a single train could occupy the rails. In Cooke's original system, a single-needle telegraph was adapted to indicate just two messages: "Line Clear" and "Line Blocked". The [signaller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signalman_(rail) "Signalman (rail)") would adjust his line-side signals accordingly. As first implemented in 1844 each station had as many needles as there were stations on the line, giving a complete picture of the traffic. As lines expanded, a sequence of pairs of single-needle instruments were adopted, one pair for each block in each direction.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-34)

### Wigwag

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Telegraphy&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Wigwag")]

Main article: [Wigwag (flag signals)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wigwag_(flag_signals) "Wigwag (flag signals)")

Wigwag is a form of [flag signalling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_signals "Flag signals") using a single flag. Unlike most forms of flag signalling, which are used over relatively short distances, wigwag is designed to maximise the distance covered—up to 32 km (20 mi) in some cases. Wigwag achieved this by using a large flag—a single flag can be held with both hands unlike flag semaphore which has a flag in each hand—and using motions rather than positions as its symbols since motions are more easily seen. It was invented by US Army surgeon [Albert J. Myer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_J._Myer "Albert J. Myer") in the 1850s who later became the first head of the [Signal Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signal_Corps_(United_States_Army) "Signal Corps (United States Army)"). Wigwag was used extensively during the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War") where it filled a gap left by the electrical telegraph. Although the electrical telegraph had been in use for more than a decade, the network did not yet reach everywhere and portable, ruggedized equipment suitable for military use was not immediately available. Permanent or semi-permanent stations were established during the war, some of them towers of enormous height and the system was extensive enough to be described as a communications network.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-36)

### Heliograph

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Telegraphy&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Heliograph")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/67/Australian_Heliograph_in_Egyptian_Desert_1940.png/250px-Australian_Heliograph_in_Egyptian_Desert_1940.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Australian_Heliograph_in_Egyptian_Desert_1940.png)

Australian troops using a Mance mk.V heliograph in the [Western Desert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Desert_(Egypt) "Western Desert (Egypt)") in November 1940

Main article: [Heliograph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heliograph "Heliograph")

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/11903A_LO_with_Heliograph_CA_1912_%2822762702845%29.jpg/330px-11903A_LO_with_Heliograph_CA_1912_%2822762702845%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:11903A_LO_with_Heliograph_CA_1912_(22762702845).jpg)

[US Forest Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Forest_Service "US Forest Service") lookout using a Colomb shutter type heliograph in 1912 at the end of a telephone line

A [heliograph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heliograph "Heliograph") is a telegraph that transmits messages by flashing sunlight with a mirror, usually using Morse code. The idea for a telegraph of this type was first proposed as a modification of surveying equipment ([Gauss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss "Carl Friedrich Gauss"), 1821). Various uses of mirrors were made for communication in the following years, mostly for military purposes, but the first device to become widely used was a heliograph with a moveable mirror ([Mance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Christopher_Mance "Henry Christopher Mance"), 1869). The system was used by the French during the [1870–71 siege of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Paris_(1870%E2%80%9371) "Siege of Paris (1870–71)"), with night-time signalling using [kerosene lamps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerosene_lamp "Kerosene lamp") as the source of light. An improved version (Begbie, 1870) was used by British military in many colonial wars, including the [Anglo-Zulu War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Zulu_War "Anglo-Zulu War") (1879). At some point, a morse key was added to the apparatus to give the operator the same degree of control as in the electric telegraph.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Woods2-37)

Another type of heliograph was the [heliostat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heliostat "Heliostat") or [heliotrope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heliotrope_(instrument) "Heliotrope (instrument)") fitted with a Colomb shutter. The heliostat was essentially a surveying instrument with a fixed mirror and so could not transmit a code by itself. The term _heliostat_ is sometimes used as a synonym for _heliograph_ because of this origin. The Colomb shutter ([Bolton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Bolton "Francis Bolton") and [Colomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Howard_Colomb "Philip Howard Colomb"), 1862) was originally invented to enable the transmission of morse code by [signal lamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signal_lamp "Signal lamp") between [Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy "Royal Navy") ships at sea.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Woods2-37)

The heliograph was heavily used by [Nelson A. Miles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_A._Miles "Nelson A. Miles") in [Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona "Arizona") and [New Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Mexico "New Mexico") after he took over command (1886) of the fight against [Geronimo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geronimo "Geronimo") and other [Apache](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apache "Apache") bands in the [Apache Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apache_Wars "Apache Wars"). Miles had previously set up the first heliograph line in the US between [Fort Keogh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Keogh "Fort Keogh") and [Fort Custer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Custer_(Montana) "Fort Custer (Montana)") in [Montana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montana "Montana"). He used the heliograph to fill in vast, thinly populated areas that were not covered by the electric telegraph. Twenty-six stations covered an area 320 by 480 km (200 by 300 mi). In a test of the system, a message was relayed 640 km (400 mi) in four hours. Miles' enemies used [smoke signals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smoke_signal "Smoke signal") and flashes of sunlight from metal, but lacked a sophisticated telegraph code.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-38) The heliograph was ideal for use in the American Southwest due to its clear air and mountainous terrain on which stations could be located. It was found necessary to lengthen the morse dash (which is much shorter in American Morse code than in the modern International Morse code) to aid differentiating from the morse dot.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Woods2-37)

Use of the heliograph declined from 1915 onwards, but remained in service in Britain and [British Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Commonwealth "British Commonwealth") countries for some time. Australian forces used the heliograph as late as 1942 in the [Western Desert Campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Desert_Campaign "Western Desert Campaign") of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). Some form of heliograph was used by the [mujahideen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mujahideen "Mujahideen") in the [Soviet–Afghan War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet%E2%80%93Afghan_War "Soviet–Afghan War") (1979–1989).[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Woods2-37)

### Teleprinter

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Telegraphy&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Teleprinter")]

Main article: [Teleprinter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teleprinter "Teleprinter")

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/79/Clavier_Baudot.jpg/250px-Clavier_Baudot.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Clavier_Baudot.jpg)

A Baudot keyboard, 1884

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/Bundesarchiv_Bild_183-2008-0516-500%2C_Fernschreibmaschine_mit_Telefonanschluss.jpg/330px-Bundesarchiv_Bild_183-2008-0516-500%2C_Fernschreibmaschine_mit_Telefonanschluss.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bundesarchiv_Bild_183-2008-0516-500,_Fernschreibmaschine_mit_Telefonanschluss.jpg)

A Creed Model 7 teleprinter, 1931

A teleprinter is a telegraph machine that can send messages from a typewriter-like keyboard and print incoming messages in readable text with no need for the operators to be trained in the telegraph code used on the line. It developed from various earlier printing telegraphs and resulted in improved transmission speeds.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-query.nytimes.com-39) The [Morse telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morse_telegraph "Morse telegraph") (1837) was originally conceived as a system marking indentations on paper tape. A chemical telegraph making blue marks improved the speed of recording ([Bain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Bain_(inventor) "Alexander Bain (inventor)"), 1846), but was delayed by a patent challenge from Morse. The first true printing telegraph (that is printing in plain text) used a spinning wheel of [types](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sort_(typesetting) "Sort (typesetting)") in the manner of a [daisy wheel printer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daisy_wheel_printing "Daisy wheel printing") ([House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Earl_House "Royal Earl House"), 1846, improved by [Hughes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Edward_Hughes "David Edward Hughes"), 1855). The system was adopted by [Western Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Union "Western Union").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-40)

Early teleprinters used the [Baudot code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baudot_code "Baudot code"), a five-bit sequential binary code. This was a telegraph code developed for use on the French telegraph using a five-key keyboard ([Baudot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89mile_Baudot "Émile Baudot"), 1874). Teleprinters generated the same code from a full alphanumeric keyboard. A feature of the Baudot code, and subsequent telegraph codes, was that, unlike Morse code, every character has a code of the same length making it more machine friendly.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Beauchamp-41) The Baudot code was used on the earliest [ticker tape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ticker_tape "Ticker tape") machines ([Calahan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_A._Calahan "Edward A. Calahan"), 1867), a system for mass distributing information on current price of publicly listed companies.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Smith433-42)

### Automated punched-tape transmission

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Telegraphy&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Automated punched-tape transmission")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0b/Creed_model_6S-2_paper_tape_reader.jpg/500px-Creed_model_6S-2_paper_tape_reader.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Creed_model_6S-2_paper_tape_reader.jpg)

Creed paper tape reader at [The National Museum of Computing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_National_Museum_of_Computing "The National Museum of Computing") at [Bletchley Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bletchley_Park "Bletchley Park") in England

See also: [Punched tape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punched_tape "Punched tape")

In a [punched-tape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punched_tape "Punched tape") system, the message is first typed onto punched tape using the code of the telegraph system—Morse code for instance. It is then, either immediately or at some later time, run through a transmission machine which sends the message to the telegraph network. Multiple messages can be sequentially recorded on the same run of tape. The advantage of doing this is that messages can be sent at a steady, fast rate making maximum use of the available telegraph lines. The economic advantage of doing this is greatest on long, busy routes where the cost of the extra step of preparing the tape is lower than the cost of providing more telegraph lines. The first machine to use punched tape was Bain's teleprinter (Bain, 1843), but the system saw only limited use. Later versions of Bain's system achieved speeds up to 1000 words per minute, far faster than a human operator could achieve.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-43)

The first widely used system (Wheatstone, 1858) was first put into service with the British [General Post Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Post_Office "General Post Office") in 1867. A novel feature of the Wheatstone system was the use of [bipolar encoding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bipolar_encoding "Bipolar encoding"). That is, both positive and negative polarity voltages were used.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-44) Bipolar encoding has several advantages, one of which is that it permits [duplex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duplex_(telecommunications) "Duplex (telecommunications)") communication.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-45) The Wheatstone tape reader was capable of a speed of 400 words per minute.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Standage-46):190

### Oceanic telegraph cables

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Telegraphy&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Oceanic telegraph cables")]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0d/Submarine_Cornhill_1852.jpg/250px-Submarine_Cornhill_1852.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Submarine_Cornhill_1852.jpg)

The first message is received by the [Submarine Telegraph Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submarine_Telegraph_Company "Submarine Telegraph Company") in London from Paris on the [Foy–Breguet instrument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foy%E2%80%93Breguet_telegraph "Foy–Breguet telegraph") in 1851. The equipment in the background is a Cooke and Wheatstone set for onward transmission.

Main articles: [Transatlantic telegraph cable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transatlantic_telegraph_cable "Transatlantic telegraph cable") and [Submarine communications cable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submarine_communications_cable "Submarine communications cable")

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/1901_Eastern_Telegraph_cables.png/500px-1901_Eastern_Telegraph_cables.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1901_Eastern_Telegraph_cables.png)

The Eastern Telegraph Company network in 1901

A worldwide communication network meant that telegraph cables would have to be laid across oceans. On land, cables could be run uninsulated suspended from poles. Underwater, a good insulator that was both flexible and capable of resisting the ingress of seawater was required. A solution presented itself with [gutta-percha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gutta-percha "Gutta-percha"), a natural rubber from the _[Palaquium gutta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palaquium\_gutta "Palaquium gutta")_ tree, after [William Montgomerie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Montgomerie "William Montgomerie") sent samples to London from Singapore in 1843. The new material was tested by [Michael Faraday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Faraday "Michael Faraday") and in 1845 Wheatstone suggested that it should be used on the cable planned between [Dover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dover "Dover") and [Calais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calais "Calais") by [John Watkins Brett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Watkins_Brett "John Watkins Brett"). The idea was proved viable when the [South Eastern Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Eastern_Railway_(UK) "South Eastern Railway (UK)") company successfully tested a three-kilometre (two-mile) gutta-percha insulated cable with telegraph messages to a ship off the coast of [Folkestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folkestone "Folkestone").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Haigh26-47) The [cable to France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submarine_Telegraph_Company#History "Submarine Telegraph Company") was laid in 1850 but was almost immediately severed by a French fishing vessel.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-isr-48) It was relaid the next year[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-isr-48) and connections to Ireland and the [Low Countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Countries "Low Countries") soon followed.

Getting a cable across the Atlantic Ocean proved much more difficult. The [Atlantic Telegraph Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Telegraph_Company "Atlantic Telegraph Company"), formed in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") in 1856, had several failed attempts. A cable laid in 1858 worked poorly for a few days, sometimes taking all day to send a message despite the use of the highly sensitive [mirror galvanometer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirror_galvanometer "Mirror galvanometer") developed by William Thomson (the future [Lord Kelvin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Kelvin "Lord Kelvin")) before being destroyed by applying too high a voltage. Its failure and slow speed of transmission prompted Thomson and [Oliver Heaviside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Heaviside "Oliver Heaviside") to find better mathematical descriptions of long [transmission lines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transmission_line "Transmission line").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-guarnieri_7-1-49) The company finally succeeded in 1866 with an improved cable laid by [SS _Great Eastern_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SS_Great_Eastern "SS Great Eastern"), the largest ship of its day, designed by [Isambard Kingdom Brunel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isambard_Kingdom_Brunel "Isambard Kingdom Brunel").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-50)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-guarnieri_7-1-49)

An overland telegraph from Britain to India was first connected in 1866 but was unreliable, prompting a submarine telegraph cable to be connected in 1870.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-51) Several telegraph companies were combined to form the _Eastern Telegraph Company_ in 1872. Australia was first linked to the rest of the world in October 1872 by a submarine telegraph cable at [Darwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darwin,_Australia "Darwin, Australia").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-52)

From the 1850s until well into the 20th century, British submarine cable systems dominated the world system. This was set out as a formal strategic goal, which became known as the [All Red Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Red_Line "All Red Line").[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-kennedy197110-53) In 1896, there were thirty cable-laying ships in the world and twenty-four of them were owned by British companies. In 1892, British companies owned and operated two-thirds of the world's cables and by 1923, their share was still 42.7 percent.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-54) During [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"), Britain's telegraph communications were almost completely uninterrupted while it was able to quickly cut Germany's cables worldwide.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-kennedy197110-53)

### Facsimile

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Telegraphy&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Facsimile")]

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ef/Bain_improved_facsimile_1850.png/250px-Bain_improved_facsimile_1850.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bain_improved_facsimile_1850.png)

[Alexander Bain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Bain_(inventor) "Alexander Bain (inventor)")'s facsimile machine, 1850

In 1843, Scottish inventor [Alexander Bain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Bain_(inventor) "Alexander Bain (inventor)") invented a device that could be considered the first [facsimile machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facsimile_machine "Facsimile machine"). He called his invention a "recording telegraph". Bain's telegraph was able to transmit images by electrical wires. [Frederick Bakewell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Bakewell "Frederick Bakewell") made several improvements on Bain's design and demonstrated a telefax machine. In 1855, an Italian priest, [Giovanni Caselli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovanni_Caselli "Giovanni Caselli"), also created an electric telegraph that could transmit images. Caselli called his invention "[Pantelegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantelegraph "Pantelegraph")". Pantelegraph was successfully tested and approved for a telegraph line between [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris") and [Lyon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyon "Lyon").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-italianunivbio-55)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-hebrewuniversity-56)

In 1881, English inventor [Shelford Bidwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelford_Bidwell "Shelford Bidwell") constructed the _scanning phototelegraph_ that was the first telefax machine to scan any two-dimensional original, not requiring manual plotting or drawing. Around 1900, German physicist [Arthur Korn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Korn "Arthur Korn") invented the _[Bildtelegraph](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bildtelegrafie "de:Bildtelegrafie")_ widespread in continental Europe especially since a widely noticed transmission of a wanted-person photograph from Paris to London in 1908 used until the wider distribution of the radiofax. Its main competitors were the _Bélinographe_ by [Édouard Belin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89douard_Belin "Édouard Belin") first, then since the 1930s, the _[Hellschreiber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellschreiber "Hellschreiber")_, invented in 1929 by German inventor [Rudolf Hell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Hell "Rudolf Hell"), a pioneer in mechanical image scanning and transmission.

### Wireless telegraphy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Telegraphy&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Wireless telegraphy")]

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/Marconi_at_newfoundland.jpg/250px-Marconi_at_newfoundland.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Marconi_at_newfoundland.jpg)

Marconi watching associates raising the kite (a "Levitor" by B.F.S. Baden-Powell[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-57)) used to lift the antenna at [St. John's, Newfoundland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._John's,_Newfoundland_and_Labrador "St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador"), December 1901

Main article: [Wireless telegraphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wireless_telegraphy "Wireless telegraphy")

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e2/Post_Office_Engineers.jpg/250px-Post_Office_Engineers.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Post_Office_Engineers.jpg)

Post Office Engineers inspect the [Marconi Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marconi_Company "Marconi Company")'s equipment at [Flat Holm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flat_Holm "Flat Holm") in the [Bristol Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Channel "Bristol Channel"), May 1897.

The late 1880s through to the 1890s saw the discovery and then development of a newly understood phenomenon into a form of [wireless telegraphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wireless_telegraphy "Wireless telegraphy"), called _Hertzian wave_ wireless telegraphy, radiotelegraphy, or (later) simply "[radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio "Radio")". Between 1886 and 1888, [Heinrich Rudolf Hertz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinrich_Rudolf_Hertz "Heinrich Rudolf Hertz") published the results of his experiments where he was able to transmit [electromagnetic waves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnetic_waves "Electromagnetic waves") (radio waves) through the air, proving [James Clerk Maxwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Clerk_Maxwell "James Clerk Maxwell")'s 1873 theory of [electromagnetic radiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnetic_radiation "Electromagnetic radiation"). Many scientists and inventors experimented with this new phenomenon but the consensus was that these new waves (similar to light) would be just as short range as light, and, therefore, useless for long range communication.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-58)

At the end of 1894, the young Italian inventor [Guglielmo Marconi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guglielmo_Marconi "Guglielmo Marconi") began working on the idea of building a commercial wireless telegraphy system based on the use of Hertzian waves (radio waves), a line of inquiry that he noted other inventors did not seem to be pursuing.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-59) Building on the ideas of previous scientists and inventors Marconi re-engineered their apparatus by trial and error attempting to build a radio-based wireless telegraphic system that would function the same as wired telegraphy. He would work on the system through 1895 in his lab and then in field tests making improvements to extend its range. After many breakthroughs, including applying the wired telegraphy concept of grounding the transmitter and receiver, Marconi was able, by early 1896, to transmit radio far beyond the short ranges that had been predicted.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-60) Having failed to interest the Italian government, the 22-year-old inventor brought his telegraphy system to Britain in 1896 and met [William Preece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Preece "William Preece"), a Welshman, who was a major figure in the field and Chief Engineer of the [General Post Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Post_Office "General Post Office"). A series of demonstrations for the British government followed—by March 1897, Marconi had transmitted Morse code signals over a distance of about 6 km (3+1⁄2 mi) across [Salisbury Plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salisbury_Plain "Salisbury Plain").

On 13 May 1897, Marconi, assisted by George Kemp, a [Cardiff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiff "Cardiff") Post Office engineer, transmitted the first wireless signals over water to [Lavernock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lavernock "Lavernock") (near Penarth in Wales) from [Flat Holm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flat_Holm "Flat Holm").[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-61) His star rising, he was soon sending signals across the [English Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Channel "English Channel") (1899), from shore to ship (1899) and finally across the Atlantic (1901).[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-62) A study of these demonstrations of radio, with scientists trying to work out how a phenomenon predicted to have a short range could transmit "over the horizon", led to the discovery of a radio reflecting layer in the Earth's atmosphere in 1902, later called the [ionosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionosphere "Ionosphere").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-63)

Radiotelegraphy proved effective for rescue work in sea [disasters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disaster "Disaster") by enabling effective communication between ships and from ship to shore. In 1904, Marconi began the first commercial service to transmit nightly news summaries to subscribing ships, which could incorporate them into their on-board newspapers. A regular transatlantic radio-telegraph service was finally begun on 17 October 1907.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-65) Notably, Marconi's apparatus was used to help rescue efforts after the sinking of [RMS _Titanic_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titanic "Titanic"). Britain's postmaster-general summed up, referring to the _Titanic_ disaster, "Those who have been saved, have been saved through one man, Mr. Marconi...and his marvellous invention."

#### Non-radio wireless telegraphy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Telegraphy&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Non-radio wireless telegraphy")]

The successful development of radiotelegraphy was preceded by a 50-year history of ingenious but ultimately unsuccessful experiments by inventors to achieve wireless telegraphy by other means.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

##### Ground, water, and air conduction

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Telegraphy&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Ground, water, and air conduction")]

Several wireless electrical signaling schemes based on the (sometimes erroneous) idea that electric currents could be conducted long-range through water, ground, and air were investigated for telegraphy before practical radio systems became available.

The original telegraph lines used two wires between the two stations to form a complete [electrical circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_network "Electrical network") or "loop". In 1837, however, [Carl August von Steinheil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_August_von_Steinheil "Carl August von Steinheil") of [Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich "Munich"), [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany"), found that by connecting one leg of the apparatus at each station to metal plates buried in the ground, he could eliminate one wire and use a single wire for telegraphic communication. This led to speculation that it might be possible to eliminate both wires and therefore transmit telegraph signals through the ground without any wires connecting the stations. Other attempts were made to send the electric current through bodies of water, to span rivers, for example. Prominent experimenters along these lines included [Samuel F. B. Morse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_F._B._Morse "Samuel F. B. Morse") in the United States and [James Bowman Lindsay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Bowman_Lindsay "James Bowman Lindsay") in Great Britain, who in August 1854, was able to demonstrate transmission across a mill dam at a distance of 500 yards (457 metres).[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-66)

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c7/Wireless_Energy_Principle.jpg/330px-Wireless_Energy_Principle.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wireless_Energy_Principle.jpg)

[Tesla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikola_Tesla "Nikola Tesla")'s explanation in the 1919 issue of _[The Electrical Experimenter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Electrical\_Experimenter "The Electrical Experimenter")_ on how he thought his wireless system would work

US inventors [William Henry Ward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Henry_Ward "William Henry Ward") (1871) and [Mahlon Loomis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahlon_Loomis "Mahlon Loomis") (1872) developed electrical conduction systems based on the erroneous belief that there was an electrified atmospheric stratum accessible at low altitude.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-67)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-68) They thought atmosphere current, connected with a return path using "Earth currents" would allow for wireless telegraphy as well as supply power for the telegraph, doing away with artificial batteries.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-69)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-70) A more practical demonstration of wireless transmission via conduction came in [Amos Dolbear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amos_Dolbear "Amos Dolbear")'s 1879 magneto electric telephone that used ground conduction to transmit over a distance of a quarter of a mile.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Christopher_Cooper_2015,_p._165-71)

In the 1890s inventor [Nikola Tesla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikola_Tesla "Nikola Tesla") worked on an air and ground conduction [wireless electric power transmission system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wireless_power_transfer "Wireless power transfer"), similar to Loomis',[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-72)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-74) which he planned to include wireless telegraphy. Tesla's experiments had led him to incorrectly conclude that he could use the entire globe of the Earth to conduct electrical energy[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-75)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Christopher_Cooper_2015,_p._165-71) and his 1901 large scale application of his ideas, a high-voltage wireless power station, now called [Wardenclyffe Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wardenclyffe_Tower "Wardenclyffe Tower"), lost funding and was abandoned after a few years.

Telegraphic communication using earth conductivity was eventually found to be limited to impractically short distances, as was communication conducted through water, or between trenches during World War I.

##### Electrostatic and electromagnetic induction

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Telegraphy&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Electrostatic and electromagnetic induction")]

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/Pat465971.png/250px-Pat465971.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pat465971.png)

Thomas Edison's 1891 patent for a ship-to-shore wireless telegraph that used electrostatic induction

Both electrostatic and electromagnetic induction were used to develop wireless telegraph systems that saw limited commercial application. In the United States, [Thomas Edison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Edison "Thomas Edison"), in the mid-1880s, patented an electromagnetic induction system he called "grasshopper telegraphy", which allowed telegraphic signals to jump the short distance between a running train and telegraph wires running parallel to the tracks.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-76) This system was successful technically but not economically, as there turned out to be little interest by train travelers in the use of an on-board telegraph service. During the [Great Blizzard of 1888](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Blizzard_of_1888 "Great Blizzard of 1888"), this system was used to send and receive wireless messages from [trains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railroad "Railroad") buried in snowdrifts. The disabled trains were able to maintain communications via their Edison induction wireless telegraph systems,[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-77) perhaps the first successful use of wireless telegraphy to send distress calls. Edison would also help to patent a ship-to-shore communication system based on electrostatic induction.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-78)

The most successful creator of an electromagnetic induction telegraph system was [William Preece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Preece "William Preece"), chief engineer of Post Office Telegraphs of the [General Post Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Post_Office "General Post Office") (GPO) in the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"). Preece first noticed the effect in 1884 when overhead telegraph wires in [Grays Inn Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grays_Inn_Road "Grays Inn Road") were accidentally carrying messages sent on buried cables. Tests in [Newcastle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne "Newcastle upon Tyne") succeeded in sending a quarter of a mile using parallel rectangles of wire.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Kieve-23):243 In tests across the [Bristol Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Channel "Bristol Channel") in 1892, Preece was able to telegraph across gaps of about 5 kilometres (3.1 miles). However, his induction system required extensive lengths of [antenna wires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antenna_(radio) "Antenna (radio)"), many kilometers long, at both the sending and receiving ends. The length of those sending and receiving wires needed to be about the same length as the width of the water or land to be spanned. For example, for Preece's station to span the [English Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Channel "English Channel") from [Dover, England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dover,_England "Dover, England"), to the coast of [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France") would require sending and receiving wires of about 30 miles (48 kilometres) along the two coasts. These facts made the system impractical on ships, boats, and ordinary islands, which are much smaller than [Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain "Great Britain") or [Greenland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenland "Greenland"). Also, the relatively short distances that a practical Preece system could span meant that it had few advantages over [underwater telegraph cables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_telegraph_cable "Underwater telegraph cable").

### Telegram services

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Telegraphy&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Telegram services")]

Main article: [Telegram services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegram_services "Telegram services")

After [electric telegraphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_telegraph "Electric telegraph") became available, companies or public entities offered telegram services - delivering telegraphed messages directly to the recipient. Earlier optical systems were largely limited to official government and military purposes.

Historically, telegrams were sent between a network of interconnected telegraph offices. A person visiting a local telegraph office paid by the word to have a message telegraphed to another office and delivered to the addressee on a paper form.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Phillips-79):276 Messages (i.e. telegrams) sent by telegraph could be delivered by [telegraph messenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph_messenger "Telegraph messenger") faster than mail,[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Smith433-42) and even in the telephone age, the telegram remained popular for social and business correspondence. At their peak in 1929, an estimated 200 million telegrams were sent.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Phillips-79):274

Telegram services still operate in much of the world (see [worldwide use of telegrams by country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worldwide_use_of_telegrams_by_country "Worldwide use of telegrams by country")), but e-mail and [text messaging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Text_messaging "Text messaging") have rendered telegrams obsolete in many countries, and the number of telegrams sent annually has been declining rapidly since the 1980s.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-80) Where telegram services still exist, the transmission method between offices is no longer by telegraph, but by [telex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telex "Telex") or [IP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_Protocol "Internet Protocol") link.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-81)

### Telex

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Telegraphy&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Telex")]

Main article: [Telex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telex "Telex")

[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3d/ITT_Creed_Model_23B_teleprinter_%2846479610772%29.jpg/250px-ITT_Creed_Model_23B_teleprinter_%2846479610772%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ITT_Creed_Model_23B_teleprinter_(46479610772).jpg)

ITT Creed Model 23B teleprinter with telex dial-up facility

[Telex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telex "Telex") (telegraph exchange) was a public switched network of teleprinters. It used rotary-telephone-style [pulse dialling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulse_dialling "Pulse dialling") for automatic routing through the network. It initially used the [Baudot code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baudot_code "Baudot code") for messages. Telex development began in Germany in 1926, becoming an operational service in 1933 run by the _[Reichspost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reichspost "Reichspost")_ (the German imperial postal service). It had a speed of 50 baud—approximately 66 words per minute. Up to 25 telex channels could share a single long-distance telephone channel by using [voice frequency telegraphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voice_frequency_telegraphy "Voice frequency telegraphy")[multiplexing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frequency-division_multiplexing "Frequency-division multiplexing"), making telex the least expensive method of reliable long-distance communication.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-82) Telex was introduced into Canada in July 1957, and the United States in 1958.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-83) A new code, [ASCII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ASCII "ASCII"), was introduced in 1963 by the [American Standards Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Standards_Association "American Standards Association"). ASCII was a seven-bit code and could thus support a larger number of characters than Baudot. In particular, ASCII supported upper and lower case whereas Baudot was upper case only.

### Decline

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Telegraphy&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Decline")]

Telegraph use began to permanently decline around 1920.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Kieve-23):248 The decline began with the growth of the use of the [telephone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telephone "Telephone").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Kieve-23):253 Ironically, the invention of the telephone grew out of the development of the [harmonic telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_telegraph "Harmonic telegraph"), a device which was supposed to increase the efficiency of telegraph transmission and improve the profits of telegraph companies. Western Union gave up its patent battle with [Alexander Graham Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Graham_Bell "Alexander Graham Bell") because it believed the telephone was not a threat to its telegraph business. The [Bell Telephone Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell_Telephone_Company "Bell Telephone Company") was formed in 1877 and had 230 subscribers which grew to 30,000 by 1880. By 1886 there were a quarter of a million phones worldwide,[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Phillips-79):276–277 and nearly 2 million by 1900.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Standage-46):204 The decline was briefly postponed by the rise of special occasion congratulatory telegrams. Traffic continued to grow between 1867 and 1893 despite the introduction of the telephone in this period,[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Phillips-79):274 but by 1900 the telegraph was definitely in decline.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Phillips-79):277

There was a brief resurgence in telegraphy during [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") but the decline continued as the world entered the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression") years of the 1930s.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Phillips-79):277 After the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War") new technology improved communication in the telegraph industry.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-EB-84) Telegraph lines continued to be an important means of distributing news feeds from [news agencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/News_agency "News agency") by teleprinter machine until the rise of the internet in the 1990s. For Western Union, one service remained highly profitable—the [wire transfer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wire_transfer "Wire transfer") of money. This service kept Western Union in business long after the telegraph had ceased to be important.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Phillips-79):277 In the modern era, the telegraph that began in 1837 has been gradually replaced by [digital data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_data "Digital data") transmission based on [computer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer "Computer")[information systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_system "Information system").[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-EB-84)

## Social implications

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Telegraphy&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Social implications")]

Optical telegraph lines were installed by governments, often for a military purpose, and reserved for official use only. In many countries, this situation continued after the introduction of the electric telegraph. Starting in Germany and the UK, electric telegraph lines were installed by railway companies. Railway use quickly led to private telegraph companies in the UK and the US offering a telegraph service to the public using telegraph along railway lines. The availability of this new form of communication brought on widespread social and economic changes.

The electric telegraph freed communication from the time constraints of postal mail and revolutionized society and the global economy.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-85)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-eh.net-86) By the end of the 19th century, the telegraph was becoming an increasingly common medium of communication for ordinary people. The telegraph isolated the message (information) from the physical movement of objects or the process.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Carey,_James_1989_p._210-87)

There was some fear of the new technology. According to author Allan J. Kimmel, some people "feared that the telegraph would erode the quality of public discourse through the transmission of irrelevant, context-free information." [Henry David Thoreau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_David_Thoreau "Henry David Thoreau") thought of the Transatlantic cable "...perchance the first news that will leak through into the broad flapping American ear will be that Princess Adelaide has the whooping cough." Kimmel says these fears anticipate many of the characteristics of the modern internet age.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-88)

Initially, the telegraph was expensive, but it had an enormous effect on three industries: finance, newspapers, and railways. Telegraphy facilitated the growth of organizations "in the railroads, consolidated financial and commodity markets, and reduced information costs within and between firms".[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-eh.net-86) In the US, there were 200 to 300 stock exchanges before the telegraph, but most of these were unnecessary and unprofitable once the telegraph made financial transactions at a distance easy and drove down transaction costs.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Phillips-79):274–75 This immense growth in the business sectors influenced society to embrace the use of telegrams once the cost had fallen.

Worldwide telegraphy changed the gathering of information for news reporting. Journalists were using the telegraph for war reporting as early as 1846 when the [Mexican–American War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican%E2%80%93American_War "Mexican–American War") broke out. News agencies were formed, such as the [Associated Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press "Associated Press"), for the purpose of reporting news by telegraph.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Phillips-79):274–75 Messages and information would now travel far and wide, and the telegraph demanded a language "stripped of the local, the regional; and colloquial", to better facilitate a worldwide media language.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Carey,_James_1989_p._210-87) Media language had to be standardized, which led to the gradual disappearance of different forms of speech and styles of [journalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journalism "Journalism") and storytelling.

The spread of the railways created a need for an accurate [standard time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_time "Standard time") to replace local standards based on local [noon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noon "Noon"). The means of achieving this synchronisation was the telegraph. This emphasis on precise time has led to major societal changes such as the concept of the [time value of money](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_value_of_money "Time value of money").[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Phillips-79):273–74

During the telegraph era there was widespread employment of [women in telegraphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_telegraphy "Women in telegraphy"). The shortage of men to work as telegraph operators in the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War") opened up the opportunity for women of a well-paid skilled job.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Phillips-79):274 In the UK, there was widespread employment of women as telegraph operators even earlier – from the 1850s by all the major companies. The attraction of women for the telegraph companies was that they could pay them less than men. Nevertheless, the jobs were popular with women for the same reason as in the US; most other work available for women was very poorly paid.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Beauchamp-41):77[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Kieve-23):85

The economic impact of the telegraph was not much studied by economic historians until parallels started to be drawn with the rise of the internet. In fact, the electric telegraph was as important as the invention of printing in this respect. According to economist Ronnie J. Phillips, the reason for this may be that [institutional economists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institutional_economics "Institutional economics") paid more attention to advances that required greater capital investment. The investment required to build railways, for instance, is orders of magnitude greater than that for the telegraph.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Phillips-79):269–70

## In popular culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Telegraphy&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: In popular culture")]

The optical telegraph was quickly forgotten once it went out of service. While it was in operation, it was very familiar to the public across Europe. Examples appear in many paintings of the period. Poems include "_Le Télégraphe_" by [Victor Hugo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Hugo "Victor Hugo"), and the collection _Telegrafen: Optisk kalender för 1858_ by [Elias Sehlstedt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elias_Sehlstedt?action=edit&redlink=1 "Elias Sehlstedt (page does not exist)")[[sv](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elias%20Sehlstedt "sv:Elias Sehlstedt")][[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-89) is dedicated to the telegraph. In novels, the telegraph is a major component in _[Lucien Leuwen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucien\_Leuwen "Lucien Leuwen")_ by [Stendhal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stendhal "Stendhal"), and it features in _[The Count of Monte Cristo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Count\_of\_Monte\_Cristo "The Count of Monte Cristo")_, by [Alexandre Dumas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandre_Dumas "Alexandre Dumas").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Holzmann-13):vii–ix Joseph Chudy's 1796 opera, _Der Telegraph oder die Fernschreibmaschine_, was written to publicise Chudy's telegraph (a binary code with five lamps) when it became clear that Chappe's design was being taken up.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-Holzmann-13):42–43

[![Image 28](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/79/Effect_of_the_submarine_telegraph%3B_or_peace_and_good-will_between_England_and_France_LCCN2016649188.jpg/250px-Effect_of_the_submarine_telegraph%3B_or_peace_and_good-will_between_England_and_France_LCCN2016649188.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Effect_of_the_submarine_telegraph;_or_peace_and_good-will_between_England_and_France_LCCN2016649188.jpg)

An illustration declaring that the submarine cable between England and France would bring those countries peace and goodwill

[Rudyard Kipling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudyard_Kipling "Rudyard Kipling") wrote a poem in praise of submarine telegraph cables; "And a new Word runs between: whispering, 'Let us be one!'"[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-90)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-91) Kipling's poem represented a widespread idea in the late nineteenth century that international telegraphy (and new technology in general)[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-92) would bring peace and mutual understanding to the world.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-93) When a submarine telegraph cable first connected America and Britain, the _[New York Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_York\_Post "New York Post")_ declared:

> It is the harbinger of an age when international difficulties will not have time to ripen into bloody results, and when, in spite of the fatuity and perveseness of rulers, war will be impossible.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-94)

English band [Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchestral_Manoeuvres_in_the_Dark "Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark") sang about the technology on their 1983 single, "[Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph_(song) "Telegraph (song)")".[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-95)

### Newspaper names

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Telegraphy&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Newspaper names")]

Numerous newspapers and news outlets in various countries, such as _[The Daily Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Daily\_Telegraph "The Daily Telegraph")_ in Britain, _[The Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Telegraph\_(Calcutta) "The Telegraph (Calcutta)")_ in India, _[De Telegraaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De\_Telegraaf "De Telegraaf")_ in the Netherlands, and the [Jewish Telegraphic Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_Telegraphic_Agency "Jewish Telegraphic Agency") in the US, were given names which include the word "telegraph" due to their having received news by means of electric telegraphy. Some of these names are retained even though different means of news acquisition are now used.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

(Redirected from [Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Telegraph&redirect=no "Telegraph"))

Long distance transmission of text

This article is about telegraphy generally. For telegraphy over conducting wires, see [Electrical telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_telegraph "Electrical telegraph").

"Telegraph" redirects here. For other uses, see [Telegraph (disambiguation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph_(disambiguation) "Telegraph (disambiguation)").

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/94/OptischerTelegraf.jpg/250px-OptischerTelegraf.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:OptischerTelegraf.jpg)

Replica of a [Chappe telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chappe_telegraph "Chappe telegraph") on the Litermont near [Nalbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nalbach "Nalbach"), Germany

**Telegraphy** is the long-distance transmission of messages where the sender uses symbolic codes, known to the recipient, rather than a physical exchange of an object bearing the message. Thus [flag semaphore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_semaphore "Flag semaphore") is a method of telegraphy, whereas [pigeon post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pigeon_post "Pigeon post") is not. Ancient [signalling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signal "Signal") systems, although sometimes quite extensive and sophisticated as in China, were generally not capable of transmitting arbitrary text messages. Possible messages were fixed and predetermined, so such systems are thus not true telegraphs.

The earliest true telegraph put into widespread use was the [Chappe telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chappe_telegraph "Chappe telegraph"), an [optical telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optical_telegraph "Optical telegraph") invented by [Claude Chappe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Chappe "Claude Chappe") in the late 18th century. The system was used extensively in France, and European nations occupied by France, during the [Napoleonic era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleonic_era "Napoleonic era"). The [electric telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_telegraph "Electric telegraph") started to replace the optical telegraph in the mid-19th century. It was first taken up in Britain in the form of the [Cooke and Wheatstone telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooke_and_Wheatstone_telegraph "Cooke and Wheatstone telegraph"), initially used mostly as an aid to [railway signalling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railway_signalling "Railway signalling"). This was quickly followed by a different system developed in the United States by [Samuel Morse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Morse "Samuel Morse"). The electric telegraph was slower to develop in France due to the established optical telegraph system, but an electrical telegraph was put into use with a code compatible with the Chappe optical telegraph. The Morse system was adopted as the international standard in 1865, using a modified [Morse code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morse_code "Morse code") developed in Germany in 1848.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-1)

The [heliograph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heliograph "Heliograph") was a telegraph system using reflected sunlight for signalling. It was mainly used in areas where the electrical telegraph had not been established and generally used the same code. The most extensive heliograph network established was in Arizona and New Mexico during the [Apache Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apache_Wars "Apache Wars"). The heliograph was standard military equipment as late as [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). [Wireless telegraphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wireless_telegraphy "Wireless telegraphy") developed in the early 20th century became important for maritime use, and was a competitor to electrical telegraphy using [submarine telegraph cables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submarine_telegraph_cable "Submarine telegraph cable") in international communications.

[Telegrams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegrams "Telegrams") became a popular means of sending messages once telegraph prices had fallen sufficiently. Traffic became high enough to spur the development of automated systems—[teleprinters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teleprinter "Teleprinter") and [punched tape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punched_tape "Punched tape") transmission. These systems led to new [telegraph codes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph_code "Telegraph code"), starting with the [Baudot code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baudot_code "Baudot code"). However, telegrams were never able to compete with the letter post on price, and competition from the [telephone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telephone "Telephone"), which removed their speed advantage, drove the telegraph into decline from 1920 onwards. The few remaining telegraph applications were largely taken over by alternatives on the [Internet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet "Internet") towards the end of the 20th century.

## Terminology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Telegraphy&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Terminology")]

The word _telegraph_ (from [Ancient Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek "Ancient Greek"): τῆλε (_[têle](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/tele-#Ancient\_Greek "wikt:tele-")_) 'at a distance' and γράφειν (_[gráphein](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/-graphy#Ancient\_Greek "wikt:-graphy")_) 'to write') was coined by the French inventor of the [semaphore telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semaphore_telegraph "Semaphore telegraph"), [Claude Chappe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Chappe "Claude Chappe"), who also coined the word _[semaphore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semaphore "Semaphore")_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-3)

A telegraph is a device for transmitting and receiving messages over long distances, i.e., for telegraphy. The word _telegraph_ alone generally refers to an [electrical telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_telegraph "Electrical telegraph"). Wireless telegraphy is transmission of messages over radio with telegraphic codes. Telegraphy refers to the long-distance transmission of text or symbolic messages, historically most often via electrical telegraph systems.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph#cite_note-4)

Contrary to the extensive definition used by Chappe, Morse argued that the term _telegraph_ can strictly be applied only to systems that transmit _and_ record messages at a distance. This is to be distinguished from _semaphore_, which merely transmits messages. Smoke signals, for instance, are to be considered semaphore, not telegraph.
