**Helmut Josef Michael Kohl**[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-2) (3 April 1930 – 16 June 2017) was a German politician who served as [chancellor of Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancellor_of_Germany "Chancellor of Germany")[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-reunified-1) from 1982 to 1998. He was [leader of the Christian Democratic Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Christian_Democratic_Union "Leader of the Christian Democratic Union") (CDU) from 1973 to 1998 and oversaw the [end of the Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/End_of_the_Cold_War "End of the Cold War"), German reunification, and the creation of the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") (EU). Kohl's 16-year tenure is the longest in German post-war history and is the longest for any elected chancellor of Germany.

Born in [Ludwigshafen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwigshafen "Ludwigshafen") to a [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church") family, Kohl joined the CDU in 1946 at the age of 16. He earned a PhD in history at [Heidelberg University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heidelberg_University "Heidelberg University") in 1958 and worked as a business executive before becoming a full-time politician. He was elected as the youngest member of the [Parliament of Rhineland-Palatinate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landtag_of_Rhineland-Palatinate "Landtag of Rhineland-Palatinate") in 1959 and from 1969 to 1976 was [minister president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister-president "Minister-president") of the [Rhineland-Palatinate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhineland-Palatinate "Rhineland-Palatinate") state. Viewed during the 1960s and the early 1970s as a progressive within the CDU, he was elected national chairman of the party in 1973. After he had become party leader, Kohl was increasingly seen as a more conservative figure. In the [1976](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_West_German_federal_election "1976 West German federal election") and [1980](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_West_German_federal_election "1980 West German federal election") federal elections, his party performed well, but the social-liberal government of social democrat Helmut Schmidt was able to remain in power. After Schmidt had lost the support of the liberal [FDP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Democratic_Party_(Germany) "Free Democratic Party (Germany)") in 1982, Kohl was elected Chancellor through a [constructive vote of no confidence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constructive_vote_of_no_confidence "Constructive vote of no confidence"), forming a coalition government with the FDP. Kohl chaired the [G7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G7 "G7") in 1985 and 1992.

As Chancellor, Kohl was committed to [European integration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_integration "European integration") and especially to the [Franco-German relationship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France%E2%80%93Germany_relations "France–Germany relations"); he was also a steadfast ally of the United States and supported [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan")'s more aggressive policies to weaken the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union"). Following the [Revolutions of 1989](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolutions_of_1989 "Revolutions of 1989"), his government acted decisively, culminating in the German reunification in 1990. Kohl and French president [François Mitterrand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Mitterrand "François Mitterrand") were the architects of the [Maastricht Treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maastricht_Treaty "Maastricht Treaty"), which established the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") and the [Euro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro "Euro") currency.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-chambers-3) Kohl was also a central figure in the [eastern enlargement of the EU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enlargement_of_the_European_Union "Enlargement of the European Union"), and his government led the effort to push for international recognition of Croatia, Slovenia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina when the states declared independence. He played a controversial role in resolving the [Bosnian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosnian_War "Bosnian War"). Domestically Kohl's policies from 1990 focused on integrating former [East Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Germany "East Germany") into reunified Germany, and he moved the federal capital from the "provisional capital" [Bonn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonn "Bonn") back to [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin"), although he never resided there because the government offices were only relocated in 1999. Kohl also greatly increased federal spending on arts and culture. After his chancellorship, Kohl became honorary chairman of the CDU in 1998 but resigned from the position in 2000 in the wake of the [CDU donations scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CDU_donations_scandal "CDU donations scandal"), which damaged his reputation domestically.

Kohl received the 1988 [Charlemagne Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlemagne_Prize "Charlemagne Prize") and was named [Honorary Citizen of Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honorary_Citizen_of_Europe "Honorary Citizen of Europe") by the [European Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Council "European Council") in 1998. Following [his death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_and_funeral_of_Helmut_Kohl "Death and funeral of Helmut Kohl"), Kohl was honoured with the [first-ever European act of state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_act_of_state_in_honour_of_Helmut_Kohl "European act of state in honour of Helmut Kohl") in [Strasbourg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strasbourg "Strasbourg").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-auto1-4) Kohl was described as "the greatest European leader of the second half of the 20th century" by US presidents [George H. W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_H._W._Bush "George H. W. Bush")[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-5) and [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-6)

## Life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Helmut_Kohl&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life")]

### Youth and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Helmut_Kohl&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Youth and education")]

Kohl was born on 3 April 1930 in [Ludwigshafen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwigshafen "Ludwigshafen"). He was the third child of Hans Kohl (3 January 1887 – 19 October 1975),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-7) a [Bavarian army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bavarian_army "Bavarian army") veteran and civil servant, and his wife, Cäcilie (_née_ Schnur; 17 November 1892 – 1 August 1977).

Kohl's family was conservative and Catholic and remained loyal to the [Catholic Centre Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_Party_(Germany) "Centre Party (Germany)") before and after 1933. His elder brother died serving in the [Wehrmacht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wehrmacht "Wehrmacht") in [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") at the age of 18 in 1944.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-8) At the age of ten, Kohl joined, like most children in Germany at the time,[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] the _[Deutsches Jungvolk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deutsches\_Jungvolk "Deutsches Jungvolk")_, a section of the [Hitler Youth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hitler_Youth "Hitler Youth"). Aged 15, on 20 April 1945, Kohl was sworn into the Hitler Youth by leader [Artur Axmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artur_Axmann "Artur Axmann") at [Berchtesgaden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berchtesgaden "Berchtesgaden"), just days before the end of the war, as membership was mandatory for all boys of his age. Kohl was also [drafted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conscription "Conscription") for military service in 1945; he was not involved in any combat, a fact he later referred to as the "mercy of late birth" (German: _Gnade der späten Geburt_).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwarz201242%E2%80%9343-9)

Kohl attended the Ruprecht Elementary School and continued at the Max-Planck-Gymnasium.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwarz201238-10) After graduating in 1950, Kohl began to study law in [Frankfurt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frankfurt "Frankfurt") am Main, spending two semesters commuting between Ludwigshafen and Frankfurt.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwarz201262-11) Here, Kohl heard lectures from [Carlo Schmid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlo_Schmid_(German_politician) "Carlo Schmid (German politician)") and [Walter Hallstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Hallstein "Walter Hallstein"), among others.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwarz201263-12) In 1951, Kohl switched to [Heidelberg University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heidelberg_University "Heidelberg University"), where he studied history and [political science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_science "Political science"). Kohl was the first in his family to attend university.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwarz201261%E2%80%9362-13)

### Life before politics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Helmut_Kohl&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Life before politics")]

After graduating in 1956, Kohl became a fellow at the Alfred Weber Institute of Heidelberg University under [Dolf Sternberger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolf_Sternberger "Dolf Sternberger")[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwarz201264-14) where he was an active member of the student society [AIESEC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIESEC "AIESEC").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-15) In 1958, Kohl received his doctorate in history for his dissertation _Die politische Entwicklung in der Pfalz und das Wiedererstehen der Parteien nach 1945_ ("The Political Developments in the Palatinate and the Reconstruction of Political Parties after 1945"), under the supervision of the historian Walther Peter Fuchs.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwarz201268%E2%80%9369-16) After that, Kohl entered business, first as an assistant to the director of a foundry in [Ludwigshafen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwigshafen "Ludwigshafen"),[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwarz201290-17) then, in April 1960, as a manager for the Industrial Union for Chemistry in Ludwigshafen.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwarz201290-17)

### Early political career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Helmut_Kohl&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Early political career")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/KAS-Kohl%2C_Helmut-Bild-6906-3.jpg/250px-KAS-Kohl%2C_Helmut-Bild-6906-3.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:KAS-Kohl,_Helmut-Bild-6906-3.jpg)

Kohl in 1967 as the CDU [Rhineland-Palatinate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhineland-Palatinate "Rhineland-Palatinate") state party chairman

In 1946, Kohl joined the recently founded [CDU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Democratic_Union_of_Germany "Christian Democratic Union of Germany"),[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwarz201252-18) becoming a full member once he turned 18 in 1948.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwarz201257-19) In 1947, Kohl was one of the co-founders of the [Junge Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junge_Union "Junge Union")-branch in Ludwigshafen, the CDU youth organisation.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwarz201257-19) In 1953, Kohl joined the board of the Palatinate branch of the CDU. In 1954, Kohl became vice-chair of the Junge Union in [Rhineland-Palatinate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhineland-Palatinate "Rhineland-Palatinate"),[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-fruehejahre-20) being a member of the board until 1961.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwarz201274-21)

In January 1955, Kohl ran for a seat on the board of the Rhineland-Palatinate CDU, losing just narrowly to the state's Minister of Family Affairs, [Franz-Josef Wuermeling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franz-Josef_Wuermeling "Franz-Josef Wuermeling").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-fruehejahre-20) Kohl was still able to take up a seat on the board, being sent there by his local party branch as a delegate.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwarz201275-22) During his early years in the party, Kohl aimed to open it towards the young generation, turning away from a close relationship with the churches.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwarz201278%E2%80%9380-23)

In early 1959, Kohl was elected chairman of the Ludwigshafen district branch of the CDU, as well as a candidate for the upcoming state elections. On 19 April 1959, Kohl was elected as the youngest member of the state diet, the [Landtag of Rhineland-Palatinate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landtag_of_Rhineland-Palatinate "Landtag of Rhineland-Palatinate").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwarz201291%E2%80%9392-24) In 1960, he was also elected to the municipal council of Ludwigshafen, where he served as leader of the CDU party until 1969.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwarz201293-25) When the chairman of the CDU parliamentary group in the Landtag, [Wilhelm Boden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_Boden "Wilhelm Boden"), died in late 1961, Kohl moved up into a deputy position.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwarz201298%E2%80%9399-26)

In 1963, following the next state election, he took over as chairman, a position he held until he became Minister-President in 1969.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwarz201298%E2%80%9399-26) In 1966, Kohl and the incumbent minister-president and state party chairman, [Peter Altmeier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Altmeier "Peter Altmeier"), agreed to share duties. In March 1966, Kohl was elected as chairman of the party in Rhineland-Palatinate, while Altmeier once again ran for minister-president in the state elections in 1967, agreeing to hand the post over to Kohl after two years, halfway into the legislative period.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwarz2012103-27)

### Minister-President of Rhineland-Palatinate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Helmut_Kohl&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Minister-President of Rhineland-Palatinate")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/Bundesarchiv_B_145_Bild-F028914-0002%2C_Ludwigshafen%2C_CDU-Kongress%2C_Helmut_Kohl.jpg/250px-Bundesarchiv_B_145_Bild-F028914-0002%2C_Ludwigshafen%2C_CDU-Kongress%2C_Helmut_Kohl.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bundesarchiv_B_145_Bild-F028914-0002,_Ludwigshafen,_CDU-Kongress,_Helmut_Kohl.jpg)

Kohl in 1969

Kohl was elected [minister-president of Rhineland-Palatinate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister-President_of_Rhineland-Palatinate "Minister-President of Rhineland-Palatinate") on 19 May 1969, as the successor to Peter Altmeier. As of 2017, he was the youngest person ever to be elected as head of government in a German _Bundesland_.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-swr-28) While in office, Kohl acted as a reformer, focusing on school and education. His government abolished [school corporal punishment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_corporal_punishment "School corporal punishment") and the parochial school, topics that had been controversial with the conservative wing of his party.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwarz2012101%E2%80%93114-29)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-swr-28)

During his term, Kohl founded the [University of Trier-Kaiserslautern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Kaiserslautern "University of Kaiserslautern").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-30) He also finalised a territorial reform of the state, standardising codes of law and re-aligning districts, an act that he had already pursued under Altmeier's tenure, taking the chairmanship of the Landtag's committee on the reform.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-swr-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEK%C3%B6hler2014126%E2%80%93127-31) After taking office, Kohl established two new ministries, one for economy and transportation and one for social matters, with the latter going to [Heiner Geißler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heiner_Gei%C3%9Fler "Heiner Geißler"), who would work closely with Kohl for the next twenty years.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwarz2012104-32)

### Federal party level, election as chairman of the CDU

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Helmut_Kohl&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Federal party level, election as chairman of the CDU")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/Bundesarchiv_B_145_Bild-F041437-0013%2C_Hamburg%2C_CDU-Bundesparteitag%2C_Helmut_Kohl.jpg/250px-Bundesarchiv_B_145_Bild-F041437-0013%2C_Hamburg%2C_CDU-Bundesparteitag%2C_Helmut_Kohl.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bundesarchiv_B_145_Bild-F041437-0013,_Hamburg,_CDU-Bundesparteitag,_Helmut_Kohl.jpg)

Kohl at the CDU national party convention in [Hamburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg "Hamburg"), 1973

Kohl moved up into the federal board (_Vorstand_) of the CDU in 1964.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwarz2012139-33) Two years later, shortly before his election as chairman of the party in Rhineland-Palatinate, he failed at an attempt to be voted into the executive committee (_Präsidium_) of the party.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwarz2012144-34) After the CDU lost its involvement in the federal government for the first time since the [end of World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/End_of_World_War_II_in_Europe "End of World War II in Europe") in the [1969 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1969_West_German_federal_election "1969 West German federal election"), Kohl was elected into the committee.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwarz2012156-35) While former chancellor [Kurt Georg Kiesinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurt_Georg_Kiesinger "Kurt Georg Kiesinger") remained chairman of the CDU until 1971, it was now parliamentary chairman [Rainer Barzel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainer_Barzel "Rainer Barzel") who led the opposition against the newly formed social-liberal coalition of [Willy Brandt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willy_Brandt "Willy Brandt").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwarz2012157-36)

As a member of the board and the executive committee, Kohl pushed towards party reform, supporting liberal stances in education and social policies, including employee participation. When a proposal by the board was put to vote at a party convention in early 1971 in [Düsseldorf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%BCsseldorf "Düsseldorf"), Kohl was unable to prevail against protest coming from the conservative wing of the party around [Alfred Dregger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Dregger "Alfred Dregger") and the sister party [CSU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Social_Union_in_Bavaria "Christian Social Union in Bavaria"), costing him support at the liberal wing of the party. To make matters worse, in a mistake during the voting process, Kohl voted against the proposal, further angering his supporters, such as party treasurer [Walther Leisler Kiep](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Leisler_Kiep "Walther Leisler Kiep").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwarz2012158%E2%80%93159-37)

Nevertheless, when Kiesinger stepped down as party chairman in 1971, Kohl was a candidate for his succession. He was unsuccessful, losing the vote to Barzel 344 to 174.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwarz2012162-38) In April 1972, in the light of Brandt's _[Ostpolitik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostpolitik "Ostpolitik")_, the CDU aimed to depose Brandt and his government in a [constructive vote of no confidence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constructive_vote_of_no_confidence "Constructive vote of no confidence"), replacing him with Barzel. The attempt failed, as two members of the opposition voted against Barzel.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-39)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-40) After Barzel also lost the [general election later that year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_West_German_federal_election "1972 West German federal election"), the path was free for Kohl to take over. After Barzel announced on 10 May 1973 that he would not run for the post of party chairman again, Kohl succeeded him at a party convention in [Bonn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonn "Bonn") on 12 June 1973, amassing 520 of 600 votes, with him as the only candidate.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwarz2012164%E2%80%93165-41)

Facing stiff opposition from the left wing of the party, Kohl initially expected only to serve as chairman for a couple of months, as his critics planned to replace him at another convention set for November in [Hamburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg "Hamburg").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEK%C3%B6hler2014215-42) Kohl received the support of his party and remained in office, not least due to the lauded work of [Kurt Biedenkopf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurt_Biedenkopf "Kurt Biedenkopf"), whom Kohl had brought in as Secretary General of the CDU.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEK%C3%B6hler2014218%E2%80%93222-43) Kohl remained chairman until 1998.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchwarz2012166-44)

When Chancellor Brandt stepped down in May 1974 following the unravelling of the [Guillaume Affair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guillaume_Affair "Guillaume Affair"), Kohl urged his party to restrain from _[Schadenfreude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schadenfreude "Schadenfreude")_ and not to use the position of their political opponent for "cheap polemics".[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEK%C3%B6hler2014223%E2%80%93224-45) In June, Kohl campaigned during the state elections in [Lower Saxony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Saxony "Lower Saxony") for his party colleague Wilfried Hasselmann, leading the CDU to a strong result of 48.8% of the vote, even though it proved not enough to prevent a continuation of the social-liberal coalition in the state.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEK%C3%B6hler2014226-46)

### First candidacy for the chancellorship and the 1976 Bundestag election

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Helmut_Kohl&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: First candidacy for the chancellorship and the 1976 Bundestag election")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4b/Bundesarchiv_B_145_Bild-F049283-0016%2C_Berlin%2C_CDU_Bundestagswahlkampf%2C_Kohl.jpg/250px-Bundesarchiv_B_145_Bild-F049283-0016%2C_Berlin%2C_CDU_Bundestagswahlkampf%2C_Kohl.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bundesarchiv_B_145_Bild-F049283-0016,_Berlin,_CDU_Bundestagswahlkampf,_Kohl.jpg)

Kohl in [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Berlin "West Berlin") at a campaign event for the [1976 West German federal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_West_German_federal_election "1976 West German federal election")

On 9 March 1975, Kohl and the CDU faced re-election in Rhineland-Palatinate. What placed Kohl, who intended to run for chancellor, under increased pressure was the fact that the sister parties of CDU and CSU were set to decide upon their leading candidate for the [upcoming federal elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_West_German_federal_election "1976 West German federal election") in mid-1975. CSU chairman [Franz Josef Strauss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franz_Josef_Strauss "Franz Josef Strauss") had ambitions to run and publicly put Kohl under pressure over what result would be acceptable in the state elections.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEK%C3%B6hler2014232%E2%80%93234-47)

On election day, the CDU achieved a result of 53.9%, the highest-ever result in the state, consolidating Kohl's position. Strauß's bid for the chancellorship was further put into jeopardy when in March 1975 the magazine _[Der Spiegel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Der\_Spiegel "Der Spiegel")_ published a transcript of a speech held in November 1974, in which Strauß claimed that the [Red Army Faction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Army_Faction "Red Army Faction"), a West German armed struggle group responsible for multiple attacks at the time, had sympathizers in the ranks of the SPD and FDP. The scandal deeply unsettled the public and effectively ruled out Strauß for the candidacy.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEK%C3%B6hler2014232%E2%80%93234-47)

On 12 May 1975, the federal board of the CDU unanimously nominated Kohl as the candidate for the general elections, without consulting their Bavarian sister party beforehand. In reaction, the CSU nominated Strauß and only a mediation by former chancellor Kiesinger was able to resolve the issue and confirm Kohl as the candidate for both parties.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEK%C3%B6hler2014236-48) In June 1975, Kohl was also re-elected as party chairman, achieving a result of 98.44%.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEK%C3%B6hler2014237-49)

Strauß took the discord as a starting point to evaluate chances of expanding the CSU on the federal level, such as having separate electoral lists in the states of [North Rhine-Westphalia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Rhine-Westphalia "North Rhine-Westphalia"), [Lower Saxony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Saxony "Lower Saxony"), Hamburg, and [Bremen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bremen_(state) "Bremen (state)"). He hoped to draw away right-wing voters from the FDP towards the CSU and went as far as having private meetings with industrialists in North Rhine-Westphalia. These attempts led to discomfort within the membership base of the CDU and hampered both parties' chances in the upcoming elections. Kohl remained silent during these tensions, which some interpreted as a lack of leadership, while others, such as future president [Karl Carstens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Carstens "Karl Carstens"), praised him for seeking a consensus at the centre of the party.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEK%C3%B6hler2014242%E2%80%93244-50)

In the 1976 federal election, the CDU/CSU coalition performed very well, winning 48.6% of the vote. They were kept out of government by the centre-left cabinet formed by the [Social Democratic Party of Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Democratic_Party_of_Germany "Social Democratic Party of Germany") (SPD) and [Free Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Democratic_Party_(Germany) "Free Democratic Party (Germany)") (FDP), led by Social Democrat Helmut Schmidt. Kohl then retired as minister-president of Rhineland-Palatinate to become the leader of the CDU/CSU in the [Bundestag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bundestag "Bundestag"). He was succeeded by Bernhard Vogel.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-51)

### Leader of the opposition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Helmut_Kohl&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Leader of the opposition")]

In the [1980 federal elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_German_federal_election "1980 German federal election"), Kohl had to play second fiddle when CSU leader Franz Josef Strauss became the CDU/CSU's candidate for chancellor. Strauß was also unable to defeat the coalition of the SPD and the FDP. Unlike Kohl, Strauß did not want to continue as the leader of the CDU/CSU and remained Minister-President of [Bavaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bavaria "Bavaria"). Kohl remained as leader of the opposition under the third Schmidt cabinet (1980–1982). On 17 September 1982, a conflict of economic policy occurred between the governing SPD/FDP coalition partners. The FDP wanted to radically liberalise the labour market, while the SPD preferred greater job security. The FDP began talks with the CDU/CSU to form a new government.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-52)

## Chancellor of Germany (1982–1998)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Helmut_Kohl&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Chancellor of Germany (1982–1998)")]

### Rise to power and first cabinet, 1982–1983

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Helmut_Kohl&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Rise to power and first cabinet, 1982–1983")]

Main article: [First Kohl cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Kohl_cabinet "First Kohl cabinet")

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7d/Bundesarchiv_B_145_Bild-F064809-0010%2C_CDU_Bundestagswahlkampf%2C_Kohl.jpg/250px-Bundesarchiv_B_145_Bild-F064809-0010%2C_CDU_Bundestagswahlkampf%2C_Kohl.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bundesarchiv_B_145_Bild-F064809-0010,_CDU_Bundestagswahlkampf,_Kohl.jpg)

Kohl at a campaign event for the [1983 West German federal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1983_West_German_federal_election "1983 West German federal election")

On 1 October 1982, the CDU proposed a constructive vote of no confidence, which was supported by the FDP. The motion carried — to date, the only time that a chancellor has been deposed in this manner. Three days later, the Bundestag voted in a new CDU/CSU-FDP coalition cabinet, with Kohl as chancellor. Many of the important details of the new coalition had been hammered out on 20 September, though minor details were reportedly still being negotiated as the vote took place.

Though Kohl's election was done according to the [Basic Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_Law_for_the_Federal_Republic_of_Germany "Basic Law for the Federal Republic of Germany"), it came amid some controversy. The FDP had fought its 1980 campaign on the side of the SPD and even placed Chancellor Schmidt on some of their campaign posters. There were also doubts that the new government had the support of a majority of the people. In answer, the new government aimed for new elections at the earliest possible date. Polls suggested that a clear majority was indeed within reach.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-Roberts-53)

As the Basic Law only allows the dissolution of parliament after an unsuccessful confidence motion, Kohl had to take another controversial move: he called for a confidence vote only a month after being sworn in, which he intentionally lost because the members of his coalition abstained. President Karl Carstens then dissolved the Bundestag at Kohl's request and called new elections.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-Roberts-53)

The move was controversial, as the coalition parties denied their votes to the same man they had elected Chancellor a month before and whom they wanted to re-elect after the parliamentary election. However, this step was condoned by the German [Federal Constitutional Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Constitutional_Court_of_Germany "Federal Constitutional Court of Germany") as a legal instrument and was again applied by SPD Chancellor [Gerhard Schröder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerhard_Schr%C3%B6der "Gerhard Schröder") in 2005.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-Roberts-53)

During his first term in terms of economy, Kohl wanted to move back to [ordoliberalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordoliberalism "Ordoliberalism").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-54)

### Second cabinet, 1983–1987

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Helmut_Kohl&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Second cabinet, 1983–1987")]

Main article: [Second Kohl cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Kohl_cabinet "Second Kohl cabinet")

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3a/Bundesarchiv_B_145_Bild-F065185-0016%2C_Bonn%2C_Sitzung_CDU-Pr%C3%A4sidium.jpg/250px-Bundesarchiv_B_145_Bild-F065185-0016%2C_Bonn%2C_Sitzung_CDU-Pr%C3%A4sidium.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bundesarchiv_B_145_Bild-F065185-0016,_Bonn,_Sitzung_CDU-Pr%C3%A4sidium.jpg)

Kohl and former chancellor Kiesinger in 1983

In the [federal elections of March 1983](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1983_West_German_federal_election "1983 West German federal election"), Kohl won a resounding victory. The CDU/CSU won 48.8%, while the FDP won 7.0%. Some opposition members of the Bundestag, angered by what SPD figures in the Hessian regional elections had called the FDP's "betrayal in Bonn", asked the Federal Constitutional Court to declare the whole proceeding unconstitutional. It denied their claim but did set restrictions on a similar move in the future. The second Kohl cabinet pushed through several controversial plans, including the stationing of [NATO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO "NATO") midrange missiles, against major opposition from the peace movement.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-55)

On 22 September 1984, Kohl met French president [François Mitterrand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Mitterrand "François Mitterrand") at [Verdun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verdun "Verdun"), where the [Battle of Verdun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Verdun "Battle of Verdun") between France and Germany had taken place during [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"). Together, they commemorated the deaths of both World Wars. The photograph, which depicted [their minutes-long handshake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitterrand_and_Kohl_holding_hands_in_Verdun "Mitterrand and Kohl holding hands in Verdun"), became an important symbol of French-German reconciliation. Kohl and Mitterrand developed a close political relationship, forming an important motor for [European integration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_integration "European integration").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-56)

Together they laid the foundations for European projects, like [Eurocorps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurocorps "Eurocorps") and [Arte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arte "Arte"). In 1985, alongside European leaders from 16 other countries, they founded [Eureka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eureka_(organisation) "Eureka (organisation)"): a research and development network of national funding ministries and agencies (distinct from the European Union) that fund and support collaborative international projects. This French-German cooperation was also vital for important European projects, like the [Treaty of Maastricht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Maastricht "Treaty of Maastricht") and the Euro.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-57)

In 1985, Kohl and US President [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan"), as part of a plan to observe the 40th anniversary of [V-E Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V-E_Day "V-E Day"), saw an opportunity to demonstrate the strength of the friendship that existed between Germany and its former foe. During a November 1984 visit to the White House, Kohl appealed to Reagan to join him in symbolising the reconciliation of their two countries at a German military cemetery. Reagan visited Germany as part of the [11th G7 summit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/11th_G7_summit "11th G7 summit") in Bonn; then he and Kohl visited [Bergen-Belsen concentration camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergen-Belsen_concentration_camp "Bergen-Belsen concentration camp") on 5 May and the [German military cemetery at Bitburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitburg_controversy "Bitburg controversy"). There was widespread outrage when the media reported that this cemetery had the graves of SS soldiers but no Americans. Reagan considered that escalating Cold War confrontations with the Kremlin required his strong support for Kohl.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-58)

#### Domestic policies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Helmut_Kohl&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Domestic policies")]

Kohl's chancellorship presided over a number of innovative policy measures. Extensions in unemployment benefits for older claimants were introduced, while the benefit for the young unemployed was extended to age 21. In 1986, a child-rearing allowance was introduced to benefit parents when at least one was employed. Informal carers were offered an attendance allowance together with tax incentives, both of which were established with the tax reforms of 1990, and were also guaranteed up to 25 hours a month of professional support, which was supplemented by four weeks of annual holiday relief. In 1984, an early retirement scheme was introduced that offered incentives to employers to replace elderly workers with applicants off the unemployment register. In 1989, a partial retirement plan was introduced under which elderly employees could work half-time and receive 70% of their former salary, "and be credited with 90% of the full social insurance entitlement." In 1984, a Mother and Child Fund was established, providing discretionary grants "to forestall abortions on grounds of material hardship," and in 1986, a 10 Bn DM package of Erziehungsgeld (childcare allowance) was introduced, although according to various studies, this latter initiative was heavily counterbalanced by cuts. In 1989, special provisions were introduced for the older unemployed.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-59)

Kohl's time as Chancellor also saw some controversial decisions in the field of social policy. Student aid was made reimbursable to the state[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-60) while the Health Care Reform Act of 1989 introduced the concept by which patients pay up front and are reimbursed, while increasing patient co-payments for hospitalisation, spa visits, dental prostheses, and prescription drugs.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-61) In addition, while a 1986 Baby-Year Pensions reform granted women born after 1921 one year of work-credit per child, lawmakers were forced by public protest to phase in supplementary pension benefits for mothers who were born before the cut-off year.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-62)

After the [1987 federal elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_West_German_federal_election "1987 West German federal election"), Kohl won a slightly reduced majority and formed his [third cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_Kohl_III "Cabinet Kohl III"). The SPD's candidate for chancellor was the [Minister-President of North Rhine-Westphalia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister-President_of_North_Rhine-Westphalia "Minister-President of North Rhine-Westphalia"), [Johannes Rau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Rau "Johannes Rau").[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-63)

In 1987, Kohl hosted East German leader [Erich Honecker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erich_Honecker "Erich Honecker") – the [first ever visit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erich_Honecker's_1987_visit_to_West_Germany "Erich Honecker's 1987 visit to West Germany") by an East German head of state to West Germany. This is generally seen as a sign that Kohl pursued _Ostpolitik_, a policy of [détente](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%A9tente "Détente") between East and West that had been begun by the SPD-led governments (and strongly opposed by Kohl's own CDU) during the 1970s.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-64)

#### Internal struggle for CDU leadership

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Helmut_Kohl&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Internal struggle for CDU leadership")]

The CDU's general secretary, Heiner Geißler, considered the party to be in a downward spiral following the relatively poor showing in the 1987 elections. Behind the scenes, he attempted to find a majority to unseat Kohl as the party's chairman and replace him with [Lothar Späth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lothar_Sp%C3%A4th "Lothar Späth"), the [Minister-president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister-president "Minister-president") of [Baden-Württemberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baden-W%C3%BCrttemberg "Baden-Württemberg").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-65) Before the CDU party convention in [Bremen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bremen "Bremen") started on 11 September 1989, Kohl was diagnosed with an inflammation of his prostate.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-66) His doctor recommended immediate surgery, but Kohl refused to miss the convention and attended while wearing a [catheter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catheter "Catheter") and with his doctor by his side, whom he introduced as his new speech writer.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-67) In the end, the "coup" was unsuccessful, as Kohl was re-elected as chairman with 79.52% of the votes.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-68) Späth, who did not stand for the position of chairman after support for Kohl became apparent, was punished by his party, failing to be elected as vice-chairman with just 357 of 731 votes.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-69) Geißler meanwhile was relieved of his duties as general secretary and replaced by [Volker Rühe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volker_R%C3%BChe "Volker Rühe").[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-70)

#### Road to reunification

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Helmut_Kohl&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Road to reunification")]

Main article: [German reunification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_reunification "German reunification")

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/KohlModrowMomperBrandenburgerTor.jpg/250px-KohlModrowMomperBrandenburgerTor.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:KohlModrowMomperBrandenburgerTor.jpg)

Kohl speaks at the official opening of the [Brandenburg Gate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandenburg_Gate "Brandenburg Gate") in 1989.

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/96/Helmut_Kohl_%26_Fran%C3%A7ois_Mitterrand_-_1989.jpg/250px-Helmut_Kohl_%26_Fran%C3%A7ois_Mitterrand_-_1989.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Helmut_Kohl_&_Fran%C3%A7ois_Mitterrand_-_1989.jpg)

Kohl and French President [François Mitterrand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Mitterrand "François Mitterrand") at the [European Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Council "European Council") Summit in Strasbourg, 9 December 1989

Following the breach of the [Berlin Wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Wall "Berlin Wall") and the collapse of the East German Communist regime in 1989, Kohl's handling of the East German issue would become the turning point of his chancellorship. Kohl, like most West Germans, was initially caught unaware when the [Socialist Unity Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Unity_Party_of_Germany "Socialist Unity Party of Germany") was toppled in late 1989. Well aware of his constitutional mandate to seek German unity, he immediately moved to make it a reality. Taking advantage of the historic political changes occurring in East Germany, Kohl presented a ten-point plan for "Overcoming the division of Germany and Europe" without consulting his coalition partner, the FDP, or the Western Allies. In February 1990, he visited the Soviet Union seeking a guarantee from Mikhail Gorbachev that the USSR would allow German reunification to proceed. [One month later](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_East_German_general_election "1990 East German general election"), the [Party of Democratic Socialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_of_Democratic_Socialism_(Germany) "Party of Democratic Socialism (Germany)") – the renamed SED – was roundly defeated by a grand coalition headed by the East German counterpart of Kohl's CDU, which ran on a platform of speedy reunification.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-Thompson-71)

On 18 May 1990, Kohl signed an economic and social union treaty with East Germany. This treaty stipulated that when reunification took place, it would be under the quicker provisions of Article 23 of the Basic Law. That article stated that any new states could adhere to the Basic Law by a simple majority vote. The alternative would have been the more protracted route of drafting a completely new constitution for the newly reunified country, as provided by Article 146 of the Basic Law. However, the Article 146 process would have opened up contentious issues in West Germany. Even without this to consider, by this time, East Germany was in a state of utter collapse. In contrast, an Article 23 reunification could be completed in as little as six months.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-72)

Over the objections of [Bundesbank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deutsche_Bundesbank "Deutsche Bundesbank") president [Karl Otto Pöhl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Otto_P%C3%B6hl "Karl Otto Pöhl"), he allowed a 1:1 exchange rate for wages, interest and rent between the [West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_mark "German mark") and [East Marks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_German_mark "East German mark"). In the end, this policy would seriously hurt companies in the [new federal states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_states_of_Germany "New states of Germany"). Together with Foreign Minister [Hans-Dietrich Genscher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans-Dietrich_Genscher "Hans-Dietrich Genscher"), Kohl was able to resolve talks with the former Allies of World War II to allow [German reunification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_reunification "German reunification"). He received assurances from Gorbachev that a reunified Germany would be able to choose which international alliance it wanted to join, although Kohl made no secret that he wanted the reunified Germany to inherit West Germany's seats at NATO and the EC.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-73)

A reunification treaty was signed on 31 August 1990 and was overwhelmingly approved by both parliaments on 20 September 1990. At midnight [Central European Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_European_Time "Central European Time") on 3 October 1990, East Germany officially ceased to exist, and its territory joined the Federal Republic as the five states of [Brandenburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandenburg "Brandenburg"), Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, [Saxony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxony "Saxony"), Saxony-Anhalt and [Thuringia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thuringia "Thuringia"). These states had been the original five states of East Germany before being abolished in 1952 and had been reconstituted in August. East and West Berlin were reunited as a city-state, which became the capital of the enlarged Federal Republic.

After the [fall of the Berlin Wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_the_Berlin_Wall "Fall of the Berlin Wall"), Kohl affirmed that [former German territories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Former_eastern_territories_of_Germany "Former eastern territories of Germany") east of the [Oder-Neisse line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oder-Neisse_line "Oder-Neisse line") were definitively part of Poland, thereby relinquishing any claim Germany had to them in a [treaty signed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German%E2%80%93Polish_Border_Treaty "German–Polish Border Treaty") on 14 November 1990 in [Warsaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw "Warsaw"). Though earlier in March of that year, Kohl caused a diplomatic firestorm when he suggested that a reunified Germany would not accept the Oder–Neisse line, and implied that the Federal Republic might wish to restore the frontier of 1937, by force if necessary.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-74) After the statement caused a major international backlash that threatened to halt German reunification, Kohl retracted his comments after knuckling under international rebuke and assured both the United States and the Soviet Union that a reunified Germany would accept the Oder–Neisse line as the final border between Poland and Germany.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-75) In 1993, Kohl confirmed, via treaty with the Czech Republic, that Germany would no longer bring forward territorial claims as to the pre-1945 [ethnic German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnic_German "Ethnic German")[Sudetenland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudetenland "Sudetenland"). This treaty was a disappointment for the German [Heimatvertriebene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heimatvertriebene "Heimatvertriebene") ("displaced persons").[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-76)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-77)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-78)

### After reunification, 1990–1998

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Helmut_Kohl&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: After reunification, 1990–1998")]

Main articles: [Fourth Kohl cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Kohl_cabinet "Fourth Kohl cabinet") and [Fifth Kohl cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifth_Kohl_cabinet "Fifth Kohl cabinet")

Reunification placed Kohl in a momentarily unassailable position. In the [1990 elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_German_federal_election "1990 German federal election")– the first free, fair and democratic all-German elections since the [Weimar Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weimar_Republic "Weimar Republic") era – Kohl won by a landslide over opposition candidate and Minister-President of [Saarland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saarland "Saarland"), [Oskar Lafontaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oskar_Lafontaine "Oskar Lafontaine"). He then formed his [fourth cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_Kohl_IV "Cabinet Kohl IV").[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-79)

After the [federal elections of 1994](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_German_federal_election "1994 German federal election"), Kohl was reelected with a somewhat reduced majority, defeating Minister-President of Rhineland-Palatinate [Rudolf Scharping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Scharping "Rudolf Scharping"). The SPD was able to win a majority in the [Bundesrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bundesrat_of_Germany "Bundesrat of Germany"), which significantly limited Kohl's power. In foreign politics, Kohl was more successful, for instance, getting [Frankfurt am Main](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frankfurt_am_Main "Frankfurt am Main") as the seat for the [European Central Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank "European Central Bank"). In 1997, Kohl received the [Vision for Europe Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vision_for_Europe_Award "Vision for Europe Award") for his efforts in the unification of Europe.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-80)

By the late 1990s, Kohl's popularity had dropped amid rising unemployment. He was defeated by a large margin in the [1998 federal elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_German_federal_election "1998 German federal election") by the [Minister-President of Lower Saxony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister-President_of_Lower_Saxony "Minister-President of Lower Saxony"), Gerhard Schröder.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-Thompson-71)

The future Chancellor [Angela Merkel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angela_Merkel "Angela Merkel") started her political career as Kohl's protégée and was known in the 1990s as "Kohl's girl"; in January 1991, he lifted the then little-known Merkel to national prominence by appointing her to the federal cabinet.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-81)

## Retirement

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Helmut_Kohl&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Retirement")]

A [red–green coalition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red%E2%80%93green_coalition "Red–green coalition") government led by Schröder replaced Kohl's government on 27 October 1998. He immediately resigned as CDU leader and largely retired from politics. He remained a member of the Bundestag until he decided not to run for reelection in the [2002 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_German_federal_election "2002 German federal election").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-82)

### CDU finance affair, 1999–2000

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Helmut_Kohl&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: CDU finance affair, 1999–2000")]

Kohl's life after political office in the beginning was dominated by the [CDU donations scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CDU_donations_scandal "CDU donations scandal"). The party financing scandal became public in 1999 when it was discovered that the CDU had received and kept illegal donations during Kohl's leadership.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-Spiegel(08/07/2009)-83)_Der Spiegel_ reported, "It was never suggested that Kohl benefited personally from political donations – but he did lead the party financial system outside of the legal boundaries, doing such things as opening secret bank accounts and establishing civic associations that could act as middlemen, or procurement agencies, for campaign donations."[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-Spiegel(08/07/2009)-83) While his reputation in Germany suffered in the immediate years after the finance affair, it did not affect his reputation internationally; outside of Germany he was perceived as a great European statesman and remembered for his role in solving the five great problems of his era: German reunification, European integration, the relations with Russia after the fall of the Soviet Union and the [Bosnian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosnian_War "Bosnian War").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-84)

### Life after politics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Helmut_Kohl&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Life after politics")]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/30/Vladimir_Putin_6_March_2002-1.jpg/250px-Vladimir_Putin_6_March_2002-1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vladimir_Putin_6_March_2002-1.jpg)

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/HelmutKohl.PNG/250px-HelmutKohl.PNG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:HelmutKohl.PNG)

Kohl in 2012

In 2002, Kohl left the Bundestag and officially retired from politics. Later, he was largely rehabilitated by his party. After taking office, Angela Merkel invited her former patron to the Chancellor's Office and Ronald Pofalla, the Secretary-General of the CDU, announced that the CDU would cooperate more closely with Kohl, "to take advantage of the experience of this great statesman".[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-85) On 4 March 2004, he published the first of his memoirs, called _Memories 1930–1982_, covering the period from 1930 to 1982, when he became chancellor. The second part, published on 3 November 2005, included the first half of his chancellorship (1982–1990). On 28 December 2004, he was air-lifted by the [Sri Lanka Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sri_Lanka_Air_Force "Sri Lanka Air Force"), after having been stranded in a hotel by the [2004 Indian Ocean earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Indian_Ocean_earthquake "2004 Indian Ocean earthquake").[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-86) Kohl was a member of the [Club of Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_of_Madrid "Club of Madrid").[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-cdm-87)

As reported in the German press, he also gave his name to the _Helmut Kohl Centre for European Studies_ (currently _Centre for European Studies_), which is the new political foundation of the [European People's Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_People's_Party "European People's Party"). In late February 2008, Kohl suffered a stroke in combination with a fall which caused serious head injuries and required his hospitalisation, after which he was reported to be using a wheelchair due to partial paralysis and having difficulty speaking.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-88)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-89)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-90)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-91) He remained in intensive care since, marrying his 43-year-old partner, [Maike Richter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maike_Kohl-Richter "Maike Kohl-Richter"), on 8 May 2008, while still in hospital. In 2010, he had a gall bladder operation in [Heidelberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heidelberg "Heidelberg"),[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-92) and heart surgery in 2012.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-93) He was reportedly in "critical condition" in June 2015, following intestinal surgery following a hip-replacement procedure.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-94)

In 2011, Kohl, despite frail health, began giving a number of interviews and issued statements in which he sharply condemned his successor Angela Merkel, whom he had formerly mentored, on her policies in favour of strict [austerity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austerity "Austerity") in the [European debt crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_debt_crisis "European debt crisis") which he saw as opposed to his politics of peaceful bi-lateral European integration during his time as chancellor. He published the book _Aus Sorge um Europa_ ("Out of Concern for Europe") outlining these criticisms of Merkel (while also attacking his immediate successor Gerhard Schröder's Euro policy)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-95)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-96)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-WSW-97)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-98) and was widely quoted in the press as saying, "_Die macht mir mein Europa kaputt_" ("That woman is destroying my Europe").[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-99)[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-100)[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-101)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-102)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-103) Kohl thus joined former German chancellors Gerhard Schröder and Helmut Schmidt in their similar criticisms of Merkel's policies in these two fields.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-BI-104)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-WSW-97) In 2011, he also criticised Merkel for committing to nuclear power phaseout by 2022, following the [Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fukushima_Daiichi_nuclear_disaster "Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster"), saying that a nuclear phase-out would "make the world a more dangerous place", that risks are a part of life and Germany should instead focus on "taking precautionary measures and minimizing risks".[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-105)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-106)

On 19 April 2016, Kohl was visited in his [Oggersheim residence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwigshafen "Ludwigshafen") by Hungarian Prime Minister [Viktor Orbán](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viktor_Orb%C3%A1n "Viktor Orbán"). The two had a one-hour conversation and released a joint press statement regarding the [2015 European migrant crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_European_migrant_crisis "2015 European migrant crisis"), saying they doubted that Europe was capable of continuing to absorb refugees indefinitely.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-orbanvisit-107) Before the meeting, it had widely been interpreted as criticism of Angela Merkel's handling of the crisis,[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-108)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-109) but Kohl and Orbán refrained from attacking the chancellor directly, writing: "It is about a good future for Europe and peace in the world. The efforts of Merkel point in the same direction."[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-orbanvisit-107)[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-110)

In 2016, Kohl sued [Random House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_House "Random House"), his former ghost writer Heribert Schwan and co-author Tilman Jens for publishing without his consent 116 comments allegedly made by Kohl during interviews in 2001 and 2002 and published in an [unauthorised biography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unauthorised_biography "Unauthorised biography") in 2014 called _Legacy: The Kohl Protocols_. By April 2017, a German court ordered publisher Random House and the two journalists to pay Kohl damages of 1 million euros ($1.1 million) for violating his privacy, making it the highest judgment ever rendered for violations of privacy rights under German law.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-111)

## Political views

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Helmut_Kohl&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Political views")]

Main article: [Conservatism in Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservatism_in_Germany "Conservatism in Germany")

Kohl was committed to European integration, maintaining close relations with French president François Mitterrand. Parallel to this, he was committed to German reunification. Although he continued the _Ostpolitik_ of his social democratic predecessors, Kohl supported Reagan's more aggressive policies to weaken the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union").[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-112) He had a strained relationship with British prime minister and fellow conservative [Margaret Thatcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Thatcher "Margaret Thatcher"),[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-113)[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-114) although Kohl did allow her secret access to his plans on reunification in March 1990,[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-115) to allay the concerns she shared with Mitterrand.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-116)

## Personality and media portrayals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Helmut_Kohl&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Personality and media portrayals")]

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bb/Bundesarchiv_B_145_Bild-F045625-0010%2C_Bonn%2C_Pressekonferenz_CDU_Bundesvorstand%2C_Kohl.jpg/250px-Bundesarchiv_B_145_Bild-F045625-0010%2C_Bonn%2C_Pressekonferenz_CDU_Bundesvorstand%2C_Kohl.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bundesarchiv_B_145_Bild-F045625-0010,_Bonn,_Pressekonferenz_CDU_Bundesvorstand,_Kohl.jpg)

Kohl in 1975. In his years as minister-president, Kohl was treated by the media as a progressive reformer in his own party. This image changed during the 1970s with Kohl's assumption of leadership in the federal party.He experienced a fundamental animosity of journalists towards him.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Kohl faced stiff opposition from the West German political left and was mocked for his large physical stature (Standing at 193 cm (6 ft 4 in) and weighing over 136 kg (300 lb) during his leadership years), alleged provinciality, simplistic language, and (slight) local [Palatinate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palatinate_(region) "Palatinate (region)") dialect including [hypercorrections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypercorrection "Hypercorrection"). Similar to historical French cartoons of [Louis-Philippe of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis-Philippe_of_France "Louis-Philippe of France"), Hans Traxler depicted Kohl as a pear in the left-leaning satirical journal _[Titanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titanic\_(magazine) "Titanic (magazine)")_.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-117) The German word "Birne" ("pear") became a widespread nickname for and symbol of the chancellor.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-118)

Comedians like Thomas Freitag and Stefan Wald imitated the chancellor,[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-119) and books were sold with jokes rewritten with Kohl as the stupid protagonist. When Kohl died, left-wing newspaper [Die Tageszeitung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Die_Tageszeitung "Die Tageszeitung") (TAZ) presented a title page showing a flower set typical for funerals, with a pear and the caption _flourishing landscapes_, Kohl's prediction for the future of East Germany after reunification. Following protests, the editor-in-chief apologised.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-120)

The minister-president of Rhineland-Palatinate (1969–1976) was a young reformer in a somewhat backward state and a newcomer who heavily criticised the older party leaders. The national media, for as much as they took notice of him, regarded him with curiosity. But this changed when Kohl became chair of the federal party in 1973, and even more dramatically when, in late 1975, his party made him a candidate for the chancellery. His opponents within the federal party, but also journalists and other observers, had their doubts whether the parochial, though successful, moderniser of a manageable, smaller state was the right person to lead the Federal Republic, a big and complicated industrial country.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-121)

Biographer Hans Peter Schwarz names five problems of the 46-year-old candidate: being unfamiliar with the complicated relations in the Bundestag group, having no international experience, having no profound knowledge of economics, but also: a lack of charisma and no cultural acceptance in [Northern Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Germany "Northern Germany").[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-122)

In small circles, Kohl was fascinating and a perfect host; the larger the crowd, the vaguer, weaker and paler he appeared. His gaze into the TV cameras made him look helpless. When attacked, e.g. in election campaigns, he became a good fighter. But in general, he was no great orator; his speeches were lengthy and verbose, according to Schwarz. Additionally, the Catholic with his [Palatinate dialect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palatine_German_language "Palatine German language"), a folksy man who had culture but was no intellectual – to North German journalists (like from the important newspapers made in [Hamburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg "Hamburg"), including weeklies _Der Spiegel_ and _[Die Zeit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Die\_Zeit "Die Zeit")_) he just felt foreign, more than any previous CDU chairman.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-123)

Unlike many politicians of his era, including predecessors Helmut Schmidt and [Willy Brandt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willy_Brandt "Willy Brandt"), successor [Gerhard Schröder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerhard_Schr%C3%B6der "Gerhard Schröder") or rival [Franz Josef Strauss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franz_Josef_Strauss "Franz Josef Strauss"), Kohl was never regarded as charismatic or media-savvy, and many of his peculiar coinings were heavily lampooned and criticised. Nonetheless, many of them have entered the general lexicon despite or perhaps because of attempts by his opponents to mock them.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-124) Examples of "Kohlisms" that have gained some currency include his description of the 1982 change in government as "_[geistig-moralische Wende](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geistig-moralische\_Wende?action=edit&redlink=1 "Geistig-moralische Wende (page does not exist)")_"[[de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/geistig-moralische%20Wende "de:geistig-moralische Wende")] ("spiritual and moral turnaround") or the "Grace of late birth" ("_[Gnade der späten Geburt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gnade\_der\_sp%C3%A4ten\_Geburt?action=edit&redlink=1 "Gnade der späten Geburt (page does not exist)")_"[[de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gnade%20der%20sp%C3%A4ten%20Geburt "de:Gnade der späten Geburt")]) meaning that Kohl, born in 1930, was only involved in the war as a [Flakhelfer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flakhelfer "Flakhelfer") and escaped the possibility of involvement in Nazi atrocities by virtue of being too young at the time. Another frequently mocked turn of phrase by Kohl was his prediction the [New States of Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_States_of_Germany "New States of Germany") would soon turn into "_[blühende Landschaften](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bl%C3%BChende\_Landschaften?action=edit&redlink=1 "Blühende Landschaften (page does not exist)")_"[[de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/bl%C3%BChende%20Landschaften "de:blühende Landschaften")] ("flowering landscapes") with some cynics pointing out that former industrial sites were indeed turning into flowering meadows in the course of [ecological succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecological_succession "Ecological succession") as a consequence of deindustrialisation.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-125)[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-126)

Kohl was a true "people person" and loved to be in the company of others. His tremendous memory of people and their lives helped him to build up his networks in the [Christian Democratic Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Democratic_Union_of_Germany "Christian Democratic Union of Germany"), in government and abroad. In a study of German chancellorship as political leadership, Henrik Gast highlights how much time Kohl invested in personal relationships, even with the backbenchers in the [Bundestag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bundestag "Bundestag") and also party officials up to the local level. This worked because it fitted Kohl's character and was authentic.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-127)

Kohl knew that all these people were the basis of his political power and that he needed their loyalty and personal affection. He could also be rude to subordinates and assistants and confront political adversaries. "He was capable of both – being empathetic and being extremely confrontational! If you did not do what he wanted, empathy was over!", as Gast quotes a federal minister of Kohl's own party. There was also a difference between the younger Kohl and the chancellor in his later years. A parliamentary state secretary recalled: "A sense of tact and politeness? The early and the later Kohl – that was a tremendous difference. In the early years, he had all of that, in the later years no more."[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Kohl#cite_note-128)
