#### Social programs and spending

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierre_Trudeau&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Social programs and spending")]

In 1971, Trudeau's government greatly expanded [unemployment insurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unemployment_insurance "Unemployment insurance"), making coverage nearly universal as coverage for the Canadian labour force jumped to 96 percent from 75 percent. The system was sometimes called the 8/42, because one had to work for eight weeks (with at least 20 hours per week), and wait two weeks, to get benefits for the other 42 weeks of the year. This expansion also opened the UI program up to maternity, sickness, and retirement benefits, covered seasonal workers for the first time, and allowed mothers to receive up to 15 weeks of benefits if they had 20 or more insurable weeks. The reforms increased the maximum benefit period to 50 weeks, though the benefit duration was calculated using a complex formula depending on labour force participation and the regional and national unemployment rates.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-88)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-89)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-CanadianLabourUI-90)[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-WelfareCanadianEncyclopedia-91) In 1977, the government simplified the benefit duration formula but introduced a variable entrance requirement dependent on the unemployment rate in the applicant's region; the changes also mandated that workers in areas with low unemployment regions work twice as long to be eligible for benefits as workers in high unemployment regions.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-CanadianLabourUI-90)

In 1973, Trudeau's government amended the _[National Housing Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National\_Housing\_Act\_(Canada) "National Housing Act (Canada)")_ to provide financial assistance for [new home buying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-time_home_buyer_grant "First-time home buyer grant"), loans for [co-operative housing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Co-operative_housing "Co-operative housing"), and low interest loans for municipal and private non-profit housing.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-:2-92) The amendments saw the introduction the Rental Rehabilitation Assistance Program, which established that homeowners and occupants in low-income neighbourhoods could qualify for small grants to be used for home repair. Also introduced was the Assisted Home Ownership Program which allowed the [Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_Mortgage_and_Housing_Corporation "Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation") (CMHC) to start providing grants and subsidized interest rates to low income families (though in 1978 an amendment discontinued the provision of grant money to these families, which led to a high incidence of defaults, and in turn, necessitated that the federal government provide financial assistance to the CMHC). The amendments saw the passage of the _Rent Supplement Act_, which enabled the CMHC to partner with private landlords, cooperatives, and not-for-profit associations to provide affordable housing; in addition, the act saw the CMHC agree to fund the difference between market rental prices and rent prices geared to the specific occupant's income. Lastly, the Canada Rental Supply Program was introduced to provide interest-free loans for 15 years to developers who agreed to allocate a proportion of units toward social housing initiatives. In order to ensure that loans contributed to the provision of low income housing, the CMHC was restricted to giving loans amounting to $7,500 or less per unit.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-:1-93)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-:7-94)

Legislation passed in November 1968 widened eligibility for farm credit,[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-95) and in 1970 legislation was introduced aimed at improving compensation for merchant seamen and also to establish a right to maternity leave.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-96) In 1972, an Act was passed providing for the indexation of various pensions and allowances to the consumer price index. Certain eligibility requirements for receiving training allowances were also removed.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-97) One-pensioner couples benefited from a new Spouse's Allowance,[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-98) while various improvements in superannuation arrangements[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-99) and in family allowances were also carried out.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-100)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-101)

The [registered home ownership savings plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Registered_home_ownership_savings_plan "Registered home ownership savings plan") (RHOSP) was introduced in the government's [November 1974 budget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/November_1974_Canadian_federal_budget "November 1974 Canadian federal budget"). Similar to [RRSPs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Registered_retirement_savings_plan "Registered retirement savings plan"), proceeds from the RHOSP could be received tax-free for either.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-BG574-102) a down payment for the acquisition of an owner-occupied dwelling or to buy furnitures for the dwelling (or the spouse's dwelling).[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-103) Individuals who already owned a home (either owner-occupied or rented to another person) could not deduct RHOSP contributions.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-104)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-105) In 1976, Trudeau's government allowed for transfers of funds between the RHOSP (for instance to select a plan with better returns).[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-106)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTES.C._1976-77,_ch._4s_57-107) In 1977, the government tightened the rules of the RHOSP (the reforms removed the purchase of furnitures from the list of usage allowed for tax-free use of RHOSP proceeds starting in 1978;[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTES.C._1977,_ch._1s_73(3),_73(14)-108) disallowed deductible contributions for a taxpayer whose spouse owned a home;[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTES.C._1977,_ch._1s_73(1)-109) suspended tax-free rollover of RHSOP funds to an RRSP; and capped the lifetime of the RHOSP at 20 years).[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTES.C._1977,_ch._1s_73(5)-110)

In 1977, Trudeau's government established the financial program [Established Programs Financing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Established_Programs_Financing "Established Programs Financing") to help finance the [provincially](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provinces_of_Canada "Provinces of Canada")-run [healthcare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Healthcare_in_Canada "Healthcare in Canada") and post-secondary education system, through [transfer payments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transfer_payments "Transfer payments"), by [cash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cash "Cash") and [tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax "Tax")[points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basis_point "Basis point"). This system lasted until 1995.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-WelfareCanadianEncyclopedia-91)[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-111)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-DF94-112)

In 1979, Trudeau's government restructured [family allowances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_Allowance_Act "Family Allowance Act") by increasing the role of the tax system in child support and decreasing the role of family allowances. The government established an annual Refundable Child Tax Credit of $200 for families with incomes of $18,000 or less. As incomes increased above this level, benefits would be taxed away to disappear completely at $26,000. Since the median income for families during this time was $19,500, the majority of families received some benefit from the new program.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-113)

#### Taxation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierre_Trudeau&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Taxation")]

In 1969, Trudeau's first [finance minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_Finance_(Canada) "Minister of Finance (Canada)"), [Edgar Benson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Benson "Edgar Benson"), introduced a white paper on tax reform which included [tax deductions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_deduction "Tax deduction") for [child care](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_care "Child care") and advocated shifting the tax burden from the poor to the wealthy. Measures to fulfill the latter proposal included a [capital gains tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_gains_tax "Capital gains tax"), which was severely criticized by corporate Canada and the business community (notably [Israel Asper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_Asper "Israel Asper")). The bill was debated in Parliament for over a year, with its more radical proposals being removed in parliamentary committee. The reforms managed to be passed through the use of [closure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloture "Cloture"), with the capital gains tax (that had an inclusion rate of 50 percent) coming into effect on January 1, 1972, as prescribed by the [1971 budget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1971_Canadian_federal_budget "1971 Canadian federal budget").[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-Bensonglobeandmail-114)[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-115)[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-:LeaderPost-116) Also implemented in 1972 was the child care expense deduction which allowed for a deduction of up to $500 per child.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-117) As Benson had now become a political liability, Trudeau replaced him with [John Turner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner "John Turner") (who was seen as a "[Business Liberal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Grit "Blue Grit")") in 1972.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-Bensonglobeandmail-114)[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-118)

In 1973, Trudeau's government fully indexed the [person income tax system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Income_tax_in_Canada "Income tax in Canada") (both the exemptions and the brackets) to match inflation. The indexation was made effective in 1974; during that year, inflation had jumped from six percent to double digits.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-119) The government also implemented three personal income tax cuts from 1973 to 1975.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTECohenGranatstein1998238%E2%80%93239-120)

#### Inflation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierre_Trudeau&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Inflation")]

While popular with the electorate, Trudeau's promised minor reforms had little effect on the growing rate of inflation, and he struggled with conflicting advice on the crisis.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2009246-121) In September 1975, [finance minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_Finance_(Canada) "Minister of Finance (Canada)") John Turner resigned over refusing to implement [wage and price controls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wage_and_price_controls "Wage and price controls").[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-122) In December 1975, in an embarrassing about-face, Trudeau and new finance minister [Donald Macdonald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Stovel_Macdonald "Donald Stovel Macdonald") introduced wage and price controls by passing the _[Anti-Inflation Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Inflation\_Act "Anti-Inflation Act")_, despite campaigning against them in the 1974 election. Amongst its many controls, it limited pay increases for federal government employees and employees in companies with over 500 workers to 10 percent in 1976, 8 percent in 1977, and 6 percent in 1978. The Act also established the anti-inflation board which oversaw the implementation of wage and price controls and had the ability to recommend decreases in prices of goods, wage cuts, and rebates to customers of various services.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-Wageandpricecontrols-123) The breadth of the legislation, which touched on many powers traditionally considered the purview of the provinces, prompted [a Supreme Court reference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reference_re_Anti-Inflation_Act "Reference re Anti-Inflation Act") that only upheld the legislation as an [emergency requiring Federal intervention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace,_Order,_and_Good_Government "Peace, Order, and Good Government") under the _[British North America Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British\_North\_America\_Act "British North America Act")_. During the annual 1975 Christmas interview with [CTV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CTV_Television_Network "CTV Television Network"), Trudeau discussed the economy, citing market failures and stating that more state intervention would be necessary. However, the academic wording and hypothetical solutions posed during the complex discussion led much of the public to believe he had declared capitalism itself a failure, creating a lasting distrust among increasingly [neoliberal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoliberalism "Neoliberalism") business leaders.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2009290%E2%80%9394-124) The controls lasted until 1978 and the anti-inflation board was dissolved in 1979.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-Wageandpricecontrols-123)

#### Energy policy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierre_Trudeau&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Energy policy")]

On September 4, 1973, Trudeau requested that the [Western Canadian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Canadian "Western Canadian") provinces agree to a voluntary freeze on oil prices during [the ongoing Arab oil embargo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_oil_crisis "1973 oil crisis"). Nine days later, the Trudeau government imposed a 40-cent tax on every barrel of [Canadian oil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petroleum_industry_in_Canada "Petroleum industry in Canada") exported to the United States to combat rising inflation and oil prices. The tax was equivalent to the difference between domestic and international oil prices, and the revenues were used to subsidize oil imports for [Eastern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Canada "Eastern Canada")[refiners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil_refinery "Oil refinery"). The [Premier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premier_of_Alberta "Premier of Alberta") of oil-rich [Alberta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alberta "Alberta"), [Peter Lougheed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Lougheed "Peter Lougheed"), called the decision "the most discriminatory action taken by a federal government against a particular province in the entire history of [Confederation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Confederation "Canadian Confederation")." While revenues decreased for Western provinces (particularly Alberta) and for the petroleum industry, Trudeau's government subsidized Eastern consumers, angering Alberta, who successfully fought for control of its natural resources in 1930.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-125)

In the early 1970s, the [petroleum industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petroleum_industry "Petroleum industry") was largely under foreign (mainly American) control, the recent discovery of oil in [Alaska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska "Alaska") put corporate pressure on the [Canadian Arctic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arctic_Archipelago "Arctic Archipelago"), and Canada's energy sector increasingly focused on North American rather than domestic needs. Trudeau's government initially rejected the idea of creating a nationalized oil company (which was perceived to secure supplies, improve revenue collection, and give governments better information on the global energy market), arguing it would be costly and inefficient. However, after the [late 1973 oil crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_oil_crisis "1973 oil crisis") saw global oil prices quadruple, questions arose about whether Canada should continue importing oil. Though Canada also exported oil at times, the provinces of Quebec and Atlantic Canada were at risk of a cut-off of imports; as a result, Canada was in need of knowing more about its potential to produce energy. In late October 1973, Trudeau's government adopted a motion from the [New Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Democratic_Party "New Democratic Party") (which the Trudeau [minority government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minority_government "Minority government") relied on for support) to establish a nationalized oil company. The _Petro-Canada Act_ was passed in 1975 (under a Trudeau [majority government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majority_government "Majority government")), resulting in the creation of a new [crown corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_corporations_of_Canada "Crown corporations of Canada"), [Petro-Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petro-Canada "Petro-Canada"). Petro-Canada was mandated to acquire imported oil supplies, take part in energy research and development, and engage in downstream activities such as refining and marketing. The corporation started with an initial $1.5 billion in capital and had preferential access to debt capital as "an agent of Her Majesty". Trudeau's government gave itself authority over Petro-Canada's capital budget and its corporate strategy, making the company its policy arm; the government also wanted the company to be mainly active on the frontiers (the oil sands, the Arctic, and the East Coast offshore areas) rather than Western Canada, where most Canadian oil is extracted. In 1976, Trudeau appointed his friend, [Maurice Strong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Strong "Maurice Strong"), to become the first chair of the company.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-126)

**Joseph Philippe Pierre Yves Elliott Trudeau**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-1) (October 18, 1919– September 28, 2000) was a Canadian politician, lawyer, jurist, academic, author, and journalist who served as the 15th [prime minister of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_minister_of_Canada "Prime minister of Canada") from 1968 to 1979 and from 1980 to 1984. Between his non-consecutive terms as prime minister from 1979 to 1980, he served as the [leader of the Opposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Opposition_(Canada) "Leader of the Opposition (Canada)"). He [led the Liberal Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Liberal_Party_of_Canada "Leader of the Liberal Party of Canada") from 1968 until 1984.

Trudeau was born and raised in [Outremont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outremont "Outremont"), Quebec, and studied politics and law. In 1950, he co-founded _[Cité Libre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cit%C3%A9\_Libre "Cité Libre")_ and rose to prominence as a labour activist in Quebec politics by opposing the conservative [Union Nationale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Nationale_(Quebec) "Union Nationale (Quebec)") government. Trudeau was also an associate professor of law at the [Université de Montréal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universit%C3%A9_de_Montr%C3%A9al "Université de Montréal"). He was originally part of the social democratic [New Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Democratic_Party "New Democratic Party") (NDP), but then joined the [Liberal Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Party_of_Canada "Liberal Party of Canada") in 1965 on the belief that the NDP could not achieve power. In the election [that year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1965_Canadian_federal_election "1965 Canadian federal election"), he was elected to the [House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_Canada "House of Commons of Canada"), and was quickly appointed as prime minister [Lester B. Pearson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lester_B._Pearson "Lester B. Pearson")'s [parliamentary secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_secretary "Parliamentary secretary"). Trudeau was [minister of justice and attorney general](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_Justice_and_Attorney_General_of_Canada "Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada") from 1967 to 1968, during which time he liberalized [divorce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divorce "Divorce") and [abortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion_in_Canada "Abortion in Canada") laws and decriminalized [homosexuality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBTQ_people_in_Canada "LGBTQ people in Canada"). His outgoing personality and charisma caused a sensation, termed "[Trudeaumania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trudeaumania "Trudeaumania")", which helped him win the [leadership of the Liberal Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Liberal_Party_of_Canada "Leader of the Liberal Party of Canada") in [1968](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_Liberal_Party_of_Canada_leadership_election "1968 Liberal Party of Canada leadership election"). He then succeeded Pearson and became prime minister of Canada.

From the late 1960s until the mid-1980s, Trudeau dominated the Canadian political scene. After his appointment as prime minister, he led the Liberals to victory in the [1968](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_Canadian_federal_election "1968 Canadian federal election"), [1972](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Canadian_federal_election "1972 Canadian federal election"), and [1974](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_Canadian_federal_election "1974 Canadian federal election") federal elections, before narrowly losing in [1979](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1979_Canadian_federal_election "1979 Canadian federal election"). He won a fourth election victory shortly afterwards, in [1980](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Canadian_federal_election "1980 Canadian federal election"). Trudeau is the most recent prime minister to win four federal elections (having won three [majority governments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majority_government "Majority government") and one [minority government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minority_government "Minority government")) and to serve non-consecutive terms. His tenure of 15 years and 164 days makes him the [third longest-serving prime minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Prime_Ministers_of_Canada_by_time_in_office "List of Prime Ministers of Canada by time in office") in Canadian history, behind [John A. Macdonald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_A._Macdonald "John A. Macdonald") and [William Lyon Mackenzie King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Lyon_Mackenzie_King "William Lyon Mackenzie King").

[As prime minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premierships_of_Pierre_Trudeau "Premierships of Pierre Trudeau"), Trudeau pioneered [official bilingualism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_bilingualism_in_Canada "Official bilingualism in Canada") and [multiculturalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiculturalism_in_Canada "Multiculturalism in Canada"). Amid the [Quebec sovereignty movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec_sovereignty_movement "Quebec sovereignty movement"), he invoked the _[War Measures Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War\_Measures\_Act "War Measures Act")_ in response to the 1970 [October Crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_Crisis "October Crisis") and later led the federalist campaign to victory in the [1980 Quebec sovereignty-association referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Quebec_referendum "1980 Quebec referendum"). In economic policy, he introduced the [capital gains tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_gains_tax "Capital gains tax"), expanded [social programs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_programs_in_Canada "Social programs in Canada"), sharply increased [deficit spending](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deficit_spending "Deficit spending"), and responded to the [1970s recession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973%E2%80%931975_recession "1973–1975 recession") through [wage and price controls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Inflation_Act "Anti-Inflation Act"). In a bid to move the Liberal Party towards [economic nationalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_nationalism "Economic nationalism"), Trudeau established [Petro-Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petro-Canada "Petro-Canada") and launched the [National Energy Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Energy_Program "National Energy Program"), both of which generated significant controversy in [oil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petroleum_industry_in_Canada "Petroleum industry in Canada")-rich [Western Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Canada "Western Canada") and led to a rise in what was called "[Western alienation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_alienation "Western alienation")". Trudeau's government also [converted Canada to the metric system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metrication_in_Canada "Metrication in Canada"), created [Via Rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Via_Rail "Via Rail"), and enacted the _[Access to Information Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Access\_to\_Information\_Act "Access to Information Act")_ and the _[Canada Health Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada\_Health\_Act "Canada Health Act")_. In foreign policy, Trudeau reduced alignment [with the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada%E2%80%93United_States_relations "Canada–United States relations"), maintained cordial relations [with the Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada%E2%80%93Soviet_Union_relations "Canada–Soviet Union relations"), and developed strong ties [with China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada%E2%80%93China_relations "Canada–China relations") and Cuban leader [Fidel Castro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fidel_Castro "Fidel Castro"), which put him at odds with other [Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_world "Western world")[capitalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitalist "Capitalist") states. He also oversaw Canada's entry into the [G7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G7 "G7") forum. In 1982, Trudeau [patriated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriated "Patriated") the [Constitution of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Canada "Constitution of Canada") and established the _[Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian\_Charter\_of\_Rights\_and\_Freedoms "Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms")_ with the _[Constitution Act, 1982](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution\_Act,\_1982 "Constitution Act, 1982")_, which achieved full [Canadian sovereignty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_sovereignty "Canadian sovereignty").

Trudeau retired from politics shortly before the [1984 federal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Canadian_federal_election "1984 Canadian federal election"). In his retirement, he practised law at the [Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal "Montreal") law firm of [Heenan Blaikie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heenan_Blaikie "Heenan Blaikie"). He also spoke out against the [Meech Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meech_Lake_Accord "Meech Lake Accord") and [Charlottetown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlottetown_Accord "Charlottetown Accord") accords (which proposed granting Quebec certain concessions), arguing they would strengthen [Quebec nationalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec_nationalism "Quebec nationalism"). Trudeau [died](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_and_state_funeral_of_Pierre_Trudeau "Death and state funeral of Pierre Trudeau") in 2000, aged 80. He is ranked highly among scholars in [historical rankings of Canadian prime ministers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_rankings_of_prime_ministers_of_Canada "Historical rankings of prime ministers of Canada"), but remains a divisive figure in Canadian politics. Critics accused him of arrogance, economic mismanagement, and unduly centralizing Canadian decision-making to the detriment of the culture of Quebec and the economy of the [Prairies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Prairies "Canadian Prairies"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFortin_(2000-10-09)A17-2) while admirers praised what they considered to be the force of his intellect[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMallick_(2000-09-30)P04-3) and his political acumen which maintained national unity throughout the Quebec sovereignty movement. Trudeau's eldest son, [Justin Trudeau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justin_Trudeau "Justin Trudeau"), served as prime minister of Canada [from 2015 to 2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premiership_of_Justin_Trudeau "Premiership of Justin Trudeau"), and was the first prime minister to be the child of a previous prime minister.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierre_Trudeau&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

The Trudeau family can be traced to [Marcillac-Lanville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcillac-Lanville "Marcillac-Lanville") in France in the 16th century and to a Robert Truteau (1544–1589).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEG%C3%A9n%C3%A9alogie_du_Qu%C3%A9bec_(2012)-4)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-5) In 1659, the first Trudeau to arrive in Canada was [Étienne Trudeau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89tienne_Trudeau "Étienne Trudeau") or Truteau (1641–1712), a carpenter and home builder from [La Rochelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Rochelle "La Rochelle").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-6)

Pierre Trudeau was born at home in [Outremont, Quebec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outremont,_Quebec "Outremont, Quebec"), on October 18, 1919,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish20098-7) to [Charles-Émile "Charley" Trudeau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Trudeau_(businessman) "Charles Trudeau (businessman)") (1887–1935), a [French-Canadian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French-Canadian "French-Canadian") businessman and lawyer, and Grace Elliott, who was of mixed [Scottish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish-Canadian "Scottish-Canadian") and French-Canadian descent. He had an older sister named Suzette and a younger brother named Charles Jr.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-8) Trudeau remained close to both siblings for his entire life. Trudeau's paternal grandparents were French-speaking Quebec farmers.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-NYT_Kaufman_20000929_Eulogy-9) His father had acquired the B&A gas station chain (now defunct), some "profitable mines, the Belmont amusement park in Montreal and the [Montreal Royals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal_Royals "Montreal Royals"), the city's minor-league baseball team", by the time Trudeau was fifteen.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-NYT_Kaufman_20000929_Eulogy-9) When his father died in [Orlando, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orlando,_Florida "Orlando, Florida"), on April 10, 1935, Trudeau and each of his siblings inherited $5,000 (equivalent to $110,000 in 2025), a considerable sum at that time, which meant that he was financially secure and independent.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish200624-10) His mother, Grace, "doted on Pierre"[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish200625-11) and he remained close to her throughout her long life.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrudeau1993-12) After her husband died, she left the management of her inheritance to others and spent a lot of her time working for the [Roman Catholic Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Church "Roman Catholic Church") and various charities, travelling frequently to [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), Europe, and [Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine "Maine"), sometimes with her children.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish200625-11) Already in his late teens, Trudeau was "directly involved in managing a large inheritance".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish200625-11)

## Early education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierre_Trudeau&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early education")]

From the age of six until twelve, Trudeau attended the primary school Académie Querbes, in [Outremont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outremont "Outremont"), where he became immersed in the Catholic religion. The school, which was for both English and French Catholics, was an exclusive school with very small classes and he excelled in mathematics and religion.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish200625%E2%80%9327-13) From his earliest years, Trudeau was fluently bilingual, which would later prove to be a "big asset for a politician in bilingual Canada."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-economist_obituary_20001005-14) As a teenager, he attended the Jesuit [French-language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language")[Collège Jean-de-Brébeuf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coll%C3%A8ge_Jean-de-Br%C3%A9beuf "Collège Jean-de-Brébeuf"), a prestigious secondary school known for educating elite francophone families in [Quebec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec "Quebec").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish200627-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-16)

In his seventh and final academic year, 1939–1940, Trudeau focused on winning a [Rhodes Scholarship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodes_Scholarship "Rhodes Scholarship"). In his application, he wrote that he had prepared for public office by studying public speaking and publishing many articles in _Brébeuf_. His letters of recommendations praised him highly. Father Boulin, who was the head of the college, said that during Trudeau's seven years at the college (1933–1940), he had won a "hundred prizes and honourable mentions" and "performed with distinction in all fields".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish200665-17) Trudeau graduated from Collège Jean-de-Brébeuf in 1940 at the age of twenty-one.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish200647-18)

Trudeau did not win the Rhodes Scholarship. He consulted several people on his options, including [Henri Bourassa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Bourassa "Henri Bourassa"), the economist Edmond Montpetit, and Father Robert Bernier, a Franco-Manitoban. Following their advice, he chose a career in politics and a degree in law at the [Université de Montréal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universit%C3%A9_de_Montr%C3%A9al "Université de Montréal").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish200673-19)

## Second World War

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierre_Trudeau&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Second World War")]

In its obituary, _[The Economist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Economist "The Economist")_ described Trudeau as "parochial as a young man", who "dismissed" the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War") "as a squabble between the big powers, although he later regretted 'missing one of the major events of the century'."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-economist_obituary_20001005-14) In his 1993 _Memoir,_ Trudeau wrote that the outbreak of the Second World War in September 1939 and his father's death were the two "great bombshells" that marked his teenage years.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrudeau199337-20) In his first year at university, the prime topics of conversation were the [Battle of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_France "Battle of France"), the [Battle of Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Britain "Battle of Britain"), and the [London blitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Blitz "The Blitz").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrudeau199332-21) He wrote that in the early 1940s, when he was in his early twenties, he thought, "So there was a war? Tough. It wouldn't stop me from concentrating on my studies so long as that was possible...[I]f you were a French Canadian in Montreal [at that time], you did not automatically believe that this was a just war. In Montreal in the early 1940s, we still knew nothing about the [Holocaust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holocaust "Holocaust") and we tended to think of this war as a settling of scores among the superpowers."[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrudeau199332-21)

Young Trudeau opposed [conscription](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conscription "Conscription") for overseas service,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrudeau199332-21) and in 1942 he campaigned for the anti-conscription candidate [Jean Drapeau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Drapeau "Jean Drapeau") (later the [mayor of Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_Montreal "Mayor of Montreal")) in [Outremont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outremont_(electoral_district) "Outremont (electoral district)").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrudeau199334-22) Trudeau described a speech he heard in Montreal by [Ernest Lapointe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Lapointe "Ernest Lapointe"),[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrudeau199332%E2%80%9335-23) minister of justice and Prime Minister [William Lyon Mackenzie King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Lyon_Mackenzie_King "William Lyon Mackenzie King")'s [Quebec lieutenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec_lieutenant "Quebec lieutenant"). Lapointe had been a Liberal MP during the 1917 [Conscription Crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conscription_Crisis_of_1917 "Conscription Crisis of 1917"), in which the Canadian government had deployed up to 1,200 soldiers to suppress the anti-conscription Easter Riots in [Quebec City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec_City "Quebec City") in March and April 1918. In a final and bloody conflict, armed rioters fired on the troops, and the soldiers returned fire. At least five men were killed by gunfire and there were over 150 casualties and $300,000 in damage.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-CHR_Auger_2008-24):504[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-Granastein_1977-25):60 In 1939, it was Lapointe who helped draft the Liberals' policy against conscription for service overseas. Lapointe was aware that a new conscription crisis would destroy the national unity that Mackenzie King had been trying to build since the end of the [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_World_War "First World War").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-Betcherman_2002-26) Trudeau believed Lapointe had lied and broken his promise. His criticisms of King's wartime policies, such as "suspension of habeas corpus", the "farce of bilingualism and French-Canadian advancement in the army," and the "forced 'voluntary' enrolment", were scathing.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2006191-27)

As a university student, Trudeau joined the [Canadian Officers' Training Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Officers'_Training_Corps "Canadian Officers' Training Corps") (COTC), which trained at the local armoury in Montreal during the school term and undertook further training at Camp Farnham each summer.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrudeau199334-22) Although the _[National Resources Mobilization Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National\_Resources\_Mobilization\_Act "National Resources Mobilization Act")_, enacted in 1940, originally provided that conscripts could not be required to serve outside of Canada,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-28) Parliament amended the act and removed that restriction in 1942.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-29) The [Conscription Crisis of 1944](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conscription_Crisis_of_1944 "Conscription Crisis of 1944") arose in response to the [Allied invasion of Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Overlord "Operation Overlord") in June 1944.

## Education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierre_Trudeau&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Education")]

Trudeau continued his full-time studies in law at the Université de Montréal while in the COTC from 1940 until his graduation in 1943. Following his graduation, he [articled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Articled_clerk "Articled clerk") for a year and, in late 1944, began his master's degree in [political economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_economy "Political economy") at [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University")'s Graduate School of Public Administration (now the [John F. Kennedy School of Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy_School_of_Government "John F. Kennedy School of Government")). In his _Memoir_, he admitted that it was at Harvard's "super-informed environment" that he realized the "historic importance" of the war and that he had "missed one of the major events of the century in which [he] was living.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrudeau199337-20) Harvard had become a major intellectual centre, as fascism in Europe led to a great migration of intellectuals to the United States.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2006124-30)

Trudeau's Harvard dissertation was on the topic of communism and Christianity.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2006146-31) At Harvard, an American and predominantly Protestant university, Trudeau, a French Canadian Catholic living outside the province of Quebec for the first time, felt like an outsider.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2006134-32) As his sense of isolation deepened,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2006137-33) he decided in 1947 to continue his work on his Harvard dissertation in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris"),[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2006141-34) where he studied at the [Institut d'Études Politiques de Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institut_d'%C3%89tudes_Politiques_de_Paris "Institut d'Études Politiques de Paris") (Sciences Po). The Harvard dissertation remained unfinished when Trudeau briefly entered a doctoral program to study under the socialist economist [Harold Laski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Laski "Harold Laski") at the [London School of Economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_School_of_Economics "London School of Economics") (LSE).[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2006166-35) This cemented Trudeau's belief that [Keynesian economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keynesian_economics "Keynesian economics") and social sciences were essential to the creation of the "good life" in a democratic society.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2006296-36) Over a five-week period he attended many lectures and became a follower of [personalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personalism "Personalism") after being influenced most notably by [Emmanuel Mounier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmanuel_Mounier "Emmanuel Mounier").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2006147-37) He also was influenced by [Nikolai Berdyaev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikolai_Berdyaev "Nikolai Berdyaev"), particularly his book _Slavery and Freedom_.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-NemniNemni2011-38)[Max](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Nemni "Max Nemni") and [Monique Nemni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monique_Nemni "Monique Nemni") argue that Berdyaev's book influenced Trudeau's rejection of nationalism and separatism.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-NemniNemni2011-38)

In mid 1948, Trudeau embarked on world travels to find a sense of purpose.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2006176-39) At the age of twenty-eight, he travelled to [Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poland "Poland") where he visited [Auschwitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auschwitz_concentration_camp "Auschwitz concentration camp"), then [Czechoslovakia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czechoslovakia "Czechoslovakia"), [Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria "Austria"), [Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary "Hungary"), [Yugoslavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Federal_Republic_of_Yugoslavia "Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia"), [Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria "Bulgaria"), and the [Middle East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_East "Middle East"), including [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey"), [Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan "Jordan") and southern [Iraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq "Iraq").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2006176%E2%80%93179-40) Although he was wealthy, Trudeau travelled with a backpack in "self-imposed hardship".[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-economist_obituary_20001005-14) He used his British passport instead of his Canadian passport in his travels through [Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan"), [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"), China, and [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan"), often wearing local clothing to blend in.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2006180%E2%80%93190-41) According to _The Economist_, when Trudeau returned to Canada in 1949 after an absence of five months, his mind was "seemingly broadened" from his studies at Harvard, Sciences Po, and the LSE, as well as his travels. He was "appalled at the narrow nationalism in his native French-speaking Quebec, and the authoritarianism of the province's government".[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-economist_obituary_20001005-14)

## Quiet Revolution

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierre_Trudeau&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Quiet Revolution")]

Main article: [Quiet Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quiet_Revolution "Quiet Revolution")

Beginning while Trudeau was travelling overseas, several events took place in Quebec that were precursors to the [Quiet Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quiet_Revolution "Quiet Revolution"). These included the 1948 release of the anti-establishment manifesto [Refus global](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refus_global "Refus global"), the publication of _[Les insolences du Frère Untel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les\_insolences\_du\_Fr%C3%A8re\_Untel "Les insolences du Frère Untel")_, the 1949 [Asbestos Strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asbestos_Strike "Asbestos Strike"), and the 1955 [Richard Riot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Riot "Richard Riot"). Artists and intellectuals in Quebec signed the _Refus global_ on August 9, 1948, in opposition to the repressive rule of Quebec [Premier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premier_of_Quebec "Premier of Quebec")[Maurice Duplessis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Duplessis "Maurice Duplessis") and the decadent "social establishment" in Quebec, including the Catholic Church.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-Borduas_19480809-42)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-Ellenwood_200910-43) When he returned to Montreal in 1949, Trudeau quickly became a leading figure opposing Duplessis's rule. He actively supported the workers in the [Asbestos strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asbestos_strike "Asbestos strike") which opposed Duplessis in 1949. Trudeau was the co-founder and editor of _[Cité Libre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cit%C3%A9\_Libre "Cité Libre")_, a dissident journal that helped provide the intellectual basis for the Quiet Revolution. In 1956, he edited an important book on the subject, _La grève de l'amiante_, which argued that the asbestos miners' strike of 1949 was a seminal event in Quebec's history, marking the beginning of resistance to the conservative, [Francophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francophone "Francophone") clerical establishment and [Anglophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language") business class that had long ruled the province.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2006289%E2%80%93292-44)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierre_Trudeau&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Career")]

Because of Trudeau's labour union activities in Asbestos, Duplessis blacklisted him, and he was unable to teach law at the Université de Montréal.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-economist_obituary_20001005-14) He surprised his closest friends in Quebec when he became a civil servant in [Ottawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa "Ottawa") in 1949. Until 1951, he worked in the [Privy Council Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privy_Council_Office_(Canada) "Privy Council Office (Canada)") of the Liberal prime minister [Louis St. Laurent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_St._Laurent "Louis St. Laurent") as an economic policy advisor. He wrote in his memoirs that he found this period very useful when he entered politics later on, and that senior civil servant [Norman Robertson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Robertson "Norman Robertson") tried unsuccessfully to persuade him to stay on.

Trudeau's progressive values and his close ties with [Co-operative Commonwealth Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Co-operative_Commonwealth_Federation "Co-operative Commonwealth Federation") (CCF) intellectuals (including [F. R. Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F._R._Scott "F. R. Scott"), [Eugene Forsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugene_Forsey "Eugene Forsey"), [Michael Kelway Oliver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Kelway_Oliver "Michael Kelway Oliver") and [Charles Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Taylor_(philosopher) "Charles Taylor (philosopher)")) led to his support of and membership in the party throughout the 1950s.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2006364-45)

An associate professor of law at the Université de Montréal from 1961 to 1965, Trudeau's views evolved towards a liberal position in favour of individual rights counter to the state and made him an opponent of Quebec nationalism. He admired labour unions, which were tied to the [Cooperative Commonwealth Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooperative_Commonwealth_Federation "Cooperative Commonwealth Federation") (CCF), and tried to infuse his Liberal Party with some of their reformist zeal. By the late 1950s, Trudeau began to reject social democratic and labour parties, arguing that they should put their narrow goals aside and join forces with Liberals to fight for democracy first.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-46) In economic theory, he was influenced by professors [Joseph Schumpeter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Schumpeter "Joseph Schumpeter") and [John Kenneth Galbraith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kenneth_Galbraith "John Kenneth Galbraith") while he was at Harvard. In 1963, Trudeau criticized the Liberal Party of [Lester B. Pearson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lester_B._Pearson "Lester B. Pearson") when it supported arming [Bomarc missiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_CIM-10_Bomarc "Boeing CIM-10 Bomarc") in Canada with [nuclear warheads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapon "Nuclear weapon").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2006183%E2%80%93185-47)

During his time as a professor at the Université de Montréal, he was featured in [Denis Héroux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denis_H%C3%A9roux "Denis Héroux")'s 1964 student film _[Over My Head](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Over\_My\_Head\_(film) "Over My Head (film)") (Jusqu'au cou)_, appearing as himself in a political debate.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-48)

Trudeau was offered a position at [Queen's University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen's_University_at_Kingston "Queen's University at Kingston") teaching political science by [James Corry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Corry_(academic) "James Corry (academic)"), who later became Principal of Queen's, but turned it down because he preferred to teach in Quebec.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrudeau199363%E2%80%9364-49)

## Early political career (1965–1967)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierre_Trudeau&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Early political career (1965–1967)")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3c/Trudeau_Nomination.jpg/250px-Trudeau_Nomination.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Trudeau_Nomination.jpg)

Trudeau after being nominated to represent the riding of Mount Royal, June 6, 1965

See also: [Electoral history of Pierre Trudeau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_history_of_Pierre_Trudeau "Electoral history of Pierre Trudeau")

In 1965, Trudeau joined the Liberal Party, along with his friends [Gérard Pelletier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%A9rard_Pelletier "Gérard Pelletier") and [Jean Marchand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Marchand "Jean Marchand"). Dubbed the "three wise men" by the media, they ran successfully for the Liberals in the [1965 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1965_Canadian_federal_election "1965 Canadian federal election"). Trudeau himself was elected in the safe Liberal riding of [Mount Royal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Royal_(electoral_district) "Mount Royal (electoral district)") in Montreal. He would hold this seat until his retirement from politics in 1984, winning each election with large majorities. His decision to join the Liberals rather than the CCF's successor, the [New Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Democratic_Party_(Canada) "New Democratic Party (Canada)") (NDP), was partly based on his belief that the federal NDP could not achieve power. He also doubted the feasibility of the NDP's centralizing policies and felt that the party leadership tended toward a "_deux nations_" approach he could not support.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2006364%E2%80%93365-50)

Upon arrival in Ottawa, Trudeau was appointed as [parliamentary secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_secretary "Parliamentary secretary") to Prime Minister Lester B. Pearson and spent much of the next year travelling abroad, representing Canada at international meetings and bodies, including the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations"). In 1967, he was appointed to Pearson's [Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_Canada "Cabinet of Canada") as [Minister of Justice and Attorney General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_Justice_and_Attorney_General_of_Canada "Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrudeau1993?-51)

## Minister of Justice and Attorney General (1967–1968)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierre_Trudeau&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Minister of Justice and Attorney General (1967–1968)")]

![Image 8: Spoken Wikipedia icon](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg/60px-Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/1/1a/Trudeau%2C_Turner%2C_Chretien%2C_and_Pearson.jpg/250px-Trudeau%2C_Turner%2C_Chretien%2C_and_Pearson.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Trudeau,_Turner,_Chretien,_and_Pearson.jpg)
