Pearson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lester_B._Pearson "Lester B. Pearson"), in 1967

As Justice Minister and Attorney General, Trudeau was responsible for introducing the landmark _[Criminal Law Amendment Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criminal\_Law\_Amendment\_Act,\_1968%E2%80%9369 "Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968–69")_, an [omnibus bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omnibus_bill "Omnibus bill") whose provisions included, among other things, the decriminalization of homosexual acts between consenting adults, new gun ownership restrictions and the legalization of contraception, abortion and lotteries, as well as the authorization of [breathalyzer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breathalyzer "Breathalyzer") tests on suspected drunk drivers. Trudeau famously defended the segment of the bill decriminalizing homosexual acts by telling reporters that "there's no place for the state in the bedrooms of the nation", adding that "what's done in private between adults doesn't concern the [Criminal Code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criminal_Code_(Canada) "Criminal Code (Canada)")".[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTECBC_News_(1967-12-21)-52) Trudeau paraphrased the term from [Martin O'Malley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_O'Malley_(journalist) "Martin O'Malley (journalist)")'s editorial piece in _[The Globe and Mail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Globe\_and\_Mail "The Globe and Mail")_ on December 12, 1967.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTECBC_News_(1967-12-21)-52)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEO'Malley_(1967-12-12)6-53) Trudeau also liberalized divorce laws, and clashed with Quebec Premier [Daniel Johnson, Sr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Johnson,_Sr. "Daniel Johnson, Sr.") during constitutional negotiations.

### Liberal leadership convention (1968)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierre_Trudeau&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Liberal leadership convention (1968)")]

Further information: [1968 Liberal Party of Canada leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_Liberal_Party_of_Canada_leadership_election "1968 Liberal Party of Canada leadership election")

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/d/db/Trudeau_podium2.JPG/250px-Trudeau_podium2.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Trudeau_podium2.JPG)

Trudeau at the Liberal convention after winning the leadership

At the end of [Canada's centennial year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Centennial "Canadian Centennial") in 1967, Pearson announced his intention to step down, and Trudeau entered the race to succeed him as party leader and Prime Minister. His energetic campaign attracted widespread media attention and mobilized many young people, who saw Trudeau as a symbol of generational change. However, many Liberals still had reservations, given that he had only joined the party in 1965. During the convention, prominent Cabinet Minister [Judy LaMarsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judy_LaMarsh "Judy LaMarsh") was caught on television profanely stating that Trudeau was not a Liberal.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-Don't_let_the_bastard_win-54)

Nevertheless, at the April [1968 Liberal leadership convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_Liberal_Party_of_Canada_leadership_election "1968 Liberal Party of Canada leadership election"), Trudeau was elected leader on the fourth ballot, with the support of 51 percent of the delegates. He defeated several prominent and long-serving Liberals, including [Paul Martin Sr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Martin_Sr. "Paul Martin Sr."), [Robert Winters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Winters "Robert Winters") and [Paul Hellyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Hellyer "Paul Hellyer").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2006476%E2%80%93479-55)

## First premiership (1968–1979)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierre_Trudeau&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: First premiership (1968–1979)")]

Main article: [Premierships of Pierre Trudeau §First premiership (1968–1979)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premierships_of_Pierre_Trudeau#First_premiership_(1968%E2%80%931979) "Premierships of Pierre Trudeau")

### Swearing-in and subsequent election

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierre_Trudeau&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Swearing-in and subsequent election")]

As the new leader of the governing Liberals, Trudeau was sworn in as prime minister on April 20. He became the third [French Canadian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Canadian "French Canadian") prime minister of Canada after [Wilfrid Laurier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilfrid_Laurier "Wilfrid Laurier") and [Louis St. Laurent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_St._Laurent "Louis St. Laurent"). Although the term of the Parliament was not due to expire until November 1970, Pearson's government had almost fallen before the leadership contest could even take place after a tax bill was voted down in Parliament, leading to much confusion over whether this counted as a [matter of confidence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matter_of_Confidence "Matter of Confidence") in the government. [Governor General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_General_of_Canada "Governor General of Canada")[Roland Michener](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roland_Michener "Roland Michener") ultimately ruled that it did not, and the government subsequently won an actual confidence motion, but the incident made it clear that the minority government Trudeau had inherited would not realistically last the full parliamentary term, and that he would soon need to call an early election in order to win a parliamentary majority.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-56) Trudeau eventually called this election for June 25, 1968.

Trudeau's campaign benefited from an unprecedented wave of personal popularity called "[Trudeaumania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trudeaumania "Trudeaumania")",[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-Collison-57)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZink1972Backcover-58)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTECanada.com-59) which saw him mobbed by throngs of youths. His main national opponents were [PC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_Conservative_Party_of_Canada "Progressive Conservative Party of Canada") leader [Robert Stanfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Stanfield "Robert Stanfield") and [NDP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Democratic_Party_of_Canada "New Democratic Party of Canada") leader [Tommy Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommy_Douglas "Tommy Douglas"), both popular figures who had been premiers of [Nova Scotia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premier_of_Nova_Scotia "Premier of Nova Scotia") and [Saskatchewan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premier_of_Saskatchewan "Premier of Saskatchewan") respectively (albeit in Trudeau's native Quebec, the main competition to the Liberals was from the [Ralliement créditiste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralliement_cr%C3%A9ditiste "Ralliement créditiste"), led by [Réal Caouette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%A9al_Caouette "Réal Caouette")). As a candidate, Trudeau espoused [participatory democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Participatory_democracy "Participatory democracy") as a means of making Canada a "[Just Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just_Society "Just Society")". He vigorously defended the newly implemented [universal health care](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_health_care "Universal health care") and [regional development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_development "Regional development") programs, as well as the recent reforms found in the Omnibus bill.

On the eve of the election, during the annual [Saint-Jean-Baptiste Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Jean-Baptiste_Day "Saint-Jean-Baptiste Day") parade in Montreal, rioting [Quebec sovereigntists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec_separatism "Quebec separatism") threw rocks and bottles at the grandstand where Trudeau was seated, chanting "Trudeau au poteau!" ("Trudeau to the stake!"). Rejecting the pleas of aides that he take cover, Trudeau stayed in his seat, facing the rioters, without any sign of fear. The image of the defiant Prime Minister impressed the public. The next day, Trudeau handily won the [1968 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_Canadian_federal_election "1968 Canadian federal election") with a strong [majority government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majority_government "Majority government"); this was the Liberals' first majority since [1953](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1953_Canadian_federal_election "1953 Canadian federal election").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTECBC_News_(1968-06-24)-60)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMaclean's_Magazine_(1998-04-06)-61)

### Social policy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierre_Trudeau&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Social policy")]

#### Bilingualism and multiculturalism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierre_Trudeau&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Bilingualism and multiculturalism")]

Trudeau's first major legislative push was implementing the majority of recommendations from Pearson's [Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Commission_on_Bilingualism_and_Biculturalism "Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism") via the _[Official Languages Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official\_Languages\_Act\_(Canada) "Official Languages Act (Canada)")_, which made French and English the co-equal official languages of the federal government.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-62) More controversial than the declaration (which was backed by the NDP and, with some opposition in caucus, the PCs) was the implementation of the Act's principles: between 1966 and 1976, the francophone proportion of the civil service and military doubled, causing alarm in some sections of anglophone Canada who felt they were being disadvantaged.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2009141-63)

Trudeau's Cabinet fulfilled Part IV of the Royal Commission's report by announcing a "[Multiculturalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiculturalism "Multiculturalism") Policy" on October 8, 1971. It was the first of its kind in the world,[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2009142-64) subsequently being emulated by several provinces such as Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba; even other countries, most notably Australia, which has had a similar history and immigration pattern, emulated the policy. Beyond the specifics of the policy itself, this action signalled an openness to the world and coincided with a more open immigration policy that Pearson had brought in. The policy recognized that while Canada was a country of two official languages, it recognized a plurality of cultures – "a multicultural policy within a bilingual framework".[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2009145-65) This annoyed public opinion in Quebec, which believed that it challenged Quebec's claim of Canada being a country of two nations.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2009146-66)

#### Immigration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierre_Trudeau&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Immigration")]

During Pierre Trudeau's time as prime minister, [Canada's immigration levels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immigration_to_Canada "Immigration to Canada") were much lower and more stable, with total arrivals often in the tens of thousands annually. The period between 1968 and 1975 averaged over 165,000 newcomers annually, with a peak of 218,500 immigrants in 1974. Due to a weakening economy, the numbers declined, averaging around 114,000 newcomers from 1976 to 1984.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-67)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-Maclean's-Pierre_Trudeau-68) The government introduced official immigration quotas in the mid-1970s, with a target of 100,000 in 1979.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-Maclean's-Pierre_Trudeau-68)

Following the [Vietnam War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War"), a refugee crisis was caused by the flight of the [boat people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnamese_boat_people "Vietnamese boat people") from Vietnam, as thousands of people, mostly ethnic Chinese, fled the country in makeshift boats across the [South China Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_China_Sea "South China Sea"), usually to the [British colony of Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Hong_Kong "British Hong Kong"). The Trudeau government was generous in granting asylum to the refugees.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGranatsteinBothwell1991218-69) By 1980, Canada had accepted about 44,000 boat people, making it one of the top destinations for them.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGranatsteinBothwell1991219-70)

#### Indigenous issues

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierre_Trudeau&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Indigenous issues")]

Further information: [The Canadian Crown and Indigenous peoples of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Canadian_Crown_and_Indigenous_peoples_of_Canada "The Canadian Crown and Indigenous peoples of Canada")

In 1969, Trudeau, along with his then-[Minister of Indian Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_Crown%E2%80%93Indigenous_Relations "Minister of Crown–Indigenous Relations")[Jean Chrétien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Chr%C3%A9tien "Jean Chrétien"), proposed the [1969 White Paper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1969_White_Paper "1969 White Paper") (officially entitled "Statement of the Government of Canada on Indian policy"). The Paper proposed the general assimilation of First Nations into the Canadian body politic through the elimination of the _[Indian Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian\_Act "Indian Act")_ and Indian status, the parcelling of reserve land to private owners, and the elimination of the [Department of Indian and Northern Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown%E2%80%93Indigenous_Relations_and_Northern_Affairs_Canada "Crown–Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada"). The White Paper was widely seen as racist and an attack on Canada's indigenous peoples, and prompted the first major national mobilization of indigenous activists against the federal government's proposal, leading Trudeau to set aside the legislation.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-71)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-72)

#### Death penalty

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierre_Trudeau&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Death penalty")]

On July 14, 1976, after a long and emotional debate, Bill C-84 was passed by the House of Commons by a vote of 130 to 124, abolishing the [death penalty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_punishment_in_Canada "Capital punishment in Canada") for all criminal offences (other than military offences) and instituting a life sentence without parole for 25 years for first-degree murder.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-Radio_Canada-73)

### Quebec

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierre_Trudeau&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Quebec")]

#### October Crisis

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierre_Trudeau&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: October Crisis")]

Trudeau's first serious test as prime minister came during the [October Crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_Crisis "October Crisis") of 1970, when a Marxist-influenced Quebec separatist group, the [Front de libération du Québec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Front_de_lib%C3%A9ration_du_Qu%C3%A9bec "Front de libération du Québec") (FLQ), kidnapped British Trade Consul [James Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Cross "James Cross") at his residence on October 5. Five days later, the group also kidnapped Quebec Labour Minister [Pierre Laporte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Laporte "Pierre Laporte"). Trudeau, with the acquiescence of Quebec Premier [Robert Bourassa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Bourassa "Robert Bourassa"), responded by invoking the _[War Measures Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War\_Measures\_Act "War Measures Act")_, which gave the government sweeping powers of arrest and detention without trial. Trudeau presented a determined public stance during the crisis; when questioned by [CBC Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBC_Television "CBC Television") journalist [Tim Ralfe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Ralfe "Tim Ralfe") regarding how far he would go to stop the violence, Trudeau answered, "[Just watch me](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just_watch_me "Just watch me")". Laporte was found dead on October 17 in the trunk of a car. Five of the FLQ members were flown to [Cuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuba "Cuba") in 1970 as part of a deal in exchange for James Cross' life, although they eventually returned to Canada years later, where they served time in prison.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMunroe2012-74)

Although Trudeau's response is still controversial and was opposed at the time as excessive by parliamentarians like Tommy Douglas and [David Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Lewis_(Canadian_politician) "David Lewis (Canadian politician)"), it was met with only limited objections from the public.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJanigan_(1975-11-01)3-75)

#### Quebec provincial affairs

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierre_Trudeau&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Quebec provincial affairs")]

After consultations with the provincial premiers, Trudeau agreed to attend a conference called by [British Columbia Premier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premier_of_British_Columbia "Premier of British Columbia")[W. A. C. Bennett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._A._C._Bennett "W. A. C. Bennett") to attempt to finally [patriate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriation "Patriation") the [Canadian constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Canada "Constitution of Canada").[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2009135-76) Negotiations between the provinces and Justice Minister [John Turner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner "John Turner") created a draft agreement, known as the [Victoria Charter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Charter "Victoria Charter"), that entrenched a charter of rights, bilingualism, and a guarantee of a veto of constitutional amendments for Ontario and Quebec, as well as regional vetoes for [Western Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Canada "Western Canada") and [Atlantic Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Canada "Atlantic Canada"), within the new constitution.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2009135-76) The agreement was acceptable to the nine predominantly-English speaking provinces, but Quebec's premier Robert Bourassa requested two weeks to consult with his cabinet.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2009135-76) After a strong backlash of popular opinion against the agreement in Quebec, Bourassa stated that Quebec would not accept it.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2009136-77)

Trudeau faced increasing challenges in Quebec, starting with bitter relations with Bourassa and his [Quebec Liberal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec_Liberal_Party "Quebec Liberal Party") government. Following a rise in the polls after the rejection of the Victoria Charter, the Quebec Liberals had taken a more confrontational approach with the federal government on the constitution, [French language laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_22 "Bill 22"), and the language of [air traffic control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_traffic_control "Air traffic control") in Quebec.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2009302%E2%80%93306-78) Trudeau responded with increasing anger at what he saw as nationalist provocations against Ottawa's bilingualism and constitutional initiatives, at times expressing his personal contempt for Bourassa.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2009302%E2%80%93306-78)

Partially in an attempt to shore up his support, Bourassa called a [surprise election in 1976](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_Quebec_general_election "1976 Quebec general election") that resulted in [René Lévesque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_L%C3%A9vesque "René Lévesque") and the sovereigntist [Parti Québécois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parti_Qu%C3%A9b%C3%A9cois "Parti Québécois") (PQ) winning a majority government. The PQ had chiefly campaigned on a "good government" platform, but promised a referendum on independence to be held within their first mandate. Trudeau and Lévesque had been personal rivals, with Trudeau's intellectualism contrasting with Lévesque's more working-class image. While Trudeau claimed to welcome the "clarity" provided by the PQ victory, the unexpected rise of the [Quebec sovereignty movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec_sovereignty_movement "Quebec sovereignty movement") became, in his view, his biggest challenge.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2009308-79)

As the PQ began to take power, Trudeau faced the prolonged breakdown of his marriage, which the English-language press covered in lurid detail on a day-by-day basis. Trudeau's reserve was seen as dignified by contemporaries, and his poll numbers actually rose during the height of coverage,[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2009329-80) but aides felt the personal tensions left him uncharacteristically emotional and prone to outbursts.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2009327%E2%80%93328-81)

### Economic policy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierre_Trudeau&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Economic policy")]

Trudeau's first government implemented many procedural reforms to make Parliament and the Liberal caucus meetings run more efficiently, significantly expanded the size and role of the prime minister's office,[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrudeau199322%E2%80%9324-82) and substantially expanded social-welfare programs.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTELyonVan_Die2000137%E2%80%93144-83)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTELaxerLaxer197722%E2%80%9324-84)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-85)

#### Deficit spending

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierre_Trudeau&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Deficit spending")]

Trudeau's government ran large budget [deficits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deficit_spending "Deficit spending") throughout its time in office.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-86) The government's [first budget in 1968](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_Canadian_federal_budget "1968 Canadian federal budget") produced a deficit of $667 million, while the [1969 budget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1969_Canadian_federal_budget "1969 Canadian federal budget") produced a surplus of $140 million. However, the [1970 budget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1970_Canadian_federal_budget "1970 Canadian federal budget") (which produced a deficit of over $1 billion) marked the start of consecutive budget deficits run by the Trudeau government; the budget would not be [balanced](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balanced_budget "Balanced budget") until [1997](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_Canadian_federal_budget "1997 Canadian federal budget"). By the time Trudeau's first tenure ended in 1979, the deficit grew to $12 billion.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-:CBCgraph-87)

#### Social programs and spending

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierre_Trudeau&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Social programs and spending")]

In 1971, Trudeau's government greatly expanded [unemployment insurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unemployment_insurance "Unemployment insurance"), making coverage nearly universal as coverage for the Canadian labour force jumped to 96 percent from 75 percent. The system was sometimes called the 8/42, because one had to work for eight weeks (with at least 20 hours per week), and wait two weeks, to get benefits for the other 42 weeks of the year. This expansion also opened the UI program up to maternity, sickness, and retirement benefits, covered seasonal workers for the first time, and allowed mothers to receive up to 15 weeks of benefits if they had 20 or more insurable weeks. The reforms increased the maximum benefit period to 50 weeks, though the benefit duration was calculated using a complex formula depending on labour force participation and the regional and national unemployment rates.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-88)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-89)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-CanadianLabourUI-90)[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-WelfareCanadianEncyclopedia-91) In 1977, the government simplified the benefit duration formula but introduced a variable entrance requirement dependent on the unemployment rate in the applicant's region; the changes also mandated that workers in areas with low unemployment regions work twice as long to be eligible for benefits as workers in high unemployment regions.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-CanadianLabourUI-90)

In 1973, Trudeau's government amended the _[National Housing Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National\_Housing\_Act\_(Canada) "National Housing Act (Canada)")_ to provide financial assistance for [new home buying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-time_home_buyer_grant "First-time home buyer grant"), loans for [co-operative housing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Co-operative_housing "Co-operative housing"), and low interest loans for municipal and private non-profit housing.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-:2-92) The amendments saw the introduction the Rental Rehabilitation Assistance Program, which established that homeowners and occupants in low-income neighbourhoods could qualify for small grants to be used for home repair. Also introduced was the Assisted Home Ownership Program which allowed the [Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_Mortgage_and_Housing_Corporation "Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation") (CMHC) to start providing grants and subsidized interest rates to low income families (though in 1978 an amendment discontinued the provision of grant money to these families, which led to a high incidence of defaults, and in turn, necessitated that the federal government provide financial assistance to the CMHC). The amendments saw the passage of the _Rent Supplement Act_, which enabled the CMHC to partner with private landlords, cooperatives, and not-for-profit associations to provide affordable housing; in addition, the act saw the CMHC agree to fund the difference between market rental prices and rent prices geared to the specific occupant's income. Lastly, the Canada Rental Supply Program was introduced to provide interest-free loans for 15 years to developers who agreed to allocate a proportion of units toward social housing initiatives. In order to ensure that loans contributed to the provision of low income housing, the CMHC was restricted to giving loans amounting to $7,500 or less per unit.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-:1-93)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-:7-94)

Legislation passed in November 1968 widened eligibility for farm credit,[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-95) and in 1970 legislation was introduced aimed at improving compensation for merchant seamen and also to establish a right to maternity leave.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-96) In 1972, an Act was passed providing for the indexation of various pensions and allowances to the consumer price index. Certain eligibility requirements for receiving training allowances were also removed.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-97) One-pensioner couples benefited from a new Spouse's Allowance,[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-98) while various improvements in superannuation arrangements[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-99) and in family allowances were also carried out.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-100)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-101)

The [registered home ownership savings plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Registered_home_ownership_savings_plan "Registered home ownership savings plan") (RHOSP) was introduced in the government's [November 1974 budget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/November_1974_Canadian_federal_budget "November 1974 Canadian federal budget"). Similar to [RRSPs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Registered_retirement_savings_plan "Registered retirement savings plan"), proceeds from the RHOSP could be received tax-free for either.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-BG574-102) a down payment for the acquisition of an owner-occupied dwelling or to buy furnitures for the dwelling (or the spouse's dwelling).[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-103) Individuals who already owned a home (either owner-occupied or rented to another person) could not deduct RHOSP contributions.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-104)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-105) In 1976, Trudeau's government allowed for transfers of funds between the RHOSP (for instance to select a plan with better returns).[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-106)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTES.C._1976-77,_ch._4s_57-107) In 1977, the government tightened the rules of the RHOSP (the reforms removed the purchase of furnitures from the list of usage allowed for tax-free use of RHOSP proceeds starting in 1978;[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTES.C._1977,_ch._1s_73(3),_73(14)-108) disallowed deductible contributions for a taxpayer whose spouse owned a home;[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTES.C._1977,_ch._1s_73(1)-109) suspended tax-free rollover of RHSOP funds to an RRSP; and capped the lifetime of the RHOSP at 20 years).[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTES.C._1977,_ch._1s_73(5)-110)

In 1977, Trudeau's government established the financial program [Established Programs Financing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Established_Programs_Financing "Established Programs Financing") to help finance the [provincially](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provinces_of_Canada "Provinces of Canada")-run [healthcare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Healthcare_in_Canada "Healthcare in Canada") and post-secondary education system, through [transfer payments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transfer_payments "Transfer payments"), by [cash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cash "Cash") and [tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax "Tax")[points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basis_point "Basis point"). This system lasted until 1995.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-WelfareCanadianEncyclopedia-91)[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-111)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-DF94-112)

In 1979, Trudeau's government restructured [family allowances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_Allowance_Act "Family Allowance Act") by increasing the role of the tax system in child support and decreasing the role of family allowances. The government established an annual Refundable Child Tax Credit of $200 for families with incomes of $18,000 or less. As incomes increased above this level, benefits would be taxed away to disappear completely at $26,000. Since the median income for families during this time was $19,500, the majority of families received some benefit from the new program.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-113)

#### Taxation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierre_Trudeau&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Taxation")]

In 1969, Trudeau's first [finance minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_Finance_(Canada) "Minister of Finance (Canada)"), [Edgar Benson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Benson "Edgar Benson"), introduced a white paper on tax reform which included [tax deductions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_deduction "Tax deduction") for [child care](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_care "Child care") and advocated shifting the tax burden from the poor to the wealthy. Measures to fulfill the latter proposal included a [capital gains tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_gains_tax "Capital gains tax"), which was severely criticized by corporate Canada and the business community (notably [Israel Asper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_Asper "Israel Asper")). The bill was debated in Parliament for over a year, with its more radical proposals being removed in parliamentary committee. The reforms managed to be passed through the use of [closure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloture "Cloture"), with the capital gains tax (that had an inclusion rate of 50 percent) coming into effect on January 1, 1972, as prescribed by the [1971 budget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1971_Canadian_federal_budget "1971 Canadian federal budget").[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-Bensonglobeandmail-114)[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-115)[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-:LeaderPost-116) Also implemented in 1972 was the child care expense deduction which allowed for a deduction of up to $500 per child.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-117) As Benson had now become a political liability, Trudeau replaced him with [John Turner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Turner "John Turner") (who was seen as a "[Business Liberal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Grit "Blue Grit")") in 1972.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-Bensonglobeandmail-114)[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-118)

In 1973, Trudeau's government fully indexed the [person income tax system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Income_tax_in_Canada "Income tax in Canada") (both the exemptions and the brackets) to match inflation. The indexation was made effective in 1974; during that year, inflation had jumped from six percent to double digits.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-119) The government also implemented three personal income tax cuts from 1973 to 1975.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTECohenGranatstein1998238%E2%80%93239-120)

#### Inflation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierre_Trudeau&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Inflation")]

While popular with the electorate, Trudeau's promised minor reforms had little effect on the growing rate of inflation, and he struggled with conflicting advice on the crisis.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2009246-121) In September 1975, [finance minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_Finance_(Canada) "Minister of Finance (Canada)") John Turner resigned over refusing to implement [wage and price controls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wage_and_price_controls "Wage and price controls").[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-122) In December 1975, in an embarrassing about-face, Trudeau and new finance minister [Donald Macdonald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Stovel_Macdonald "Donald Stovel Macdonald") introduced wage and price controls by passing the _[Anti-Inflation Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Inflation\_Act "Anti-Inflation Act")_, despite campaigning against them in the 1974 election. Amongst its many controls, it limited pay increases for federal government employees and employees in companies with over 500 workers to 10 percent in 1976, 8 percent in 1977, and 6 percent in 1978. The Act also established the anti-inflation board which oversaw the implementation of wage and price controls and had the ability to recommend decreases in prices of goods, wage cuts, and rebates to customers of various services.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-Wageandpricecontrols-123) The breadth of the legislation, which touched on many powers traditionally considered the purview of the provinces, prompted [a Supreme Court reference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reference_re_Anti-Inflation_Act "Reference re Anti-Inflation Act") that only upheld the legislation as an [emergency requiring Federal intervention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace,_Order,_and_Good_Government "Peace, Order, and Good Government") under the _[British North America Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British\_North\_America\_Act "British North America Act")_. During the annual 1975 Christmas interview with [CTV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CTV_Television_Network "CTV Television Network"), Trudeau discussed the economy, citing market failures and stating that more state intervention would be necessary. However, the academic wording and hypothetical solutions posed during the complex discussion led much of the public to believe he had declared capitalism itself a failure, creating a lasting distrust among increasingly [neoliberal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoliberalism "Neoliberalism") business leaders.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEnglish2009290%E2%80%9394-124) The controls lasted until 1978 and the anti-inflation board was dissolved in 1979.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-Wageandpricecontrols-123)

#### Energy policy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierre_Trudeau&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Energy policy")]

On September 4, 1973, Trudeau requested that the [Western Canadian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Canadian "Western Canadian") provinces agree to a voluntary freeze on oil prices during [the ongoing Arab oil embargo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_oil_crisis "1973 oil crisis"). Nine days later, the Trudeau government imposed a 40-cent tax on every barrel of [Canadian oil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petroleum_industry_in_Canada "Petroleum industry in Canada") exported to the United States to combat rising inflation and oil prices. The tax was equivalent to the difference between domestic and international oil prices, and the revenues were used to subsidize oil imports for [Eastern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Canada "Eastern Canada")[refiners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil_refinery "Oil refinery"). The [Premier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premier_of_Alberta "Premier of Alberta") of oil-rich [Alberta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alberta "Alberta"), [Peter Lougheed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Lougheed "Peter Lougheed"), called the decision "the most discriminatory action taken by a federal government against a particular province in the entire history of [Confederation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Confederation "Canadian Confederation")." While revenues decreased for Western provinces (particularly Alberta) and for the petroleum industry, Trudeau's government subsidized Eastern consumers, angering Alberta, who successfully fought for control of its natural resources in 1930.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-125)

In the early 1970s, the [petroleum industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petroleum_industry "Petroleum industry") was largely under foreign (mainly American) control, the recent discovery of oil in [Alaska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska "Alaska") put corporate pressure on the [Canadian Arctic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arctic_Archipelago "Arctic Archipelago"), and Canada's energy sector increasingly focused on North American rather than domestic needs. Trudeau's government initially rejected the idea of creating a nationalized oil company (which was perceived to secure supplies, improve revenue collection, and give governments better information on the global energy market), arguing it would be costly and inefficient. However, after the [late 1973 oil crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_oil_crisis "1973 oil crisis") saw global oil prices quadruple, questions arose about whether Canada should continue importing oil. Though Canada also exported oil at times, the provinces of Quebec and Atlantic Canada were at risk of a cut-off of imports; as a result, Canada was in need of knowing more about its potential to produce energy. In late October 1973, Trudeau's government adopted a motion from the [New Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Democratic_Party "New Democratic Party") (which the Trudeau [minority government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minority_government "Minority government") relied on for support) to establish a nationalized oil company. The _Petro-Canada Act_ was passed in 1975 (under a Trudeau [majority government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majority_government "Majority government")), resulting in the creation of a new [crown corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_corporations_of_Canada "Crown corporations of Canada"), [Petro-Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petro-Canada "Petro-Canada"). Petro-Canada was mandated to acquire imported oil supplies, take part in energy research and development, and engage in downstream activities such as refining and marketing. The corporation started with an initial $1.5 billion in capital and had preferential access to debt capital as "an agent of Her Majesty". Trudeau's government gave itself authority over Petro-Canada's capital budget and its corporate strategy, making the company its policy arm; the government also wanted the company to be mainly active on the frontiers (the oil sands, the Arctic, and the East Coast offshore areas) rather than Western Canada, where most Canadian oil is extracted. In 1976, Trudeau appointed his friend, [Maurice Strong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Strong "Maurice Strong"), to become the first chair of the company.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Trudeau#cite_note-126)

**Nikita Sergeyevich Khrushchev**[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-4)[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-pronunciation-5) (15 April [[O.S.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Style "Old Style") 3 April] 1894– 11 September 1971) was the [First Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Secretary_of_the_Communist_Party_of_the_Soviet_Union "First Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union") from 1953 to 1964 and the [Chairman of the Council of Ministers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chairman_of_the_Council_of_Ministers_of_the_Soviet_Union "Chairman of the Council of Ministers of the Soviet Union") from 1958 to 1964. As leader of the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union"), he shocked the world by denouncing his predecessor [Joseph Stalin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Stalin "Joseph Stalin"), embarking on a campaign of [de-Stalinization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De-Stalinization "De-Stalinization"), and presiding over the [Cuban Missile Crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuban_Missile_Crisis "Cuban Missile Crisis") in 1962.

Born in a village near [Kursk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kursk "Kursk"), Khrushchev was employed as a [metal worker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metal_worker "Metal worker") during his youth and was a [political commissar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_commissar "Political commissar") in the [Russian Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Civil_War "Russian Civil War"). Under the sponsorship of [Lazar Kaganovich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lazar_Kaganovich "Lazar Kaganovich"), he rose through the ranks of the Soviet hierarchy. During Stalin's rule, he actively supported the [Great Purge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Purge "Great Purge") and approved thousands of arrests, and in 1938 was sent to govern the [Ukrainian SSR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukrainian_Soviet_Socialist_Republic "Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic"), where he continued the purges. During [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), Khrushchev was again a commissar, serving as an intermediary between Stalin and his generals. He was also present at the [Battle of Stalingrad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Stalingrad "Battle of Stalingrad"), a fact in which he took great pride. After the war, Khrushchev returned to Ukraine before eventually being recalled to Moscow as one of Stalin's close advisers.

On 5 March 1953, the [death of Stalin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_and_state_funeral_of_Joseph_Stalin "Death and state funeral of Joseph Stalin") triggered a power struggle in which Khrushchev ultimately emerged victorious upon consolidating his authority as First Secretary of the party's Central Committee and eliminating his rival [Lavrentiy Beria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lavrentiy_Beria "Lavrentiy Beria"). On 25 February 1956, at the [20th Party Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th_Congress_of_the_Communist_Party_of_the_Soviet_Union "20th Congress of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union"), he delivered the "[Secret Speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Cult_of_Personality_and_Its_Consequences "On the Cult of Personality and Its Consequences")", which denounced Stalin's purges and ushered in [a less repressive era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khrushchev_Thaw "Khrushchev Thaw") in the Soviet Union. His domestic policies, aimed at bettering the lives of ordinary citizens, were often ineffective, especially in agriculture. Hoping eventually to rely on missiles for national defense, Khrushchev ordered major cuts in conventional forces. Despite such cuts, Khrushchev's time in office saw the tensest years of the Cold War, culminating in the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis.

As leader of the Soviet Union, Khrushchev enjoyed considerable popularity during the late 1950s due to the successful launching of [Sputnik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sputnik_1 "Sputnik 1") in 1957 as well as favorable outcomes in the [1956 Suez Crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suez_Crisis "Suez Crisis"), [1957 Syrian Crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syrian_Crisis_of_1957 "Syrian Crisis of 1957"), and the [1960 U-2 incident](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1960_U-2_incident "1960 U-2 incident"). However, by the early 1960s, Khrushchev's hold on power had been significantly weakened by his domestic policy failures and handling of the Cuban Missile Crisis. As a result, his rivals consolidated enough support among the _[nomenklatura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nomenklatura "Nomenklatura")_ to oust him from the Soviet leadership on 14 October 1964. Following his forced retirement, Khrushchev spent much of his time composing a series of lengthy memoirs which were smuggled to the West and published in part in 1970. He died the next year in his [dacha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dacha "Dacha").

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nikita_Khrushchev&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Nikita Sergeyevich Khrushchev was born on 15 April 1894[[e]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-birth-6)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETompson19952-7) in [Kalinovka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalinovka,_Khomutovsky_District,_Kursk_Oblast "Kalinovka, Khomutovsky District, Kursk Oblast"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200320-8) a Russian village in what is now the [Khomutovsky District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khomutovsky_District "Khomutovsky District") of [Kursk Oblast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kursk_Oblast "Kursk Oblast"), near the [present Ukrainian border](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia%E2%80%93Ukraine_border "Russia–Ukraine border").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200318-9) At the time, Kalinovka was part of [Dmitriyevsky Uyezd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dmitriyevsky_Uyezd "Dmitriyevsky Uyezd") in the [Kursk Governorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kursk_Governorate "Kursk Governorate") of the [Russian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Empire "Russian Empire"). His parents, Sergei Khrushchev and Kseniya Khrushcheva were poor Russian peasants,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200321-10) and had a daughter two years Nikita's junior, Irina.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETompson19952-7) Sergei Khrushchev was employed in a number of positions in the [Donbas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donbas "Donbas") area of far eastern Ukraine, working as a railwayman, as a miner, and laboring in a brick factory. Wages were much higher in the Donbas than in the Kursk region, and Sergei Khrushchev generally left his family in Kalinovka, returning when he had enough money.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETompson19952%E2%80%933-11) When Nikita was six or seven, the family moved to Yuzovka (now [Donetsk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donetsk "Donetsk")) for about a year before returning to Kalinovka.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETompson19953-12)

Kalinovka was a peasant village; Khrushchev's teacher, Lydia Shevchenko, later stated that she had never seen a village as poor.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200327-13) Nikita worked as a [herdsboy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herder "Herder") from an early age. He was schooled for a total of four years, part in the village school and part under Shevchenko's tutelage in Kalinovka's state school. According to Khrushchev's memoirs, Shevchenko was a [freethinker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freethought "Freethought") who upset the villagers by not attending church, and when her brother visited, she gave Khrushchev books which had been banned by the Imperial Government.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200326-14) She urged Nikita to seek further education, but family finances did not permit this.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200326-14)

In 1908, Sergei Khrushchev moved to the Donbas city of Yuzovka; fourteen-year-old Nikita followed later that year, while Kseniya Khrushcheva and her daughter came after.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200330-15) Yuzovka, which was renamed Stalino in 1924 and Donetsk in 1961, was at the heart of one of the most industrialized areas of the Russian Empire.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200330-15) After working briefly in other fields, Khrushchev's parents found Nikita a place as a metal fitter's apprentice. Upon completing that apprenticeship, the teenage Khrushchev was hired by a factory.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETompson19956%E2%80%937-16) He lost that job when he collected money for the families of the victims of the [Lena Goldfields massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lena_Goldfields_massacre "Lena Goldfields massacre"), and was hired to mend underground equipment by a mine in nearby Ruchenkovo,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200337%E2%80%9338-17) where his father was the union organizer, and he helped distribute copies and organize public readings of _[Pravda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pravda "Pravda")_.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETompson19958-18) He later stated that he considered emigrating to the United States for better wages, but did not do so.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarlson2009141-19)

When [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") broke out in 1914, Khrushchev was exempt from [conscription](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conscription "Conscription") because he was a skilled metal worker. He was employed by a workshop that serviced ten mines, and he was involved in several strikes that demanded higher pay, better working conditions, and an end to the war.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETompson19958%E2%80%939-20) In 1914, he married Yefrosinia Pisareva, daughter of the lift operator at the Rutchenkovo mine. In 1915, they had a daughter, Yulia, and in 1917, a son, Leonid.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200338%E2%80%9340-21)

After the abdication of [Tsar Nicholas II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_II "Nicholas II") in 1917, the new [Russian Provisional Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Provisional_Government "Russian Provisional Government") in [Petrograd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Petersburg "Saint Petersburg") had little influence over Ukraine. Khrushchev was elected to the worker's council (or [_soviet_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union#Etymology "Soviet Union")) in Rutchenkovo, and in May he became its chairman.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200347-22) He did not join the [Bolsheviks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolsheviks "Bolsheviks") until 1918, a year in which the [Russian Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Civil_War "Russian Civil War"), between the Bolsheviks and a coalition of opponents known as the [White Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Army "White Army"), began in earnest. His biographer, [William Taubman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Taubman "William Taubman"), suggests that Khrushchev's delay in affiliating himself with the Bolsheviks was because he felt closer to the [Mensheviks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mensheviks "Mensheviks") who prioritized economic progress, whereas the Bolsheviks sought political power.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200347%E2%80%9348-23) In his memoirs, Khrushchev indicated that he waited because there were many groups, and it was difficult to keep them all straight.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200347%E2%80%9348-23)

In March 1918, as the Bolshevik government concluded [a separate peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Brest-Litovsk "Treaty of Brest-Litovsk") with the [Central Powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Powers "Central Powers"), [the Germans occupied the Donbas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukrainian_War_of_Independence#German_intervention "Ukrainian War of Independence") and Khrushchev fled to Kalinovka. In late 1918 or early 1919, he was mobilized into the [Red Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Army "Red Army") as a [political commissar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_commissar "Political commissar").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200348%E2%80%9349-24) The post of political commissar had recently been introduced as the Bolsheviks came to rely less on worker activists and more on military recruits; its functions included the indoctrination of recruits in the tenets of Bolshevism, and promoting troop morale and battle readiness.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200350-25) Beginning as commissar to a construction platoon, Khrushchev rose to become commissar to a construction battalion and was sent from the front for a two-month political course. The young commissar came under fire many times,[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETompson199512-26) though many of the war stories he would tell in later life dealt more with cultural awkwardness rather than combat.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200350-25) In 1921, the civil war ended, and Khrushchev was demobilized and assigned as commissar to a labor brigade in the Donbas, where he and his men lived in poor conditions.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200350-25)

The wars had caused widespread devastation and famine, and one of the victims was Khrushchev's wife, Yefrosinia, who died of [typhus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typhus "Typhus") in Kalinovka while Khrushchev was in the army. The commissar returned for the funeral and, loyal to his [Bolshevik principles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_anti-religious_legislation "Soviet anti-religious legislation"), refused to allow his wife's coffin to enter the local church. With the only way into the churchyard through the church, he had the coffin lifted and passed over the fence into the burial ground, shocking the village.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200350-25)

## Party official

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nikita_Khrushchev&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Party official")]

### Donbas years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nikita_Khrushchev&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Donbas years")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/1916._Khrushhev-s-zhenojj-efrosinejj.jpg/250px-1916._Khrushhev-s-zhenojj-efrosinejj.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1916._Khrushhev-s-zhenojj-efrosinejj.jpg)

Khrushchev and his first wife Euphrasinia (Yefrosinia) in 1916

Through the intervention of a friend, Khrushchev was assigned in 1921 as assistant director for political affairs for the Rutchenkovo mine in the [Donbas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donbas "Donbas") region, where he had previously worked.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200352-27) There were as yet few Bolsheviks in the area. At that time, the movement was split by [Lenin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Lenin "Vladimir Lenin")'s [New Economic Policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Economic_Policy "New Economic Policy").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200352-27) While Khrushchev's responsibility lay in political affairs, he involved himself in the practicalities of resuming full production at the mine after the chaos of the war years. He helped restart the machines (key parts and papers had been removed by the pre-Soviet mine-owners) and he wore his old mine outfit for inspection tours.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200354%E2%80%9355-28)

Khrushchev was highly successful at the Rutchenkovo mine, and in mid-1922 he was offered the directorship of the nearby Pastukhov mine. However, he refused the offer, seeking to be assigned to [the newly established technical college](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donetsk_National_Technical_University "Donetsk National Technical University") (_tekhnikum_) in Yuzovka, though his superiors were reluctant to let him go. As he had only four years of formal schooling, he applied to the training program (_[rabfak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabfak "Rabfak")_, short for Рабочий факультет / Rabotchyi Fakultyet, or Worker's Faculty) attached to the _tekhnikum_ that was designed to bring undereducated students to high-school level, a prerequisite for entry into the _tekhnikum_.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200355-29) While enrolled in the _rabfak_, Khrushchev continued his work at the Rutchenkovo mine.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETompson199514-30)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/37/NikitaNina.JPG/250px-NikitaNina.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:NikitaNina.JPG)

Khrushchev's second wife (though they only officially married in 1965) was Ukrainian-born [Nina Petrovna Kukharchuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nina_Kukharchuk-Khrushcheva "Nina Kukharchuk-Khrushcheva"), whom he met in 1922. Photo taken in 1924

One of his teachers later described him as a poor student.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200355-29) He was more successful in advancing in the [Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_Party_of_the_Soviet_Union "Communist Party of the Soviet Union"); soon after his admission to the _rabfak_ in August 1922, he was appointed party secretary of the entire _tekhnikum_, and became a member of the bureau—the governing council—of the party committee for the town of Yuzovka (renamed Stalino in 1924). He briefly joined supporters of [Leon Trotsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leon_Trotsky "Leon Trotsky") against those of [Joseph Stalin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Stalin "Joseph Stalin") over the question of party democracy.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200356%E2%80%9357-31) All of these activities left him with little time for his schoolwork, and while he later said he had finished his _rabfak_ studies, it is unclear whether this was true.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200356%E2%80%9357-31)

According to William Taubman, Khrushchev's studies were aided by [Nina Petrovna Kukharchuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nina_Petrovna_Khrushcheva "Nina Petrovna Khrushcheva"), a well-educated Party organizer and daughter of well-to-do Ukrainian peasants.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200358%E2%80%9359-32) The family was poor, according to Nina's own recollections. The two lived together as husband and wife for the rest of Khrushchev's life, though they never registered their marriage. They had three children together: daughter Rada was born in 1929, son [Sergei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Khrushchev "Sergei Khrushchev") in 1935, and daughter Elena in 1937.

In mid-1925, Khrushchev was appointed Party secretary of the Petrovo-Marinsky _[raikom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raikom "Raikom")_, or district, near Stalino. The _raikom_ was about 1,000 square kilometres (400 sq mi) in area, and Khrushchev was constantly on the move throughout his domain, taking an interest in even minor matters.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETompson199516%E2%80%9317-33) In late 1925, Khrushchev was elected a non-voting delegate to the [14th Congress of the USSR Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/14th_Congress_of_the_All-Union_Communist_Party_(b) "14th Congress of the All-Union Communist Party (b)") in Moscow.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200363-34)

### Kaganovich protégé

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nikita_Khrushchev&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Kaganovich protégé")]

[![Image 10](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/31/Lazar_Kaganovich_1935.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lazar_Kaganovich_1935.jpg)

[Lazar Kaganovich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lazar_Kaganovich "Lazar Kaganovich"), one of the chief enforcers of Stalin's dictatorship and Khrushchev's main patron.

Khrushchev met [Lazar Kaganovich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lazar_Kaganovich "Lazar Kaganovich") as early as 1917. In 1925, Kaganovich became Party head in Ukraine[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200364%E2%80%9366-35) and Khrushchev, falling under his patronage,[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhitman1971-36) was rapidly promoted. He was appointed second in command of Stalin's party apparatus in late 1926. Within nine months his superior, Konstantin Moiseyenko, was ousted, which, according to Taubman, was due to Khrushchev's instigation.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200364%E2%80%9366-35) Kaganovich transferred Khrushchev to [Kharkov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kharkov "Kharkov"), then the capital of Ukraine, as head of the Organizational Department of the Ukrainian Party's Central Committee.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200366-37) In 1928, Khrushchev was transferred to [Kiev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiev "Kiev"), where he served as head of the organizational department,[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-memofkhr-38) second-in-command of the Party organization there.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200368-39)

In 1929, Khrushchev again sought to further his education, following Kaganovich (now in the [Kremlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kremlin "Kremlin") as a close associate of Stalin) to Moscow and enrolling in the [Stalin Industrial Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_Academy_(Moscow) "Industrial Academy (Moscow)"). Khrushchev never completed his studies there, but his career in the Party flourished.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200373-40) When the school's Party cell elected a number of rightists to an upcoming district Party conference, the cell was attacked in _[Pravda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pravda "Pravda")_.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETompson199531%E2%80%9332-41) Khrushchev emerged victorious in the ensuing power struggle, becoming Party secretary of the school, arranging for the delegates to be withdrawn, and, afterward, purging the cell of the rightists.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETompson199531%E2%80%9332-41) Khrushchev rose rapidly through the Party ranks, first becoming Party leader for the Bauman district, site of the academy, before taking the same position in the Krasnopresnensky district, the capital's largest and most important. By 1932, Khrushchev had become second in command, behind Kaganovich, of the [Moscow city Party organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow_City_Committee_of_the_Communist_Party_of_the_Soviet_Union "Moscow City Committee of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union"), and in 1934, he became Party leader for the city[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200373-40) and a member of the [Party's Central Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Committee_of_the_Communist_Party_of_the_Soviet_Union "Central Committee of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200378-42) Khrushchev attributed his rapid rise to his acquaintance with fellow Academy student [Nadezhda Alliluyeva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadezhda_Alliluyeva "Nadezhda Alliluyeva"), Stalin's wife. In his memoirs, Khrushchev stated that Alliluyeva spoke well of him to her husband. His biographer, William Tompson, downplays the possibility, stating that Khrushchev was too low in the Party hierarchy to enjoy Stalin's patronage and that if influence was brought to bear on Khrushchev's career at this stage, it was by Kaganovich.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETompson199533%E2%80%9334-43)

While head of the Moscow city organization, Khrushchev superintended the construction of the [Moscow Metro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow_Metro "Moscow Metro"), a highly expensive undertaking, with Kaganovich in overall charge. Faced with an already-announced opening date of 7 November 1934, Khrushchev took considerable risks in the construction and spent much of his time down in the tunnels. When the inevitable accidents did occur, they were depicted as heroic sacrifices in a great cause. The Metro did not open until 1 May 1935, but Khrushchev received the [Order of Lenin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Lenin "Order of Lenin") for his role in its construction.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200394%E2%80%9395-44) Later that year, he was selected as First Secretary of the [Moscow Regional Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow_Regional_Committee_of_the_Communist_Party_of_the_Soviet_Union "Moscow Regional Committee of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union") which was responsible for [Moscow _oblast_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow_Oblast "Moscow Oblast"), a province with a population of 11 million.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200373-40)

### Involvement in purges

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nikita_Khrushchev&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Involvement in purges")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/Joseph_Stalin_and_Nikita_Khrushchev_1930s.jpg/330px-Joseph_Stalin_and_Nikita_Khrushchev_1930s.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Joseph_Stalin_and_Nikita_Khrushchev_1930s.jpg)

Khrushchev (second from right) poses for a photo alongside [Joseph Stalin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Stalin "Joseph Stalin") (far right) sometime during the 1930s.

Stalin's office records show meetings at which Khrushchev was present as early as 1932. The two increasingly built a good relationship. Khrushchev greatly admired the dictator and treasured informal meetings with him and invitations to Stalin's _dacha_, while Stalin felt warm affection for his young subordinate.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman2003105%E2%80%93106-45) Beginning in 1934, Stalin began a campaign of political repression known as the [Great Purge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Purge "Great Purge"), during which many were executed or sent to the [Gulag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulag "Gulag"). Central to this campaign were the [Moscow Trials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow_Trials "Moscow Trials"), a series of [show trials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Show_trial "Show trial") of the purged top leaders of the party and the military. In 1936, as the trials proceeded, Khrushchev expressed his vehement support:

> Everyone who rejoices in the successes achieved in our country, the victories of our party led by the great Stalin, will find only one word suitable for the mercenary, fascist dogs of the Trotskyite-[Zinovievite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grigory_Zinoviev "Grigory Zinoviev") gang. That word is execution.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200398-46)

Khrushchev assisted in the purge of many friends and colleagues in the Moscow _oblast_.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200399-47) Of 38 top Party officials in Moscow city and province, 35 were killed[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200399-47)—the three survivors were transferred to other parts of the USSR.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETompson199557-48) Of the 146 Party secretaries of cities and districts outside Moscow city in the province, only 10 survived the purges.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200399-47) In his memoirs, Khrushchev noted that almost everyone who worked with him was arrested.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman200399%E2%80%93100-49) By Party protocol, Khrushchev was required to approve these arrests and did little or nothing to save his friends and colleagues.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman2003100-50)

Party leaders were given numerical quotas of "enemies" to be turned in and arrested.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman2003100-50) In June 1937, the [Politburo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politburo_of_the_Central_Committee_of_the_Communist_Party_of_the_Soviet_Union "Politburo of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union") set a quota of 35,000 enemies to be arrested in Moscow province; 5,000 of these were to be executed. In reply, Khrushchev asked that 2,000 wealthy peasants, or _[kulaks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kulak "Kulak")_ living in Moscow be killed in part fulfillment of the quota. In any event, only two weeks after receiving the order, Khrushchev was able to report to Stalin that 41,305"criminal and _kulak_ elements" had been arrested. Of the arrestees, according to Khrushchev, 8,500 deserved execution.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman2003100-50)

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/%D0%92%D1%80%D1%83%D1%87%D0%B5%D0%BD%D0%B8%D0%B5_%D0%BE%D1%80%D0%B4%D0%B5%D0%BD%D0%BE%D0%B2_%D0%A6%D0%98%D0%9A_%D0%A1%D0%A1%D0%A1%D0%A0.jpg/250px-%D0%92%D1%80%D1%83%D1%87%D0%B5%D0%BD%D0%B8%D0%B5_%D0%BE%D1%80%D0%B4%D0%B5%D0%BD%D0%BE%D0%B2_%D0%A6%D0%98%D0%9A_%D0%A1%D0%A1%D0%A1%D0%A0.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:%D0%92%D1%80%D1%83%D1%87%D0%B5%D0%BD%D0%B8%D0%B5_%D0%BE%D1%80%D0%B4%D0%B5%D0%BD%D0%BE%D0%B2_%D0%A6%D0%98%D0%9A_%D0%A1%D0%A1%D0%A1%D0%A0.jpg)

Regional party leaders in 1935. In the front row sits Nikita Khrushchev (Moscow), [Andrei Zhdanov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrei_Zhdanov "Andrei Zhdanov") (Leningrad), [Lazar Kaganovich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lazar_Kaganovich "Lazar Kaganovich") (Ukraine), [Lavrentiy Beria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lavrentiy_Beria "Lavrentiy Beria") (Georgia), and [Nestor Lakoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nestor_Lakoba "Nestor Lakoba") (Abkhazia) (behind him stands [Mir Jafar Baghirov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir_Jafar_Baghirov "Mir Jafar Baghirov")).

Khrushchev had no reason to think himself immune from the purges, and in 1937, confessed his own 1923 dalliance with Trotskyism to Kaganovich, who, according to Khrushchev, "blanched" (for his protégé's sins could affect his own standing) and advised him to tell Stalin. The dictator took the confession in his stride, and, after initially advising Khrushchev to keep it quiet, suggested that Khrushchev tell his tale to the Moscow party conference. Khrushchev did so, to applause, and was immediately reelected to his post.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman2003103%E2%80%93104-51) Khrushchev related in his memoirs that he was also denounced by an arrested colleague. Stalin told Khrushchev of the accusation personally. Khrushchev speculated in his memoirs that had Stalin doubted his reaction, he would have been categorized as an [enemy of the people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enemy_of_the_people "Enemy of the people") then and there.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaubman2003104-52) Nonetheless, Khrushchev became a candidate member of the Politburo on 14 January 1938 and a full member in March 1939.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev#cite_note-FOOTNOTETompson199569-53)
