A 2014 poll of American international relations scholars conducted by the College of William & Mary ranked Kissinger as the most effective Secretary of State in the 50 years prior to 2015.[7] In 1972, Time commented that "a streak of suspicion seems to underlie all that he does" and "His jokes about his paranoia have an uncomfortable edge of truth". He was so often seen escorting Hollywood starlets that the Village Voice charged he was "a secret square posing as a swinger".[267] The insight, "Power is the ultimate aphrodisiac", is widely attributed to him, although Kissinger was paraphrasing Napoleon Bonaparte.[268]

Historian Jeffrey Kimball developed the theory that Kissinger and the Nixon administration accepted a South Vietnamese collapse provided a face-saving decent interval passed between U.S. withdrawal and defeat.[269] Similarly, in his book Henry Kissinger and the American Century, Jeremi Suri wrote: "By 1971 [Kissinger] and Nixon would accept a 'decent interval' between U.S. disengagement and a North Vietnamese takeover in the south. Secret talks with Hanoi would allow Kissinger to manage this process, preserving the image of American strength and credibility."[270] In his first meeting with Zhou Enlai in 1971, Kissinger "laid out in detail the settlement terms that would produce such a delayed defeat: total American withdrawal, return of all American POWs, and a ceasefire-in-place for '18 months or some period'", in the words of historian Ken Hughes.[269] On October 6, 1972, Kissinger told Nixon twice that the terms of the Paris Peace Accords would probably destroy South Vietnam: "I also think that Thieu is right, that our terms will eventually destroy him."[271][272] However, Kissinger denied using a "decent interval" strategy, writing "All of us who negotiated the agreement of October 12 were convinced that we had vindicated the anguish of a decade not by a 'decent interval' but by a decent settlement."[273] Johannes Kadura offers a positive assessment of Nixon and Kissinger's strategy, arguing that the two men "simultaneously maintained a Plan A of further supporting Saigon and a Plan B of shielding Washington should their maneuvers prove futile." According to Kadura, the "decent interval" concept has been "largely misrepresented", in that Nixon and Kissinger "sought to gain time, make the North turn inward, and create a perpetual equilibrium" rather than acquiescing in the collapse of South Vietnam.[274]

Kissinger's record was brought up during the 2016 Democratic Party presidential primaries. Hillary Clinton had cultivated a close relationship with Kissinger, describing him as a "friend" and a source of "counsel".[275] During the Democratic primary debates, Clinton touted Kissinger's praise for her record as secretary of state.[276][277] In response, candidate Bernie Sanders criticized Kissinger and said: "I am proud to say that Henry Kissinger is not my friend. I will not take advice from Henry Kissinger."[278]

Kissinger was an immensely beloved figure within China, with China News Service describing him in his obituary as someone "who had a sharp vision and a thorough understanding of world affairs".[279][280]

Legacy and reception

Kissinger has generally received a polarizing reception; some have portrayed him as a strategic genius who was willing to act in a utilitarian manner, others have portrayed his foreign policy decisions as immoral and profoundly damaging in the long run.[281]

Positive views

Historian Niall Ferguson has argued that Kissinger was one of the most effective secretaries of state in American history.[282] The editorial board of The Wall Street Journal stated in the aftermath of his death "Kissinger was a target of both the right and left in those perilous Cold War years, often unfairly". The article noted that he was often criticized by American conservatives for overlooking human rights in China, while saying "he had no illusions about the Communist Party or its nationalist ambitions. His view was that the U.S. and China had to achieve some modus vivendi to avoid war despite their profound cultural and political differences" while claiming that "the alternatives then, as now, weren't usually [democracy advocates] of the left's imagining. They were often Communists who would have aligned themselves with the Soviets ... . The U.S. provided covert aid to Allende's political opponents, but declassified briefings from the time show the U.S. was unaware of the military coup that deposed him. Kissinger wasn't responsible for Augusto Pinochet's coup or its bloody excesses. Chile eventually became a democracy ... Cuba remains a dictatorship."[283]

Negative views

A number of journalists, activists, and human rights lawyers accused Kissinger of being responsible for war crimes during his tenure in government.[8][284] Some sought civil and even criminal penalties against Kissinger, but none of these attempts were successful.[170] In September 2001, relatives and survivors of General Rene Schneider filed civil proceedings in federal court in Washington, D.C.[285] The suit was later dismissed.[174] In April 2002, a petition for Kissinger's arrest was filed in the High Court of Justice in London by human rights campaigner Peter Tatchell, citing the destruction of civilian populations and the environment in Indochina during the years 1969–1975.[286][287] The petition was rejected one day after filing.[288]

One of his most prominent critics was American-British journalist and author Christopher Hitchens. Hitchens authored The Trial of Henry Kissinger, in which he called for the prosecution of Kissinger "for war crimes, for crimes against humanity, and for offenses against common or customary or international law, including conspiracy to commit murder, kidnap, and torture".[289][290][291][292] American chef and TV personality Anthony Bourdain wrote in A Cook's Tour: "Once you've been to Cambodia, you'll never stop wanting to beat Henry Kissinger to death with your bare hands... Witness what [he] did... and you will never understand why he's not sitting in the dock at The Hague next to Milošević."[293][294]

Author Robert D. Kaplan and historian Niall Ferguson have disputed these notions and argued that there is a double standard in how Kissinger is judged in comparison to others. They have defended Kissinger by arguing that American power to advocate for human rights in other nations is often counterproductive and limited, that taking into consideration geopolitical realities is an inevitable part of any effective foreign policy, and that there are utilitarian reasons to defend most of the decisions of his tenure.[295]

Other perspectives

Several historians have rejected both prominent reputations of Kissinger. David Greenberg argued that each are exaggerated caricatures that overstate both his genius and immorality:

In fact, if there's a single word I'd apply to Kissinger, it's 'overrated.' He was overrated as a scholar (famous mainly for writing a very long dissertation). He was overrated as a strategist (he often gave bad advice, as he did in urging George W. Bush not to withdraw troops from Iraq). He was even overrated as a villain – the 'Christopher Hitchenses' of the world loved to call him a 'war criminal,' but this was a fundamentally unserious charge. The Defense Department, not the State Department, prosecutes wars, and the president oversees it – but the Hitchenses preferred to go after Kissinger rather than (Defense Secretaries) Mel Laird or James Schlesinger or even Nixon.[296]

Similarly, Mario Del Pero argued:

He was not particularly original or bold, once we scratch away from his writings the deliberately opaque and convoluted prose he often used, possibly to try to render more original thoughts and reflections that were in reality fairly conventional. ... In short, he wasn't a war criminal, he wasn't a very deep or sophisticated thinker, he rarely challenged the intellectual vogues of the time (even because it would have meant to challenge those in power, something he always was—and still is—reluctant to do), and once in government he displayed a certain intellectual laziness vis-à-vis the intricacies and complexities of a world that he still tended to see in black-and-white.[297]

Family and personal life
Nancy and Henry Kissinger in their New York City apartment with their dog Tyler, 1978

Kissinger married Anneliese "Ann" Fleischer (born November 6, 1925, in Fürth, Germany) on February 6, 1949. They had two children, Elizabeth and David, and divorced in 1964. In 1955, he met Austrian poet Ingeborg Bachmann during a symposium at Harvard; the two had a romantic relationship that lasted several years.[298] On March 30, 1974, he married Nancy Maginnes.[299][300] They lived in Kent, Connecticut, and in New York City. Kissinger's son David served as an executive with NBC Universal Television Studio before becoming head of Conaco, Conan O'Brien's production company, in 2005.[301] In February 1982, at the age of 58, Henry Kissinger underwent coronary bypass surgery. On May 27, 2023, he turned 100.[302]

Soccer

Daryl Grove characterized Kissinger as one of the most influential people in the growth of soccer in the United States.[303] Kissinger was named chairman of the North American Soccer League board of directors in 1978.[304] He helped bring Brazilian star Pelé to the New York Cosmos after calling the Brazilian foreign minister and telling him that Pele's move to America would substantially improve relations between the United States and Brazil. Previously, the military dictatorship in Brazil had been reluctant to let a designated national treasure leave the country.[305] In a 2023 interview, Kissinger said soccer was "at the highest level complexity masquerading as simplicity."[306]

Since his childhood, Kissinger had been a fan of his hometown's soccer club, SpVgg Fürth (now SpVgg Greuther Fürth). Even during his time in office, the German Embassy informed him about the team's results every Monday morning. He was an honorary member[307] with lifetime season tickets.[308] In September 2012, Kissinger attended a home game in which Greuther Fürth lost 0–2 against Schalke, after promising years previously that he would attend a Greuther Fürth home game if they were promoted to the Bundesliga from the 2. Bundesliga.[309] From 1989 onward, he was an honorary member of Bayern Munich.[310]

Death
Henry and Nancy Kissinger at the Metropolitan Opera opening in 2008

Kissinger died from heart failure at his home in Kent, Connecticut, on November 29, 2023, at the age of 100.[311] At the time of his death, he was the last living former U.S. Cabinet member who served in the Richard Nixon administration.[312][313][314][315] He was survived by his wife, Nancy Maginnes Kissinger; two children, David and Elizabeth; and five grandchildren.[316] His death was announced by Kissinger Associates, his consulting firm.[316] Kissinger Associates announced that the funeral would be private.[317] He was buried in Arlington National Cemetery.[318]

International reactions

Kissinger was one of the most well-known Americans in China and praised by the Chinese Communist Party. He was responsible for beginning US-China relations in the 1970s and recognising PRC as the One China, attracting antagonism in Taiwan (ROC).[319] Government figures on state media uniformly released posts mourning his death. Chinese social media expressed widespread sorrow after news of his death was released, and hashtags idolizing Kissinger became the most searched trend in China.[320][280] China News Service stated in its obituary for Kissinger that "Today, this 'old friend of the Chinese people,' who had a sharp vision and a thorough understanding of world affairs, has completed his legendary life". China Central Television, the state broadcaster, called Kissinger a "legendary diplomat" and a "living fossil" who had witnessed the development of China-U.S. relations.[279] Shortly before his death, Chinese president Xi Jinping stated: "The Chinese people never forget their old friends, and Sino-U.S. relations will always be linked with the name of Henry Kissinger".[279]

Former British prime ministers mourned Kissinger.[321] Tony Blair, the former leader of the Labour Party and prime minister of the United Kingdom, released a statement saying: "There is no-one like Henry Kissinger... From the first time I met him as a new Labour Party opposition leader in 1994, struggling to form views on foreign policy, to the last occasion when I visited him in New York and, later, he spoke at my institute's annual gathering, I was in awe of him... If it is possible for diplomacy, at its highest level, to be a form of art, Henry was an artist."[322] David Cameron stated "He was a great statesman and a deeply respected diplomat who will be greatly missed on the world stage... Even at 100, his wisdom and thoughtfulness shone through". Boris Johnson said: "The world needs him now. If ever there was an author of peace and lover of concord, that man was Henry Kissinger".[323]

European Council president Charles Michel called Kissinger a "strategist with attention to the smallest detail" and "a kind human and a brilliant mind who, over 100 years, shaped the [destinies] of some of the most important events of the century." Russian president Vladimir Putin stated in a telegram to Kissinger's widow Nancy that he was a "wise and farsighted statesman".[324] Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu stated that he "had the privilege of meeting Dr. Kissinger on numerous occasions, the most recent being just two months ago in New York. Each meeting with him was not just a lesson in diplomacy but also a masterclass in statesmanship. His understanding of the complexities of international relations and his unique insights into the challenges facing our world were unparalleled." German chancellor Olaf Scholz stated: "The world has lost a great diplomat".[325]

Chile's ambassador to the United States, Juan Gabriel Valdés, released a statement saying he possessed "brilliance" but also "profound moral wretchedness". This statement was reposted by President Gabriel Boric.[326][327] The Bangladeshi foreign minister AK Abdul Momen said that Kissinger did "inhumane things", adding that "he should have apologized to the people of Bangladesh for what he has done".[328]

Domestic reactions

The announcement of Kissinger's death saw a widespread mix of tribute and criticism on American social media.[329]

Joe Biden praised Kissinger's "fierce intellect" while noting that they often "disagreed strongly".[330] Former president George W. Bush stated: "America has lost one of the most dependable and distinctive voices on foreign affairs with the passing of Henry Kissinger. I have long admired the man who fled the Nazis as a young boy from a Jewish family, then fought them in the United States Army". Cindy McCain, the widow of John McCain, wrote: "Henry Kissinger was ever present in my late husband's life. While John was a prisoner of war, and in the later years, as a senator and statesman. The McCain family will miss his wit, charm, and intelligence terribly".[325]

Kissinger at the LBJ Library in 2016

Many negative reactions to Kissinger's death argued his decisions in government violated American values.[312][331] House of Representative members Jim McGovern, Gerry Connolly, and Greg Casar issued critical reactions to his death, with Connolly stating Kissinger's "indifference to human suffering will forever tarnish his name and shape his legacy".[332] The front page of HuffPost labeled him "The Beltway Butcher", while another HuffPost article described him as "America's Most Notorious War Criminal".[333][334] Teen Vogue mocked Kissinger with the headline: "War Criminal Responsible for Millions of Deaths Dies at 100",[335] a statement similar to that of Nick Turse of The Intercept.[336] A CNN op-ed by Peter Bergen entitled "Christopher Hitchens was right about Henry Kissinger" stated that to Kissinger "the ends almost always justified the means,"[337] referencing Hitchens's 2001 book The Trial of Henry Kissinger. Socialist magazine Jacobin released a book-length anthology entitled The Good Die Young.[338] The introduction by historian Greg Grandin notes "We all live now in the Kissingerian void."[339]

Kissinger was defended by conservative commentator David Harsanyi in an op-ed on the New York Post, where he stated that "the left disgustingly dances on Kissinger's grave because it hates America".[340] The New York Sun also defended Kissinger, describing him as "one of the most remarkable figures in American history".[341]

Awards, honors, and associations
Kissinger and Lê Đức Thọ were jointly offered the 1973 Nobel Peace Prize for their work on the Paris Peace Accords which prompted the withdrawal of American forces from the Vietnam War. Lê Đức Thọ declined to accept the award on the grounds that peace had not actually been achieved in Vietnam.[342] Kissinger donated his prize money to charity, did not attend the award ceremony and later offered to return his prize medal after the fall of South Vietnam to North Vietnamese forces 18 months later.[61][62]
In 1973, Kissinger received the U.S. Senator John Heinz Award for Greatest Public Service by an Elected or Appointed Official, an award given out annually by Jefferson Awards.[343]
In 1976, Kissinger became the first honorary member of the Harlem Globetrotters.[344][345]
On January 13, 1977, Kissinger received the Presidential Medal of Freedom with distinction from President Gerald Ford.[346]
In 1980, Kissinger won the National Book Award in History (hardcover)[c] for the first volume of his memoirs, The White House Years.[347]
In 1986, Kissinger was one of twelve recipients of the Medal of Liberty.[348]
In 1995, Kissinger was made an honorary Knight Commander of the Most Distinguished Order of St Michael and St George.[349]
In 2000, Kissinger received the Sylvanus Thayer Award at United States Military Academy at West Point.[350]
In 2002, Kissinger became an honorary member of the International Olympic Committee.[351]
On March 1, 2012, Kissinger was awarded Israel's President's Medal.[352]
In October 2013, Kissinger was awarded the Henry A. Grunwald Award for Public Service by Lighthouse International.[353]
Kissinger was a member of the Founding Council of the Rothermere American Institute, University of Oxford.[354]
Kissinger was a member of the following groups:

Atlantic Council[356]
Bilderberg Group[357][358]

Kissinger served on the board of Theranos, a health technology company,[369] from 2014 to 2017.[370]
He received the Theodore Roosevelt American Experience Award from the Union League Club of New York in 2009.
He became the Honorary Chair of the advisory board for the Bloomberg New Economy Forum[371] in 2018.
He also received the Ellis Island Medal of Honor.[372]
In 2023, he received the Bavarian Maximilian Order for Science and Art from Minister-President of Bavaria Markus Söder.[citation needed]
He was an Honorary Member of Bayern Munich.[310]

[Shrimati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shrimati "Shrimati")**Indira Priyadarshini Gandhi**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi#cite_note-2) ([née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_name#Maiden_and_married_names "Birth name")**Nehru**; 19 November 1917 – 31 October 1984)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi#cite_note-3) was an Indian stateswoman who twice served as the [Prime Minister of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_India "Prime Minister of India") from 1966 to 1977 and again from 1980 until her [assassination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Indira_Gandhi "Assassination of Indira Gandhi") in 1984. She was India's first and only female prime minister, and a central figure in Indian politics as the leader of the [Indian National Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_National_Congress "Indian National Congress") (INC). Gandhi also served as chairperson of the [Non-Aligned Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-Aligned_Movement "Non-Aligned Movement") (NAM) from 1983 to 1984, becoming the first Indian to hold the position. She was the daughter of [Jawaharlal Nehru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jawaharlal_Nehru "Jawaharlal Nehru"), the first prime minister of India, and the mother of [Rajiv Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rajiv_Gandhi "Rajiv Gandhi"), who succeeded her as prime minister. Her cumulative tenure of 15 years and 350 days, spanning four terms, makes her the second-longest-serving Indian prime minister after her father and the longest-serving female head of government at the time of her death.

During her father Jawaharlal Nehru's premiership from 1947 to 1964, Gandhi was his hostess and accompanied him on his numerous foreign trips. In 1959, she played a part in the dissolution of the [communist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist "Communist")-led [Kerala state government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala_state_government "Kerala state government") as then-[president of the Indian National Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Indian_National_Congress "President of the Indian National Congress"), otherwise a ceremonial position to which she was elected earlier that year. [Lal Bahadur Shastri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lal_Bahadur_Shastri "Lal Bahadur Shastri"), who had succeeded Nehru as prime minister upon [his death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_and_state_funeral_of_Jawaharlal_Nehru "Death and state funeral of Jawaharlal Nehru") in 1964, appointed her [minister of information and broadcasting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_Information_and_Broadcasting_(India) "Minister of Information and Broadcasting (India)") in [his government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shastri_ministry "Shastri ministry"); the same year she was elected to the [Rajya Sabha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rajya_Sabha "Rajya Sabha"), the upper house of the [Indian Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Parliament "Indian Parliament"). After Shastri's death in January 1966, Gandhi defeated her rival, [Morarji Desai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morarji_Desai "Morarji Desai"), in the INC's parliamentary leadership election to become leader and also succeeded Shastri as prime minister. With her premiership of India she became the [world's second female prime minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_elected_and_appointed_female_heads_of_state_and_government "List of elected and appointed female heads of state and government") after her Sri Lankan counterpart [Sirimavo Bandaranaike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sirimavo_Bandaranaike "Sirimavo Bandaranaike"). She led the Congress to victory in two subsequent elections, starting with the [1967 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_Indian_general_election "1967 Indian general election"), in which she was first elected to the lower house of the Indian parliament, the [Lok Sabha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lok_Sabha "Lok Sabha"). In 1971, her party secured its first [landslide victory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landslide_victory "Landslide victory") since her father's sweep in [1962](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1962_Indian_general_election "1962 Indian general election"), focusing on issues such as poverty.

As prime minister, Gandhi was known for her uncompromising political stances and [centralisation of power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centralised_government "Centralised government") within the [executive branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_branch "Executive branch"). In 1967, she headed a [military conflict with China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathu_La_and_Cho_La_clashes "Nathu La and Cho La clashes") in which India repelled Chinese incursions into the [Himalayas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalayas "Himalayas").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi#cite_note-Chellaney-4) In 1971, she went to [war with Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indo-Pakistani_War_of_1971 "Indo-Pakistani War of 1971") in support of the [independence movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Six_point_movement "Six point movement") and [war of independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh_Liberation_War "Bangladesh Liberation War") in [East Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Pakistan "East Pakistan"), which resulted in an Indian victory, the end of the [Bangladeshi genocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladeshi_genocide "Bangladeshi genocide"), and the independence of [Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh"), as well as an increase in India's influence to the point where it became the sole [regional power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_power "Regional power") in [South Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Asia "South Asia").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi#cite_note-j653-5) Another military operation against Pakistan, codenamed [Operation Meghdoot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Meghdoot "Operation Meghdoot"), occurred during her tenure in 1984, which led to India expanding the territory it effectively controlled in the disputed Kashmir region.

Gandhi also played a crucial role in initiating India's first successful [nuclear weapon test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smiling_Buddha "Smiling Buddha") in 1974. Her rule saw India grow closer to the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") by signing a [friendship treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indo-Soviet_Treaty_of_Friendship_and_Cooperation "Indo-Soviet Treaty of Friendship and Cooperation") in 1971 to ward off perceived geopolitical threat as a result of the U.S. warming up to China. India received military, financial, and diplomatic support from the Soviet Union during its conflict with Pakistan in the same year.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi#cite_note-6) Though India was at the forefront of the [Non-Aligned Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-Aligned_Movement "Non-Aligned Movement"), Gandhi made it one of the Soviet Union's closest allies in Asia, each often supporting the other in proxy wars and at the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi#cite_note-7)

Responding to separatist tendencies and a call for revolution, she instituted a [state of emergency from 1975 to 1977](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Emergency_(India) "The Emergency (India)"), during which she [ruled by decree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_by_decree "Rule by decree") and basic civil liberties were suspended.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi#cite_note-:5-8) More than 100,000 political opponents, journalists and dissenters were imprisoned.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi#cite_note-:5-8) Following the Emergency, the INC lost the [1977 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1977_Indian_general_election "1977 Indian general election") in the midst of massive anti-incumbency sentiment—the first such loss for the INC in the history of the Republic of India. She even lost her own parliamentary constituency. However, due to her portrayal as a strong leader and the weak governance of the [Janata Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Janata_Party "Janata Party"), her party won the [next election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Indian_general_election "1980 Indian general election") by a landslide and she returned to the premiership.

She faced the [Sikh separatist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sikh_separatism "Sikh separatism") movement throughout her fourth premiership; in response, she ordered [Operation Blue Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Blue_Star "Operation Blue Star"), which involved military action in the [Golden Temple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Temple "Golden Temple") and killed hundreds of [Sikhs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sikhs "Sikhs"). On 31 October 1984, she was assassinated by two of her bodyguards, both of whom were Sikh nationalists seeking retribution for the events at the temple.

Gandhi was cremated at the site now known as [Shakti Sthal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakti_Sthal "Shakti Sthal") (transl. 'Place of strength'). The site is marked by a large monolithic rock of iron ore commemorating her as the "Iron Lady of India".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi#cite_note-advani-9)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi#cite_note-chopra-10) Gandhi is remembered as one of the most powerful women in the world.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi#cite_note-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi#cite_note-12) Her supporters cite her leadership during victories over geopolitical rivals China and Pakistan, the [Green Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Revolution_in_India "Green Revolution in India"), [a growing economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_policy_of_the_Indira_Gandhi_government "Economic policy of the Indira Gandhi government") in the early 1980s, and her [anti-poverty campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garibi_Hatao "Garibi Hatao") that led her to be known as Mother Indira among the country's poor and rural population. Critics note her [cult of personality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult_of_personality "Cult of personality") and authoritarian rule of India during the Emergency. In 1999, she was named "Woman of the Millennium" in an online poll organised by the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi#cite_note-BBCPOLL-13) In 2020, she was named by [_Time_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_(magazine) "Time (magazine)") magazine among the 100 women who defined the past century as counterparts to the magazine's previous choices for [Man of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Person_of_the_Year "Time Person of the Year").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi#cite_note-14)

## Early life and career

Indira Gandhi was born in [British ruled India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Raj "British Raj") as Indira Nehru, into a [Kashmiri Pandit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashmiri_Pandit "Kashmiri Pandit") family on 19 November 1917 in Allahabad (present-day [Prayagraj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prayagraj "Prayagraj")) in [Uttar Pradesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uttar_Pradesh "Uttar Pradesh").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrank201013-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi#cite_note-Indira_Priyadarshini-16) Her father, [Jawaharlal Nehru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jawaharlal_Nehru "Jawaharlal Nehru"), was a leading figure in the [Indian movement for independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_movement_for_independence "Indian movement for independence") from [British rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Raj "British Raj"), and became the first Prime Minister of the [Dominion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominion_of_India "Dominion of India") (and later [Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India")) of India.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGupte20123-17) Indira was her parents' only surviving child (she had a younger brother who died while young);[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrank201031-18) she grew up with her mother, [Kamala Nehru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Nehru "Kamala Nehru"), at the [Anand Bhavan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swaraj_Bhavan "Swaraj Bhavan"), a large family estate in Allahabad.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrank201016-19) In 1930, the Nehru family donated the mansion to the Indian National Congress and renamed it [Swaraj Bhavan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swaraj_Bhavan "Swaraj Bhavan") (meaning abode of freedom). A new mansion was built nearby to serve as the family residence and given the name of the old [Anand Bhavan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anand_Bhavan "Anand Bhavan").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrank201016-19) Indira had a lonely and unhappy childhood.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrank201025-20) Her father was often away, directing political activities or incarcerated, while her mother was frequently bedridden with illness and later suffered an early death from [tuberculosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuberculosis "Tuberculosis").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrank201032-21) Indira had limited contact with her father, mostly through letters.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrank201055-22)

Nehru tried to return to England through [Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal "Portugal") but was left stranded for nearly two months. She managed to enter England in early 1941, and from there returned to India without completing her studies at Oxford. The university later awarded her an honorary degree. In 2010, Oxford honoured her further by selecting her as one of the ten Oxasians, illustrious [Asian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_people "Asian people") graduates from the [University of Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi#cite_note-35)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi#cite_note-degree-1) During her stay in Britain, Nehru frequently met her future husband [Feroze Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feroze_Gandhi "Feroze Gandhi") (no relation to [Mahatma Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahatma_Gandhi "Mahatma Gandhi")). In March 1942 they were married in Allahabad according to [Adi Dharm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adi_Dharm "Adi Dharm") rituals, although Feroze belonged to a [Zoroastrian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoroastrian "Zoroastrian")[Parsi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parsi "Parsi") family of [Gujarat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gujarat "Gujarat").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi#cite_note-36) The couple had two sons, [Rajiv Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rajiv_Gandhi "Rajiv Gandhi") (born 1944) and [Sanjay Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanjay_Gandhi "Sanjay Gandhi") (born 1946).[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi#cite_note-37)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi#cite_note-Auerbach-1984-38)

In September 1942, Indira Gandhi was arrested over her role in the [Quit India Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quit_India_Movement "Quit India Movement"). She was released from jail in April 1943.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi#cite_note-Duda_2006-39) "Mud entered our souls in the drabness of prison," she later recalled her time in the jail. She added, "When I came out, it was such a shock to see colors again I thought I would go out of my mind."[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi#cite_note-Washington_Post1-40)
