#### Constitutional issues

After sidestepping the political landmine for most of the first year of his time as prime minister, much as all the post-Charlottetown Accord prime ministers had done, Harper's hand was forced to reopen the [Quebec sovereignty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec_sovereignty_movement "Quebec sovereignty movement") debate after the opposition Bloc Québécois were to introduce a motion in the House that called for recognition of Quebec as a "nation". On November 22, 2006, Harper introduced [his own motion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qu%C3%A9b%C3%A9cois_nation_motion "Québécois nation motion") to recognize that "the [Québécois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French-Canadian "French-Canadian") form a nation within a united Canada."[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-158) Five days later, Harper's motion passed, with a margin of 266–16; all federalist parties, and the Bloc Québécois, supported it.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-159)

In 2004, Harper said "the Upper House remains a dumping ground for the favoured cronies of the prime minister".[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-senatestar-160) Between 2006 and 2008, by which time Harper was prime minister, he did not put any names to the governor general for appointment to the Senate, resulting in 16 Senate vacancies by the October 2008 election.[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-theglobeandmail1-161) The one exception was [Michael Fortier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Fortier "Michael Fortier"). When Harper took office, he advised the governor general to appoint Michael Fortier to both the Senate and the [Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_Canada "Cabinet of Canada"), arguing the government needed [representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_representation "Political representation") from the city of Montreal.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-162) Although there is a precedent for this action in Canadian history, the appointment led to criticism from opponents who claimed Harper was reneging on his push for an elected Senate. In 2008, Fortier gave up his Senate seat and sought election as an MP, but was defeated by a large margin by the incumbent Bloc Québécois MP.[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-163)

After the October 2008 election, Harper again named Senate reform as a priority.[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-theglobeandmail1-161) By December, he recommended the appointment of 18 senators and, in 2009, provided an additional nine people for appointment as senators. Many of those appointed had close ties with the Conservative Party, including the campaign manager of the Conservative Party, [Doug Finley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doug_Finley "Doug Finley"). Critics accused Harper of hypocrisy (the Liberals coined the term "Harpocrisy"). Conservative senator Bert Brown defended Harper's appointments and said "the only way [the Senate]'s ever been filled is by having people that are loyal to the prime minister who's appointing them".[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-senatestar-160)

#### Economic management

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/Stephen-Harper-January-26-2012.png/250px-Stephen-Harper-January-26-2012.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Stephen-Harper-January-26-2012.png)

Harper during the 'Special Address' at the 2012 Annual Meeting of the [World Economic Forum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Economic_Forum "World Economic Forum") at the congress centre in Davos, Switzerland, January 26, 2012.

During Harper's tenure, Canada had budgetary surpluses in [2006](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Canadian_federal_budget "2006 Canadian federal budget") and [2007](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_Canadian_federal_budget "2007 Canadian federal budget") of $13.8 and $9.6 billion respectively. Following the [2008 financial crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_financial_crisis "2008 financial crisis"), Canada ran deficits from [2008](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Canadian_federal_budget "2008 Canadian federal budget")–[2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Canadian_federal_budget "2013 Canadian federal budget"). The deficit was $55.6 billion in [2009](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_Canadian_federal_budget "2009 Canadian federal budget") and was gradually lowered to $5.2 billion in 2013. Harper cut both the GST and corporate taxes aggressively. In [2014](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Canadian_federal_budget "2014 Canadian federal budget"), the federal budget was balanced with a surplus of $1.9 billion.[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-164) For [2015–2016](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Canadian_federal_budget "2015 Canadian federal budget"), the federal government initially projected a $1.4-billion surplus. Following Harper's defeat in the [2015 Canadian federal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Canadian_federal_election "2015 Canadian federal election") and the change in party control, the 2015 fiscal year ended in a $1 billion deficit instead.[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-cbc.ca-165) In 2010, Canada had the lowest [debt-to-GDP ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debt-to-GDP_ratio "Debt-to-GDP ratio") in the G7 economies.[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-166)_The Economist_ magazine stated that Canada had come out the recession stronger than any other rich country in the G7.[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-167)[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-168) In 2013, Canada came out with [Global Markets Action Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada's_Global_Markets_Action_Plan "Canada's Global Markets Action Plan") to generate employment opportunities for Canadians.[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-GMAP-169)[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-TNFAVSF-170)[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-TIMFPTT-171)

#### 2011 Census

Ahead of the [Canada 2011 Census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_2011_Census "Canada 2011 Census"), the government announced that the long-form questionnaire (which collects detailed demographic information) will no longer be mandatory. According to [Minister of Industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_Industry_(Canada) "Minister of Industry (Canada)") Tony Clement, the change was made because of privacy-related complaints and after consulting with [Statistics Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_Canada "Statistics Canada").[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-:1-172) However, the federal [privacy commissioner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privacy_Commissioner_of_Canada "Privacy Commissioner of Canada") reported only receiving three complaints between 1995 and 2010, according to a report in the _Toronto Sun_.[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-:2-173)

[Munir Sheikh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munir_Sheikh "Munir Sheikh"), the [chief statistician of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_Statistician_of_Canada "Chief Statistician of Canada")—appointed on Harper's advice—resigned on July 21, 2010, in protest of the government's change in policy.[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-174)[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-175)[Ivan Fellegi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Fellegi "Ivan Fellegi"), a former chief statistician, criticized the government's decision, saying that those who are most vulnerable (such as the poor, new immigrants, and aboriginals) are least likely to respond to a voluntary form, which weakens information about their demographic.[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-176)

The move was opposed by some governmental and non-governmental organizations.[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-177)[Federation of Canadian Municipalities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Canadian_Municipalities "Federation of Canadian Municipalities"); the [Toronto government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Municipal_government_of_Toronto "Municipal government of Toronto");[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-178)[Canadian Jewish Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Jewish_Congress "Canadian Jewish Congress"); [Evangelical Fellowship of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelical_Fellowship_of_Canada "Evangelical Fellowship of Canada");[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-179)[Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Conference_of_Catholic_Bishops "Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops");[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-180)[Canadian Medical Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Medical_Association "Canadian Medical Association");[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-181)[Statistical Society of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_Society_of_Canada "Statistical Society of Canada"); the [American Statistical Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Statistical_Association "American Statistical Association");[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-182) and [Registered Nurses Association of Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Registered_Nurses_Association_of_Ontario "Registered Nurses Association of Ontario") all opposed the change. However, the [Fraser Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fraser_Institute "Fraser Institute") supported the change.[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-183) The provincial governments of [Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Ontario "Government of Ontario"), [Quebec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Quebec "Government of Quebec"), [New Brunswick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_New_Brunswick "Government of New Brunswick"), [Prince Edward Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Prince_Edward_Island "Government of Prince Edward Island"), and [Manitoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Manitoba "Government of Manitoba"), also opposed the change.[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-184)

**Stephen Joseph Harper** (born April 30, 1959) is a Canadian politician who served as the 22nd [prime minister of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_minister_of_Canada "Prime minister of Canada") from 2006 to 2015. He is to date the only prime minister to have been a member of the modern-day [Conservative Party of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada "Conservative Party of Canada"), being the party's co-founder and serving as its first [leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Canadian_conservative_leaders "List of Canadian conservative leaders") from 2004 to 2015. Since 2018, he has been the [chairman of the International Democracy Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Democracy_Union#Chairmen "International Democracy Union").

Born in [Leaside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leaside "Leaside"), now a neighbourhood of [Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto "Toronto"), Ontario, Harper studied economics, earning his bachelor's and master's degrees in 1985 and 1991, respectively, from the [University of Calgary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Calgary "University of Calgary"). He was a founder of the [Reform Party of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_Party_of_Canada "Reform Party of Canada") and was first elected to the [House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_Canada "House of Commons of Canada") in the [1993 federal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_Canadian_federal_election "1993 Canadian federal election") in the [riding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_district_(Canada) "Electoral district (Canada)") of [Calgary West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calgary_West "Calgary West"). He did not seek re-election in [1997](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_Canadian_federal_election "1997 Canadian federal election") and instead joined and later led the [National Citizens Coalition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Citizens_Coalition "National Citizens Coalition"), a conservative lobbyist group. In [2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Alliance_leadership_elections#2002_leadership_election "Canadian Alliance leadership elections"), Harper defeated [Stockwell Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockwell_Day "Stockwell Day") to become leader of the [Canadian Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Alliance "Canadian Alliance"), the successor to the Reform Party, and returned to Parliament as the [leader of the Opposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Official_Opposition_(Canada) "Leader of the Official Opposition (Canada)"). In 2003, Harper and [Progressive Conservative Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_Conservative_Party_of_Canada "Progressive Conservative Party of Canada") leader [Peter MacKay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_MacKay "Peter MacKay") agreed to merge the Canadian Alliance with the Progressive Conservatives to form the [Conservative Party of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada "Conservative Party of Canada"). Harper was elected as the party's first leader in [2004](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Conservative_Party_of_Canada_leadership_election "2004 Conservative Party of Canada leadership election"). He led the Conservatives in the [2004 federal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Canadian_federal_election "2004 Canadian federal election"), which it lost to [Paul Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Martin "Paul Martin")'s [Liberal Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Party_of_Canada "Liberal Party of Canada"). In the [2006 federal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Canadian_federal_election "2006 Canadian federal election"), Harper led the Conservatives to a [minority government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minority_governments_in_Canada "Minority governments in Canada").

During [Harper's premiership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premiership_of_Stephen_Harper "Premiership of Stephen Harper"), he faced the [In and Out scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_and_Out_scandal "In and Out scandal"), reduced the [goods and services tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goods_and_services_tax_(Canada) "Goods and services tax (Canada)") (GST) to 5%, and passed the _[Federal Accountability Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal\_Accountability\_Act "Federal Accountability Act")_, the [Québécois nation motion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qu%C3%A9b%C3%A9cois_nation_motion "Québécois nation motion"), and the _[Veterans' Bill of Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veterans'\_Bill\_of\_Rights "Veterans' Bill of Rights")_. Harper led the Conservatives to a larger minority government in the [2008 federal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Canadian_federal_election "2008 Canadian federal election"), after which he [prorogued Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prorogation_in_Canada "Prorogation in Canada") to avoid defeat by a [proposed coalition of opposition parties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008%E2%80%932009_Canadian_parliamentary_dispute "2008–2009 Canadian parliamentary dispute"), advanced the [Economic Action Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_Canadian_federal_budget "2009 Canadian federal budget") of personal income tax cuts and infrastructure investments in response to the [Great Recession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Recession "Great Recession"), introduced the [tax-free savings account](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax-free_savings_account "Tax-free savings account"), and authorized [military intervention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Mobile "Operation Mobile") during the [First Libyan Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libyan_civil_war_(2011) "Libyan civil war (2011)"). In March 2011, [Harper's government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/28th_Canadian_Ministry "28th Canadian Ministry") was found in a vote of no confidence to be in [contempt of Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contempt_of_Parliament "Contempt of Parliament"), triggering [a federal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Canadian_federal_election "2011 Canadian federal election") in which he led the Conservatives to a [majority government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majority_government "Majority government"). He subsequently repealed the [long-gun registry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Firearms_Registry "Canadian Firearms Registry"), privatized the [Canadian Wheat Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Wheat_Board "Canadian Wheat Board"), enacted the _[Anti-terrorism Act, 2015](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-terrorism\_Act,\_2015 "Anti-terrorism Act, 2015")_, and reduced Canada's [budget deficit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budget_deficit "Budget deficit") from $55.6 billion in 2009 to $2.9 billion in [2015](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Canadian_federal_budget "2015 Canadian federal budget"). In foreign policy, Harper [withdrew Canada from the Kyoto Protocol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_and_the_Kyoto_Protocol "Canada and the Kyoto Protocol"), launched [Canada's Global Markets Action Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada's_Global_Markets_Action_Plan "Canada's Global Markets Action Plan"), negotiated [free trade agreements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_trade_agreements_of_Canada "Free trade agreements of Canada"), and authorized [Operation Impact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Impact "Operation Impact")[against ISIL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_against_the_Islamic_State "War against the Islamic State") and [Operation Unifier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Unifier "Operation Unifier") following the [Russian annexation of Crimea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Russian_annexation_of_Crimea "2014 Russian annexation of Crimea"). Harper's Conservatives also faced controversies in the [Robocall scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Canadian_federal_election_voter_suppression_scandal "2011 Canadian federal election voter suppression scandal") and the [Canadian Senate expenses scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Senate_expenses_scandal "Canadian Senate expenses scandal"), and confronted the [Idle No More](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idle_No_More "Idle No More") movement.

In the [2015 federal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Canadian_federal_election "2015 Canadian federal election"), the Conservative Party was defeated by the Liberal Party led by [Justin Trudeau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justin_Trudeau "Justin Trudeau"). Harper officially stepped down as party leader in October 2015, and resigned his seat in August 2016. Since then, he has taken on several international business and leadership roles, including founding a global consulting firm, appearing in U.S. and British media, and being elected as chairman of the [International Democracy Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Democracy_Union "International Democracy Union"), an [international alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_international "Political international") of centre-right to right-wing political parties. The [longest-serving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_prime_ministers_of_Canada_by_time_in_office "List of prime ministers of Canada by time in office") conservative prime minister since [John A. Macdonald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_A._Macdonald "John A. Macdonald"), Harper ranks average to above-average in [rankings of prime ministers of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_rankings_of_prime_ministers_of_Canada "Historical rankings of prime ministers of Canada").

## Early life and education

Harper was born and raised in the [Town of Leaside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leaside "Leaside"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-3) now a neighbourhood of [Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto "Toronto"), Ontario, the first of three sons of Margaret (née Johnston) and Joseph Harris Harper, an accountant at [Imperial Oil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_Oil "Imperial Oil").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-4) The Harper family traces its ancestral roots back to [Sledmere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sledmere "Sledmere"), a village in [Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire "Yorkshire"), [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England"), with Harper's 4th great-grandfather Christopher having emigrated to [Nova Scotia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nova_Scotia "Nova Scotia") in 1774, where he later served as [justice of the peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justice_of_the_peace "Justice of the peace") in the area that is now [New Brunswick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Brunswick "New Brunswick").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-Globe_And_Mail-5)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-6)

Harper attended Northlea Public School in Leaside and, later, [John G. Althouse Middle School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_G._Althouse_Middle_School "John G. Althouse Middle School") and [Richview Collegiate Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richview_Collegiate_Institute "Richview Collegiate Institute"), both in [Etobicoke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etobicoke "Etobicoke"), Toronto. He graduated from high school in 1978, and was a member of Richview Collegiate's team on _[Reach for the Top](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reach\_for\_the\_Top "Reach for the Top")_, a televised academic quiz show for high school students.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-ReachForTheTop-7) Harper first enrolled at the [Trinity College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_College,_Toronto "Trinity College, Toronto") of the [University of Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Toronto "University of Toronto").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-Johnson-8) In an attempt to establish independence from his parents, Harper dropped out of the University of Toronto and then moved to [Edmonton, Alberta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmonton,_Alberta "Edmonton, Alberta"), where he found work in the mail room at Imperial Oil.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-Johnson-8) Later, he advanced to work on the company's computer systems. He took up post-secondary studies again at the [University of Calgary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Calgary "University of Calgary"), where he completed a bachelor's degree in economics in 1985. He later returned there to earn a master's degree in economics, completed in 1991.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-Historica-9) Throughout his career, Harper has kept strong links to the University of Calgary. Trained as an economist, Harper was the first prime minister with an economics degree since Pierre Trudeau and the first prime minister without a law degree since [Joe Clark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Clark "Joe Clark").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-10)

## Political beginnings

Harper became involved in politics as a member of his high school's [Young Liberals club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young_Liberals_of_Canada "Young Liberals of Canada").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-canadiancontent1-11) He later changed his political allegiance because he disagreed with the [National Energy Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Energy_Program "National Energy Program") (NEP) of Pierre Trudeau's Liberal government.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-12) He became executive assistant to Progressive Conservative (PC) Member of Parliament (MP) [Jim Hawkes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Hawkes "Jim Hawkes") in 1985 but later became disillusioned with the party and the government of [Brian Mulroney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Mulroney "Brian Mulroney"), citing the administration's economic policy. He left the PC Party the next year.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-13)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-14)

Harper was then recommended by the University of Calgary's economist Bob Mansell to [Preston Manning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preston_Manning "Preston Manning"), the founder and leader of the [right-wing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right-wing_politics "Right-wing politics")[populist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right-wing_populism "Right-wing populism")[Reform Party of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_Party_of_Canada "Reform Party of Canada"). At that time, Harper "didn't see himself as a politician", Mansell told CBC News in 2002, adding, "Politics was not his first love."[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-cbc-bio-15)

Manning invited him to participate in the party, and Harper gave a speech at Reform's 1987 founding convention in [Winnipeg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winnipeg "Winnipeg"). He became the Reform Party's chief policy officer, and he played a major role in drafting the 1988 election platform,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-cbc-bio-15) otherwise known as the Blue Book, which helped form the principles and policies of the party. Harper was influenced by his political mentor, [Tom Flanagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Flanagan_(political_scientist) "Tom Flanagan (political scientist)"), when writing the book.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-16)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-17)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-18)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-19) Harper is credited with creating Reform's campaign slogan, "The West wants in!"[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-20)

Harper ran for the House of Commons in the [1988 federal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1988_Canadian_federal_election "1988 Canadian federal election") in Calgary West and losing by a wide margin to Hawkes, his former employer. After Reform candidate [Deborah Grey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deborah_Grey "Deborah Grey") was elected as the party's first MP in a 1989 [by-election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_Beaver_River_federal_by-election "1989 Beaver River federal by-election"), Harper became Grey's executive assistant, serving as her chief adviser and speechwriter until 1993.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-Geoff_White_1989-21) He remained prominent in the Reform Party's national organization in his role as policy chief, encouraging the party to expand beyond its Western base and arguing that strictly regional parties were at risk of being taken over by radical elements.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-22) He delivered a speech at the Reform Party's 1991 national convention, in which he condemned extremist views.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-23)

Harper's relationship with Manning became strained in 1992, because of conflicting strategies over the [Charlottetown Accord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlottetown_Accord "Charlottetown Accord"). Harper opposed the accord on principle for ideological reasons, while Manning was initially more open to compromise. Harper also criticized Manning's decision to hire [Rick Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Anderson_(political_strategist) "Rick Anderson (political strategist)") as an adviser, believing that Anderson was not sufficiently committed to the Reform Party's principles.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-24) Harper resigned as the policy chief in October 1992.

Harper stood for office again in the [1993 federal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_Canadian_federal_election "1993 Canadian federal election") and defeated Jim Hawkes amid a significant Reform breakthrough in Western Canada.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-25) The [National Citizens Coalition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Citizens_Coalition "National Citizens Coalition") (NCC) ran a $50,000 print and television campaign against Hawkes but did not endorse Harper directly.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-26)

### Reform Party MP (1993–1997)

Harper emerged a prominent member of the Reform Party caucus. He was active on constitutional issues and played a prominent role in drafting the Reform Party's strategy for the [1995 Quebec referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_Quebec_referendum "1995 Quebec referendum"). A long-standing opponent of centralized [federalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_federalism "Canadian federalism"), he stood with Preston Manning in Montreal to introduce a twenty-point plan to "decentralize and modernize" Canada in the event of a "no" victory.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-27) Harper later argued that the "no" side's narrow [plurality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plurality_(voting) "Plurality (voting)") was a worst-case scenario, in that no-one had won a mandate for change.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-28)

Harper has expressed some [socially conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_conservatism "Social conservatism") views on certain issues.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-29) In 1994, he opposed plans by federal Justice Minister [Allan Rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allan_Rock "Allan Rock") to introduce spousal benefits for same-sex couples. Citing the recent failure of a similar initiative in Ontario, he was quoted as saying, "What I hope they learn is not to get into it. There are more important social and economic issues, not to mention the unity question."[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-30) Harper also spoke against the possibility of the [Canadian Human Rights Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Human_Rights_Commission "Canadian Human Rights Commission") or the [Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Canada "Supreme Court of Canada") changing federal policy in these and other matters.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-31)

At the Reform Party's 1994 policy convention, Harper was part of a small minority of delegates who voted against restricting the definition of marriage to "the union of one man and one woman".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-32) He opposed both [same-sex marriage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Same-sex_marriage_in_Canada "Same-sex marriage in Canada") and mandated benefits for same-sex couples, but argued that political parties should refrain from taking official positions on these and other "issues of conscience".[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-33)

Harper was the only Reform MP to support the creation of the [Canadian Firearms Registry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Firearms_Registry "Canadian Firearms Registry") at [second reading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_reading "Second reading") in 1995, although he later voted against it at [third reading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_reading "Third reading") stage. He said at the time that he initially voted for the registry because of a poll showing that most of his constituents supported it, and added that he changed his vote when a second poll showed the opposite result. It was reported in April 1995, that some Progressive Conservatives opposed to [Jean Charest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Charest "Jean Charest")'s leadership wanted to remove both Charest and Manning, and unite the Reform and Progressive Conservative parties under Harper's leadership.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-34)

Despite his prominent position in the party, Harper's relationship with the Reform Party leadership was frequently strained. In early 1994, he criticized a party decision to establish a personal expense account for Manning at a time when other Reform MPs had been asked to forego parliamentary perquisites.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-35) He was formally rebuked by the Reform executive council despite winning support from some MPs. His relationship with Manning grew increasingly fractious in the mid-1990s, and he pointedly declined to express any opinion on Manning's leadership during a 1996 interview.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-36) This friction was indicative of a fundamental divide between the two men: Harper was strongly committed to conservative principles and opposed Manning's inclinations toward [populism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Populism "Populism"), which Harper saw as leading to compromise on core ideological matters.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-37)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-38)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-39)

These tensions culminated in late 1996 when Harper announced that he would not be a candidate in the [next federal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_Canadian_federal_election "1997 Canadian federal election"). He resigned his parliamentary seat on January 14, 1997, the same day that he was appointed as a vice-president of the National Citizens Coalition (NCC), a conservative think-tank and advocacy group.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-40) He was promoted to NCC president later in the year.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-41)

In April 1997, Harper suggested that the Reform Party was drifting toward social conservatism and ignoring the principles of [economic conservatism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiscal_conservatism "Fiscal conservatism").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-42) The Liberal Party lost seats but managed to retain a narrow majority government in the 1997 federal election, while Reform made only modest gains.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-43)

### Out of parliament (1997–2001)

Soon after leaving Parliament, Harper and Tom Flanagan co-authored an opinion piece entitled "Our [Benign Dictatorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enlightened_absolutism "Enlightened absolutism")", which argued that the Liberal Party only retained power through a dysfunctional political system and a divided opposition. Harper and Flanagan argued that federal conservative governments between 1917 and 1993 were founded on temporary alliances between Western populists and [Quebec nationalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec_nationalism "Quebec nationalism"), and were unable to govern because of their fundamental contradictions. The authors called for an alliance of Canada's conservative parties, and suggested that meaningful political change might require electoral reforms such as [proportional representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proportional_representation "Proportional representation"). "Our Benign Dictatorship" also commended [Conrad Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conrad_Black "Conrad Black")'s purchase of the [Southam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southam_Newspapers "Southam Newspapers") newspaper chain, arguing that his stewardship would provide for a "pluralistic" editorial view to counter the "monolithically liberal and [feminist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feminism "Feminism")" approach of the previous management.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-44)

Harper remained active in constitutional issues. He was a prominent opponent of the [Calgary Declaration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calgary_Declaration "Calgary Declaration") on national unity in late 1997, describing it as an "appeasement strategy" against Quebec nationalism. He called for federalist politicians to reject this strategy, and approach future constitutional talks from the position that "Quebec separatists are the problem and they need to be fixed".[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-45) In late 1999, Harper called for the federal government to establish clear rules for any future Quebec referendum on sovereignty.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-46) Some have identified Harper's views as an influence on the Chrétien government's _[Clarity Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarity\_Act "Clarity Act")_.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-47)

As president of the National Citizens Coalition (NCC) from 1998 to 2002, Harper launched an ultimately unsuccessful [legal battle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harper_v._Canada_(Attorney_General) "Harper v. Canada (Attorney General)") against federal election laws restricting third-party advertising.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-48) He led the NCC in several campaigns against the [Canadian Wheat Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Wheat_Board "Canadian Wheat Board"),[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-49) and supported Finance Minister [Paul Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Martin "Paul Martin")'s 2000 tax cuts as a positive first step toward tax reform.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-50)

In 1997, Harper delivered a controversial speech on [Canadian identity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_identity "Canadian identity") to the [Council for National Policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_for_National_Policy "Council for National Policy"), a conservative American [think tank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Think_tank "Think tank"). He made comments such as "Canada is a Northern European [welfare state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welfare_state "Welfare state") in the worst sense of the term, and very proud of it", "if you're like all Americans, you know almost nothing except for your own country. Which makes you probably knowledgeable about one more country than most Canadians", and "the [NDP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Democratic_Party_(Canada) "New Democratic Party (Canada)") [New Democratic Party] is kind of proof that the Devil lives and interferes in the affairs of men."[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-51) These statements were made public and criticized during the [2006 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Canadian_federal_election "2006 Canadian federal election"). Harper argued that the speech was intended as humour, and not as serious analysis.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-52)

Harper considered campaigning for the [Progressive Conservative Party leadership in 1998](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_Progressive_Conservative_leadership_election "1998 Progressive Conservative leadership election"), after Jean Charest left federal politics. Among those encouraging his candidacy were senior aides to Ontario [Premier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premier_of_Ontario "Premier of Ontario")[Mike Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Harris "Mike Harris"), including [Tony Clement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Clement "Tony Clement") and [Tom Long](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Long_(politician) "Tom Long (politician)").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-53) He eventually decided against running, arguing that it would "burn bridges to those Reformers with whom I worked for many years" and prevent an alliance of right-wing parties from taking shape.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-54) Harper was sceptical about the Reform Party's [United Alternative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Alternative "United Alternative") initiative in 1999, arguing that it would serve to consolidate Manning's hold on the party leadership.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-55) He also expressed concern that the UA would dilute Reform's ideological focus.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-56)

When the United Alternative created the Canadian Alliance in 2000 as a successor party to Reform, Harper predicted that [Stockwell Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockwell_Day "Stockwell Day") would defeat Preston Manning for the new party's leadership. He expressed reservations about Day's abilities, however, and accused Day of "[making] adherence to his social views a [litmus test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Litmus_test_(politics) "Litmus test (politics)") to determine whether you're in the party or not".[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-57) Harper endorsed Tom Long for the leadership, arguing that Long was best suited to take support from the Progressive Conservative Party.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-58) When Day placed first on the first ballot, Harper said that the Canadian Alliance was shifting "more towards being a party of the [religious right](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_right "Christian right")".[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-59)

After the death of Pierre Trudeau in 2000, Harper wrote an editorial criticizing Trudeau's policies as they affected Western Canada. He wrote that Trudeau "embraced the fashionable causes of his time, with variable enthusiasm and differing results", but "took a pass" on the issues that "truly defined his century".[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-60) Harper subsequently accused Trudeau of promoting "unabashed socialism", and argued that Canadian governments between 1972 and 2002 had restricted [economic growth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_growth "Economic growth") through "state corporatism".[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-61)

After the Canadian Alliance's poor showing in the [2000 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Canadian_federal_election "2000 Canadian federal election"), Harper joined with other Western conservatives in co-authoring a document called the "[Alberta Agenda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alberta_Agenda "Alberta Agenda")". The letter called on Alberta to reform publicly funded health care, replace the [Canada Pension Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_Pension_Plan "Canada Pension Plan") with a provincial plan and replace the [Royal Canadian Mounted Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Canadian_Mounted_Police "Royal Canadian Mounted Police") with a provincial police force. It became known as the "firewall letter", because it called on the provincial government to "build firewalls around Alberta" to stop the federal government from redistributing its wealth to less affluent regions.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-62) Alberta [Premier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premier_of_Alberta "Premier of Alberta")[Ralph Klein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Klein "Ralph Klein") agreed with some of the letter's recommendations, but distanced himself from the "firewall" comments.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-63)

Harper also wrote an editorial in late 2000 arguing that Alberta and the rest of Canada were "embark[ing] on divergent and potentially hostile paths to defining their country". He said that Alberta had chosen the "best of Canada's heritage—a combination of American enterprise and individualism with the British traditions of order and co-operation" while Canada "appears content to become a second-tier socialistic country... led by a second-world strongman appropriately suited for the task". He also called for a "stronger and much more autonomous Alberta", while rejecting calls for [separatism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alberta_separatism "Alberta separatism").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-64) In the [2001 Alberta provincial election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Alberta_general_election "2001 Alberta general election"), Harper led the NCC in a "Vote Anything but Liberal" campaign.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-65) Some articles from this period described him as a possible successor to Klein.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-66)

Harper and the NCC endorsed a private school [tax credit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_credit "Tax credit") proposed by Ontario's [Progressive Conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_Conservative_Party_of_Ontario "Progressive Conservative Party of Ontario") government in 2001, arguing that it would "save about $7,000 for each student who does not attend a [union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_union "Trade union")-run public school". [Education Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_Education_(Ontario) "Minister of Education (Ontario)")[Janet Ecker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Janet_Ecker "Janet Ecker") criticized this, saying that her government's intent was not to save money at the expense of public education.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-67)

Day's leadership of the Canadian Alliance became increasingly troubled throughout the summer of 2001, as several party MPs called for his resignation. In June, the _[National Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National\_Post "National Post")_ newspaper reported that former Reform MP [Ian McClelland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_McClelland "Ian McClelland") was organizing a possible leadership challenge on Harper's behalf.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-68) Harper announced his resignation from the NCC presidency in August 2001, to prepare a campaign.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-69)

## Opposition leader (2002–2006)

### Leader of the Canadian Alliance (2002–2003)

See also: [2002 Canadian Alliance leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Canadian_Alliance_leadership_election "2002 Canadian Alliance leadership election")

Stockwell Day called a new Canadian Alliance leadership race for 2002, and soon declared himself a candidate. Harper emerged as Day's main rival, and declared his own candidacy on December 3, 2001. He eventually won the support of at least 28 Alliance MPs,[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-70) including [Scott Reid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Reid_(politician) "Scott Reid (politician)"), [James Rajotte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Rajotte "James Rajotte")[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-71) and [Keith Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Martin_(politician) "Keith Martin (politician)").[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-72) During the campaign, Harper reprised his earlier warnings against an alliance with Quebec nationalists, and called for his party to become the federalist option in Quebec.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-73) He argued that "the French language is not imperilled in Quebec", and opposed "special status" for the province in the [Canadian constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Constitution "Canadian Constitution") accordingly.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-74) He also endorsed greater provincial autonomy on [Medicare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicare_(Canada) "Medicare (Canada)"), and said that he would not co-operate with the Progressive Conservatives as long as they were led by Joe Clark.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-75) On social issues, Harper argued for "parental rights" to use [corporal punishment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment "Corporal punishment") against their children and supported raising the age of sexual consent.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-76) He described his potential support base as "similar to what [George Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush") tapped".[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-77)

The tone of the leadership contest turned hostile in February 2002. Harper described Day's governance of the party as "amateurish",[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-78) while his campaign team argued that Day was attempting to win re-election by building a narrow support base among different groups in the religious right.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-79) The Day campaign accused Harper of "attacking ethnic and religious minorities".[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-80) In early March, the two candidates had an especially fractious debate on [CBC Newsworld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBC_Newsworld "CBC Newsworld").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-81) The leadership vote was held on March 20, 2002. Harper was elected on the first ballot with 55% support, against 37% for Day. Two other candidates split the remainder.

After winning the party leadership, Harper announced his intention to run for parliament in a by-election in [Calgary Southwest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calgary_Southwest "Calgary Southwest"), recently vacated by Preston Manning. [Ezra Levant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ezra_Levant "Ezra Levant") had been chosen as the riding's Alliance candidate and declared that he would not stand aside for Harper; he later reconsidered.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-82) The Liberals did not field a candidate, following a parliamentary tradition of allowing opposition leaders to enter the House of Commons unopposed. The Progressive Conservative candidate, [Jim Prentice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Prentice "Jim Prentice"), also chose to withdraw.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-83) Harper was elected without difficulty over New Democrat [Bill Phipps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Phipps "Bill Phipps"), a former [United Church of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Church_of_Canada "United Church of Canada") moderator. Harper told a reporter during the campaign that he "despise[d]" Phipps, and declined to debate him.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-84)

Harper officially became the [leader of the Official Opposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Official_Opposition_(Canada) "Leader of the Official Opposition (Canada)") in May 2002. Later in the same month, he said that the [Atlantic Provinces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Provinces "Atlantic Provinces") were trapped in "a culture of defeat" which had to be overcome, the result of policies designed by Liberal and Progressive Conservative governments. Many Atlantic politicians condemned the remark as patronizing and insensitive. The [Legislature of Nova Scotia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legislature_of_Nova_Scotia "Legislature of Nova Scotia") unanimously approved a motion condemning Harper's comments,[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-85) which were also criticized by [New Brunswick premier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premier_of_New_Brunswick "Premier of New Brunswick"), [Bernard Lord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Lord "Bernard Lord"), federal Progressive Conservative leader Joe Clark and others. Harper refused to apologize, and said that much of Canada was trapped by the same "can't-do" attitude.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-86)

In March 2003, their speeches in favour gaining no traction in Parliament, Harper and Day co-wrote a letter to _[The Wall Street Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Wall\_Street\_Journal "The Wall Street Journal")_ in which they condemned the Canadian government's unwillingness to participate in the [2003 invasion of Iraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_invasion_of_Iraq "2003 invasion of Iraq").[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-87)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-88)

As party leader, Harper sought to merge the Alliance with the Progressive Conservatives (PCs) to create a united [right-of-centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right-of-centre "Right-of-centre") party. The possibility of a united conservative party increased after [Peter Mackay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Mackay "Peter Mackay") was [elected](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_Progressive_Conservative_leadership_election "2003 Progressive Conservative leadership election") Progressive Conservative leader in May 2003. On October 16, 2003, Harper and Mackay agreed to merge the two parties to form the [Conservative Party of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada "Conservative Party of Canada"). After 95 percent of Alliance members voted in favour of merging with the PCs and 90 percent of 2,486 PC delegates voted in favour of merging with the Alliance, the Conservative Party of Canada was founded on December 7, 2003.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-89)

### Leader of the Conservative Party

See also: [2004 Conservative Party of Canada leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Conservative_Party_of_Canada_leadership_election "2004 Conservative Party of Canada leadership election")

On January 12, 2004, Harper announced his resignation as the leader of the Official Opposition in order to run for the leadership of the Conservative Party of Canada. Harper was elected the first leader of the Conservative Party, with a first ballot majority against [Belinda Stronach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belinda_Stronach "Belinda Stronach") and Tony Clement on March 20, 2004. Harper's victory included strong showings outside of Western Canada.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-cpac092613-90)[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-2004ridings-91)

#### 2004 federal election

Main article: [2004 Canadian federal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Canadian_federal_election "2004 Canadian federal election")

Harper led the Conservatives into the 2004 federal election. Initially, new prime minister Paul Martin held a large lead in polls, but this eroded because of infighting, the [sponsorship scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sponsorship_scandal "Sponsorship scandal") and other scandals surrounding his government. The Liberals attempted to counter this with an early election call, as this would give the Conservatives less time to consolidate their merger.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-nasty2004-92)[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-93)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-94)

This, along with an unpopular provincial budget by Liberal Premier [Dalton McGuinty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dalton_McGuinty "Dalton McGuinty") in Ontario, moved the Conservatives into a lead for a time.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-nasty2004-92) However, comments by Conservative MPs, leaked press releases accusing the then prime minister of supporting [child pornography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_pornography "Child pornography"), as well as [attack ads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack_ad "Attack ad") suggesting that the Conservatives had a secret agenda, caused Harper's party to lose some momentum.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-np042111-95)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-cbc062004-96)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-po030106-97)

The Liberals were re-elected to power with a minority government, with the Conservatives coming in second place. The Conservatives managed to make inroads into the Liberals' Ontario stronghold, primarily in the province's socially conservative central region. However, they were shut out of Quebec, marking the first time that a centre-right party did not win any seats in that province. Harper, after some personal deliberation, decided to stay on as the party leader.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-cbc120319-98)[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-99)

##### Agreement with the BQ and the NDP

Two months after the federal election, Harper privately met [Bloc Québécois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloc_Qu%C3%A9b%C3%A9cois "Bloc Québécois") leader [Gilles Duceppe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilles_Duceppe "Gilles Duceppe") and New Democratic Party leader [Jack Layton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Layton "Jack Layton") in a Montreal hotel.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-gazetteCo-Opposition-100) On September 9, 2004, the three signed a letter addressed to the [governor general](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_General_of_Canada "Governor General of Canada"), [Adrienne Clarkson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Clarkson "Adrienne Clarkson"), stating, "We respectfully point out that the opposition parties, who together constitute a majority in the House, have been in close consultation. We believe that, should a request for dissolution arise this should give you cause, as constitutional practice has determined, to consult the opposition leaders and consider all of your options before exercising your constitutional authority."[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-101)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-102) On the same day the letter was written, the three party leaders held a joint press conference at which they expressed their intent to co-operate on changing parliamentary rules, and to request that the governor general consult with them before deciding to call an election.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-Harpercoalition-103) At the news conference, Harper said, "It is the Parliament that's supposed to run the country, not just the largest party and the single leader of that party. That's a criticism I've had and that we've had and that most Canadians have had for a long, long time now so this is an opportunity to start to change that." At the time, Harper and the two other opposition leaders denied trying to form a [coalition government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coalition_government "Coalition government").[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-gazetteCo-Opposition-100) Harper said, "This is not a coalition, but this is a co-operative effort."[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-Harpercoalition-103)

On October 4, [Mike Duffy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Duffy "Mike Duffy"), who was later appointed as a Conservative senator by Harper, said: "It is possible that you could change prime minister without having an election." He added that some Conservatives wanted Harper to temporarily become prime minister without holding an election. The next day, Layton walked out on talks with Harper and Duceppe, accusing them of trying to replace Paul Martin with Harper as prime minister. Both Bloc and Conservative officials denied Layton's accusations.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-gazetteCo-Opposition-100) On March 26, 2011, Duceppe stated that Harper had tried to form a coalition government with the Bloc and NDP in response to Harper's allegations that the Liberals may form a coalition with the Bloc and the NDP.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-104)

#### 38th Parliament

The Conservative Party's first policy convention was held from March 17 to 19, 2005, in [Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal "Montreal"). Harper had been rumoured to be shifting his ideology closer to that of a [Blue Tory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Tory "Blue Tory"), and many thought he had wanted to move the party's policies closer to the centre. Any opposition to abortion or bilingualism was dropped from the Conservative platform. Harper received an 84% endorsement from delegates in the [leadership review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leadership_review "Leadership review").[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-105)

Despite the party abandoning debate over the two controversial issues, they began a concerted drive against same-sex marriage. Harper was criticized by a group of law professors for arguing that the government could override the provincial court rulings on same-sex marriage without using the "[notwithstanding clause](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Section_Thirty-three_of_the_Canadian_Charter_of_Rights_and_Freedoms "Section Thirty-three of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms")", a provision of the _[Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian\_Charter\_of\_Rights\_and\_Freedoms "Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms")_.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-gm011905-106) He also argued, in general, for lower taxes, an elected [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_Canada "Senate of Canada"), a tougher stance on crime, and closer relations with the United States.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-107)

Following the April 2005 release of [Jean Brault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Brault "Jean Brault")'s damaging testimony at the [Gomery Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gomery_Commission "Gomery Commission"), implicating the Liberals in the scandal, opinion polls placed the Conservatives ahead of Liberals.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-sink42505-108) The Conservatives had earlier abstained from the vote on the [2005 budget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_federal_budget,_2005 "Canadian federal budget, 2005") to avoid forcing an election.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-109) With the collapse in Liberal support and a controversial NDP amendment to the budget, the party exerted significant pressure on Harper to bring down the government.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-cbc062405-110)[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-111) In May, Harper announced that Martin's Liberals had lost the "moral authority to govern".[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-nyt051105-112) Shortly thereafter, the Conservatives and Bloc Québécois united to defeat the government on a vote that some considered to be either a [confidence motion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confidence_motion "Confidence motion") or else a motion requiring an immediate test of the confidence of the House.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-dam53005-113) The Martin government did not accept this interpretation and argued that vote had been on a procedural motion, although they also indicated that they would bring forward their revised budget for a confidence vote the following week. Ultimately, the effort to bring down the Martin government failed following the decision of Conservative MP Belinda Stronach to [cross the floor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossing_the_floor "Crossing the floor") to the Liberal Party. The vote on the NDP amendment to the budget tied, and with the [speaker of the House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaker_of_the_House_of_Commons_of_Canada "Speaker of the House of Commons of Canada") voting to continue the debate, the Liberals stayed in power. At the time, some considered the matter to be a [constitutional crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_crisis "Constitutional crisis").[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-dam53005-113)[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-Heard,_Andrew,_The_Confidence_Convention_and_the_May_2005_Vote_on_the_Public_Accounts_Committee_Report-114)[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-Bliss,_Michael-115)

Harper was also criticized for supporting his caucus colleague MP [Gurmant Grewal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gurmant_Grewal "Gurmant Grewal").[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-116) Grewal had produced tapes of conversations with [Tim Murphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Murphy_(Canadian_politician) "Tim Murphy (Canadian politician)"), Paul Martin's chief of staff, in which Grewal claimed he had been offered a cabinet position in exchange for his defection.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-cbc053105-117)

The Liberals' support dropped sharply after the first report from the Gomery Commission was issued, but rebounded soon after.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-flawless6-118) Later that month, Harper introduced a motion of no confidence on the Martin government, telling the House of Commons "that this government has lost the confidence of the House of Commons and needs to be removed". As the Liberals had lost NDP support in the house by refusing to accept an NDP plan to prevent health care privatization, the no-confidence motion was passed by a vote of 171–133. It was the first time that a Canadian government had been toppled by a straight motion of no confidence proposed by the opposition. As a result, Parliament was dissolved and a general election was scheduled for January 23, 2006.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-flawless6-118)[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-jack1255-119)[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-cbc112805-120)

On February 27, 2008, allegations surfaced that two Conservative Party officials offered terminally ill, independent MP [Chuck Cadman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Cadman#2005_Budget_vote "Chuck Cadman") a million-dollar life insurance policy in exchange for his vote to bring down the Liberal government in a May 2005, budget vote.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-121) If the story had been proved true, the actions may have been grounds for charges as a criminal offence as under the _[Criminal Code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criminal\_Code\_(Canada) "Criminal Code (Canada)")_, it is illegal to bribe an MP.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-cbc-2008-02-27-122)

When asked by Vancouver journalist Tom Zytaruk about the alleged life insurance offer then-opposition leader Stephen Harper states on an audio tape "I don't know the details. I know there were discussions"[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-investigate1-123) and goes on to say "The offer to Chuck was that it was only to replace financial considerations he might lose due to an election".[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-investigate1-123) Harper also stated that he had told the Conservative Party representatives that they were unlikely to succeed. "I told them they were wasting their time. I said Chuck had made up his mind."[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-investigate1-123)[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-articlenews1-124) In February 2008, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) investigated the allegations that Section 119's provisions on bribery and corruption in the _Criminal Code_ had been violated.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-125)[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-126) The RCMP concluded their investigation stating that there was no evidence for pressing charges.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-127)

Harper denied any wrongdoing and subsequently filed a civil [libel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libel "Libel") suit against the Liberal Party. Because libel laws do not apply to statements made in Parliament, the basis of the lawsuit was that statements made by Liberal Party members outside the House of Commons and in articles which appeared on the Liberal Party web site made accusations that Harper had committed a criminal act.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-articlenews1-124)[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-128)

The audio expert hired by Harper to prove that the tape containing the evidence was doctored reported that the latter part of the tape was recorded over, but the tape was unaltered where Harper's voice said "I don't know the details, I know that, um, there were discussions, um, but this is not for publication?" and goes on to say he "didn't know the details" when asked if he knew anything about the alleged offer to Cadman.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-cbctape-129)

#### 2006 federal election

Main article: [2006 Canadian federal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Canadian_federal_election "2006 Canadian federal election")

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/Harper%2C-Stephen-Jan-23-06.jpg/250px-Harper%2C-Stephen-Jan-23-06.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Harper,-Stephen-Jan-23-06.jpg)

Stephen Harper giving a victory speech to party members in [Calgary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calgary "Calgary") after the [Conservatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Canada "Conservative Party of Canada") won the [2006 federal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Canadian_federal_election "2006 Canadian federal election").

The Conservatives began the campaign period with a policy-per-day strategy, contrary to the Liberal plan of holding off major announcements until after the Christmas holidays, so Harper dominated media coverage for the first weeks of the election. Though his party showed only modest movement in the polls, Harper's personal numbers, which had always significantly trailed those of his party, began to rise. In response, the Liberals launched [negative ads targeting Harper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Harper_attack_ads "2006 Harper attack ads"), similar to their attacks in the 2004 election. However, their tactics were not sufficient to erode the Conservative's advantage, although they did manage to close what had been a ten-point advantage in public opinion. As Harper's personal numbers rose, polls found he was now considered not only more trustworthy, but a better choice for prime minister than Martin.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-130)

Immediately prior to the Christmas break, in a faxed letter to NDP candidate [Judy Wasylycia-Leis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judy_Wasylycia-Leis "Judy Wasylycia-Leis"), [RCMP commissioner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commissioner_of_the_RCMP "Commissioner of the RCMP")[Giuliano Zaccardelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuliano_Zaccardelli "Giuliano Zaccardelli") announced the RCMP had opened a criminal investigation into her complaint that it appeared Liberal Finance Minister [Ralph Goodale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Goodale "Ralph Goodale")'s office had leaked information leading to [insider trading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insider_trading "Insider trading") before making an important announcement on the taxation of [income trusts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Income_trust "Income trust"). On December 27, 2005, the RCMP confirmed that information in a press release. At the conclusion of the investigation, Serge Nadeau, a top civil servant in the [Department of Finance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Finance_(Canada) "Department of Finance (Canada)"), was charged with criminal breach of trust. No charges were laid against Goodale.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-131)

The election gave Harper's Conservatives the largest number of seats in the House, although not enough for a majority government, and shortly after midnight on January 24, Martin conceded defeat. Later that day, Martin informed Governor General [Michaëlle Jean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micha%C3%ABlle_Jean "Michaëlle Jean") that he would resign as prime minister, and at 6:45 p.m. Jean asked Harper to form a government. Harper was sworn in as Canada's 22nd prime minister on February 6, 2006.

In his first address to Parliament as prime minister, Harper opened by paying tribute to the [queen of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Canada "Monarchy of Canada"), [Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_II "Elizabeth II"), and her "lifelong dedication to duty and self-sacrifice".[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-132) He also said before the Canada-UK Chamber of Commerce that Canada and the United Kingdom were joined by "the golden circle of [the Crown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Crown "The Crown"), which links us all together with the majestic past that takes us back to the [Tudors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tudors "Tudors"), the Plantagenets, the [Magna Carta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magna_Carta "Magna Carta"), _[habeas corpus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habeas\_corpus "Habeas corpus")_, petition of rights, and English [common law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_law "Common law")".[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-133) Journalist Graham Fraser said in the _[Toronto Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto\_Star "Toronto Star")_ that Harper's speech was "one of the most monarchist speeches a Canadian prime minister has given since [John Diefenbaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Diefenbaker "John Diefenbaker")".[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-134) An analysis by [Michael D. Behiels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_D._Behiels "Michael D. Behiels") suggested that a political realignment might be underway, based on the continuance of Harper's government.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-135)

After the election, the Conservative party were charged with improper election spending, in a case that became known as the [In and Out scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_and_Out_scandal "In and Out scandal"). It dragged on for years, but in 2012 they took a plea deal, admitting both improper spending and falsifying records to hide it.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harper#cite_note-136)

## Prime Minister of Canada (2006–2015)

Main article: [Premiership of Stephen Harper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premiership_of_Stephen_Harper "Premiership of Stephen Harper")
